en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Exposition of the Vinaya:
An Introduction to the Book.
Having bowed my head to the Supreme One, the Buddha, who has no equal;
and to the Dhamma that brings about the end of existence, as well as to the stainless Saṅgha—
the community of monks and nuns— I am composed for the sake of their welfare.
I shall explain, in brief, the exposition of the Vinaya—
unconfused, uncluttered, with sweetly meaningful phrasing,
which brings about proficiency and is supreme in the sequence of the Vinaya.
For monks and for nuns who are crossing over to the further shore of the ocean of the Vinaya, it is a delightful boat.
Therefore, [I shall explain] the method of training and the determination of the Vinaya.
With an undistracted mind, understand what I say.
The Analysis of the Monks:
The Discourse on the Defeats.
In the discourse on the first *pārājika*: One who, with the intention of sexual intercourse, inserts even as much as a sesame seed into any part of the body other than the [proper] path,
having introduced the genitals, is defeated.
Whether it has been inserted or is being inserted, or whether it remains or is being withdrawn—
if one consents while having a student present, one falls from the training, setting aside the formal act.
Whether the private parts are covered by a cloth or not, or whether the place is covered or uncovered—
But when entering the path, likewise with what is spread out,
whether with something clung-to or not clung-to, or with that which is not clung-to;
if he should consent to being touched by that which is not clung-to, herein he is at fault.
If one has entered a *pārājika* zone, one is defeated (*parājita*) upon entering;
one should designate a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) for being within the zone, and a wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) as well.
This applies even when [the victim] is dead, or when [the body] is unrecognizable, or when it is mostly unrecognizable.
A man who engages in sexual intercourse commits a *pārājika* offense.
Even when more than half is displayed, and even when exactly half is displayed, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*;
for the remainder, the offense is *dukkaṭa*.
Even when the body has been devoured until only the sign remains,
if one engages in sexual intercourse with that sign, there is defeat (pārājika). Furthermore,
if [the corpse] has reached the stage of bloatedness or other such states, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in all cases.
"Regarding what is called 'eaten or uneaten,' this refers to all parts of a dead body.
However, having cut or sliced [the flesh], or having extracted the sign (nimitta),
if one [handles it] from that point on as a mere wound, one incurs a thullaccaya offense."
Then, for one who makes an effort toward a woman who has fallen [into sin] due to the passion for sexual intercourse because of a sign:
there is a *dukkaṭa* offense regarding a piece of flesh.
Even when there is only a piece of flesh or a tendon the size of a fingernail or the back of a finger, [the same applies].
While engaging in sexual intercourse, one is defeated (parājika) while the partner is alive.
If one inserts the genitals into the ear-cavities, nostrils, vagina, anus,
or into wounds out of lust, one incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya).
In the remaining parts of the body, such as the armpits, the thighs, and so forth,
for one who indulges in sexual desire with fat, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
[This applies to] the flesh of horses, cows, buffaloes, and others, as well as camels, donkeys, and elephants.
In the nostrils and the openings of the vagina, such conduct incurs a thullaccaya offense.
Likewise, in the eyes, ears, and wounds of all animals, as well as in the rest of the body,
for one who engages in such conduct, there is a dukkaṭa offense.
But for one who consorts with those who have died while their bodies are still moist,
there may be an offense of three kinds, provided that the three types of fields exist.
However, regarding the sign of a woman outside [the field] through lust for sexual intercourse:
For one who touches a mark [of a woman] with a mark [of his own], there shall be a *thullaccaya* offense.
Through lust for bodily contact, if he touches the mark of a woman with either a mark or a mouth,
it shall be a grave offense (*garuka*) for him.
Likewise, when there is lust for both [the male and female organs], even if it is the male's organ;
for one who touches with the organ, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
But when the organ touches the organ of a female animal;
For one who touches [a woman] with lust for sexual intercourse, there is a thullaccaya offense.
For touching the female form of an animal out of a desire for bodily contact,
touching form by form, it is considered a dukkaṭa offense.
Having inserted the penis into a mouth that has been made into a vagina,
and having placed it there in the air, for one who withdraws it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Likewise, [for inserting it] into the lower part of a woman's body on all four sides.
Having inserted it into one who has not yet reached orgasm, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the one who withdraws it.
If the lips, gums, or flesh have been torn apart, or if the hair has protruded outside,
or if he exerts himself upon the teeth, for him there would be a grave offense (thullaccaya).
Having made contact with bones on the road, whether semen has been emitted or not,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who makes an effort [to emit it].
For one who embraces a woman with lust for sexual intercourse, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
The same principle applies to seizing by the hand, touching, kissing, and so forth.
Snakes among those without feet, fish, pigeons, and also those with two feet;
lizards among those with four feet—these are the bases for an offense involving defeat (pārājika).
The mind desiring to have sexual intercourse, and the entry into the path upon the path—
these two factors are stated for the first and the last types of objects.
A *dukkaṭa* offense is described as being in the vicinity of the first [type of object] alone.
But for the remaining three [offenses], a grave offense (thullaccaya) is declared.
It should be understood as "no offense" for a monk who does not know [the rule],
as well as for one who accepts it unknowingly, and for one who is a first-time offender (*ādikammika*) even if he knows.
In the Vinaya, which is unsurpassed and supreme,
in the guidance that leads virtuous people to happiness,
he who delights in striving becomes proficient, not being attached to sensual pleasures.
But here, O Sāramati, he who delights in this meditation that reveals what is beneficial experiences the origin of existence as having its source in the Divine.
May he be protected by the protectors within the teaching that is the snare of Māra.
Thus ends the discussion on the first *pārājika* in the *Vinayavinicchaya*.
The Discussion on the Second Pārājika:
One who takes up, one who carries away, one who removes, one who disrupts,
or one who causes [the object] to move from its place— is defeated.
In this regard, there are ten types of theft involving multiple articles or five [kinds of] fats that should be understood by one who is discerning:
namely, taking with one's own hand, by command, relinquishment, and accomplishing a purpose.
"And the laying down of the burden"—this is the pentad of "by one's own hand.
Furthermore, the pentad beginning with "prior preparation" consists of:
prior preparation, joint effort, making an agreement, signaling, and giving a sign.
Theft by means of deception, theft by means of a trick, theft by concealment, and [theft] involving weapons and so forth—
these five types of taking what is not given should be understood by the wise.
Furthermore, these five are distinguished by way of the object, the time, the place, and the manner of consumption.
Having understood these points, a wise person should make a legal determination:
for one who goes with a thieving mind seeking either a second hoe or a basket,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the preliminary effort.
Furthermore, for one who cuts wood or a creeper grown there,
a *dukkaṭa* offense is stated in both cases due to the simultaneous application [of the act].
Also for one who digs the earth or heaps up soil;
If one touches the pot while it is still on the fire, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Having inserted a rope through the mouth [of the pot] and tied it to a stake,
the wise person should understand that the classification of the location depends upon the nature of the binding.
Furthermore, there are two instances involving a post and a jar tied to it:
either when a ring has been inserted at the base of a tree after the jar was fixed there,
or when one is pulling out the post or cutting the chain.
If he causes the pot to fall from its place, it is a thullaccaya offense once it has fallen.
However, if he first lifts the pot, and likewise again causes a stump or even a chain to fall from its place, the same principle applies.
Rubbing it back and forth, he causes it to touch the base and protects it;
while making a ring there that has gone into the air, he is defeated.
If he cuts down a tree that has grown, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense at the top of the jar.
For one who cuts [wood] nearby, there is a *pācittiya* offense arising from that very act.
However, if he causes an object inside a pot to move,
or if he removes it right there, for him there would be a *thullaccaya*.
While stealing goods from a jar, he cuts his own fist;
or having placed it inside the vessel, the monk becomes one who has committed a defeat (parājika).
Or again, a necklace or a string of beads upon a thread inside a jar—
If one shakes it according to its substance and moves it from its place, then having fallen [from the original spot],
there is defeat as soon as one has drunk even a single dose— any amount whatsoever— of ghee or other liquids,
for the purpose of filling the mouth, by means of a single action.
Having indeed laid down the burden, even if he drinks from it again and again,
and even if he drinks the entire contents of that jar, there is no defeat.
If he throws anything whatsoever— be it a vessel or oil— into the oil jar;
He certainly drinks that oil worth a foot’s weight as long as it remains in his hand;
yet, with a thieving mind, he perishes even at the mere moment it leaves his grasp—
or likewise, if he causes the oil to be poured out by shaking the jar.
Having perceived that the oil had been poured into an empty jar,
he drank that oil and, while lifting the vessel, was scalded. Likewise,
as he broke it right there and likewise discarded the oil, [he suffered the same fate].
For one who intends to burn it, or for one who performs [the act], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
This concludes the discussion on what is situated on the ground. Regarding garments that have been laid out or spread, such as shawls, bedspreads, and so forth;
For one who pulls it out after having wrapped it around, there is defeat (pārājika) once it is released from its place.
Or, when the space touched by the near side is [reached] from the far side,
there is defeat for one who drags it across, even if it is straight.
The Commentary on the Grounds:
The snout at the front, the tip of the tail at the back,
extending to both sides, and likewise the nails of the feet below.
Furthermore, as the peacock moves through the sky up to the tip of its crest,
six distinct parts are to be discerned by one who is observant.
A bhikkhu, thinking, "I shall catch the peacock while it still has its owner," pursued it as it flew into the air.
He extends his hand, or he stands before him.
Even a peacock spreads its wings in the sky, yet it does not move;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for cutting off its movement, as well as for touching it.
If, while intending to release the peacock from its place, one causes it to quiver,
then for that act of causing it to quiver, a *thullaccaya* offense is declared.
Whether not having taken hold of it or having taken hold of it with one's own hand—
If he causes a peacock to move from its place, he himself would be fallen from his own place.
If a monk [should touch] the area reached by the tip of the beak, or else by the tip of the tail-feather; or if the tail-feather-tip has been touched by the tip of the beak.
Whoever should overstep the peacock is said to displace it from its place;
this same principle is illustrated regarding the feet, the crest, and the wings.
Furthermore, as the peacock moves through the sky, it alights upon the sun.
Moving it with his own hand, he is said to "make it quiver.
If he catches that peacock with his other hand,
then because it has been moved from its place, the monk would have fallen from his state.
But as for the other [the peacock], if it brings its own tail-feather near,
there is no fault therein, for having flown up, it settles down of its own accord. Yet,
seeing that feather settled upon its limb, if one departs with a thieving mind, [there is an offense].
When it reaches the foot, there is a *thullaccaya* offense; at the second [step], there is a *parājika*.
For one standing on the ground, the wise man should explain three points:
by way of the feet and by way of the bundle.
Then, even if it is no more than a hair’s breadth,
for a bhikkhu who uproots a peacock feather from the earth, there is a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, if gold or other such items, while being cut, should fall into his bowl...
For one who lifts it with the hand, there may be a *pārājika* offense.
If, without having lifted it, he departs with a thieving mind,
he should be declared a *pārājika* at the second step.
And this same method is to be understood for [the elements] in the hand, the cloth, and the head;
that respective place of his, wherever it may be established.
The Discourse on the Space-Dweller.
If, with a thieving mind, one touches anything— whether raw meat or something that is not to be touched—
that stands upon a bed, a chair, or the like, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If the robe has been gathered and placed upon a bamboo rack, [the same applies].
Having again made the measurement from this side, and likewise from the other side and the inside,
the area touched by the robe is declared to be its "place";
however, that entire [area] is not considered to be the "robe-pole" (cīvaravaṃsa).
Whether the space is touched by one edge and the other by the other,
or touched by the other and again by the near edge;
or whether it is touched by the southern edge and the northern edge by the other.
When the spot touched by the left hand moves beyond [the boundary], there is death (defeat).
Or, for one lifting the robe upward from the bamboo pole,
when it has been lifted even the breadth of a hair-tip, there is a *pārājika* offense for him.
If a robe has been tied with a cord and set aside, there is a thullaccaya offense for loosening it;
once it is released, one incurs a pārājika offense.
For a monk who is untying [a robe] that was wrapped around and placed upon a bamboo pole:
This same principle applies to one who is cutting a bracelet or releasing it.
For when a robe has been spread out and hung on a bamboo rack,
the determination [of its status] is the same as when the robe has been gathered up and set aside.
Whatever goods have been hung up after being placed in a carrying-net,
one who takes them out from the net, or drops them together with the net;
or [goods] such as spears and the like, which are standing in a row upon the elephant-tusks.
Whether by the tip or the base, for one who seizes and drags it away,
there is a *pārājika* offense when he causes it to pass beyond the point of contact;
for one lifting it straight up, there is defeat (*parājaya*) when the hair-tip [of the organ] has passed.
If, however, while standing facing the wall, he pulls it back,
he falls from the moment the space touched by the near side reaches the limit of the other side.
The same applies to a monk who pushes it from the opposite side.
This same principle applies even when [the fruit] is placed leaning against a wall.
When a palm tree is being shaken, the fruit reaches its destination;
for when it is released from its attachment, the offense of *pārājika* occurs with respect to that [destination].
If one were to cut the cluster of a palm tree and it were an offense of defeat (pārājika),
this same principle would apply to the flowers and fruits of all other trees as well.
Discussion on those situated in the air.
For one who goes toward the location of the treasure, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every step taken;
likewise when in deep water, or when submerging oneself and so forth.
Regarding the flowers that grow there, it is by whichever flower [the vessel] becomes full.
If one cuts the flower from its base, declare that for him there is a *pārājika* offense.
But on the side of a single-stalked lotus of the *vāka* or *utpala* species, it is not severed until [the stalk] is cut;
as long as it is not cut, it protects it.
Even in the case of flowers that have been cut and set aside by the owner themselves,
the legal decision (vinicchaya) should be understood according to the method previously stated.
Regarding flowers carried as a burden, [the offense] occurs in six ways by anyone.
If, by way of its form, one causes those [flowers] to fall from their place, they are lost.
However, if one moves a cluster of flowers placed on the surface of the water and causes them to fall from their position in the water, they are considered "fallen."
If one contemplates, "I shall take it here," and guards it,
yet while lifting it from its place, it is lost— this is called "lost.
For that which has risen up, its entire place is [considered] burnt, and its whole substance is burnt.
But for one who pulls out the flower from there and draws it straight up:
if it is released as soon as the tip of the stalk touches water, it is a *pārājika*;
if it is not released while touching that water, a *thullaccaya* is declared.
If, having taken and arranged flowers, one then plucks them, the water does not remain in its place; it is lost at the very moment of being plucked.
For whoever takes fish belonging to another with a thieving mind—
Whether by means of a net, a trap, a hand,
or a basket— while he is thus catching it,
as soon as that fish which filled [the vessel] is pulled out, his defeat occurs.
For water is the sole and entire habitat of aquatic creatures;
one who releases them from their watery dwelling becomes defeated by reason of the water.
If a fish, having leaped from the water, falls upon the bank—
But for one who takes it, that offense is to be designated according to the value of the goods.
Having placed fish-poison in a pond or even in a river—
a place where fish dwell in low-lying areas— for the purpose of killing them, and having then departed;
If fish, having eaten fish-poison, float to the surface afterwards,
there is an offense of defeat (pārājika) for one who takes them with a thieving mind once the fish are dead.
There is no fault whatsoever for one who takes them with the perception that they are refuse-rags (paṃsukūla).
When owners are taking away [their property], it is declared that the value of the goods must be paid as restitution.
If the owners, having taken the fish, depart without leaving anything behind,
then for one who takes the remainder with the intent to steal, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Those who know the Vinaya say there is no offense in this case;
and this same principle applies to the remaining forbidden foods, such as tortoises and the like.
Discussion on Water-Attached [Food].
Thinking, “I will steal and take goods from a boat or what is on board a boat,” the offense for the lifting of the foot is stated for a bhikkhu proceeding in this manner.
For when a boat is moored in a violent current;
A single place is considered a bond;
for a bhikkhu, at the mere moment of being released from it,
the wise declare that he has committed a pārājika offense.
A boat moored in shallow water remains fixed—
whether being pulled from the front, from behind, or from the side;
it is touched on one side, while the other side is free.
If he causes the boat to go beyond [the limit], it shall be a *pārājika* offense for him.
Likewise:
"Even if [the boat] is released from the water by as much as the length of a hair... (121)
That which is below the waterline and that which is touched by the rim of the mouth;
furthermore, having been tied and placed on the shore where the water is still—that is considered its twofold state: the state of being bound and the place where it stands.
If there was a grave offense (thullaccaya) prior to the release from bondage,
and afterwards, by some means, one causes [the person] to fall from their position— if they have fallen—
then having first caused them to fall from their position, there is an offense of release from bondage afterwards.
And this same method is stated for a monk with a thieving mind regarding [a boat] that has been hauled up and turned upside down on dry land;
for in the case of a boat, the rim of its mouth is indeed the "place" [the measure of the offense].
The object of knowledge is the delimitation of the place;
by means of the five aspects alone;
even while causing it to move from anywhere whatsoever.
That man becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense.
This same principle should be understood to apply when a boat is tilted,
or when a boat is stationary, or likewise when [the water] is above the buckets.
If, however, having boarded a boat standing at a ferry-crossing,
one causes it to move by means of a paddle or even a pole, there is a defeat (parājika). If,
having spread out a sunshade and raised up a robe, [one causes it to move]...
Having fashioned it like a sail, one causes the wind to seize it.
But if a powerful wind comes and carries away the ship,
there is no fault whatsoever in the ship being carried off by that very wind.
If one goes to a village crossing and,
without causing anyone to move from their place, buys something and runs away,
there is no offense of theft for the bhikkhu; it is declared that the goods must be paid for.
And if he causes her, who is walking by herself, to fall from her place, she is expelled (*cuto*).
This is not a commentary on the eight [offenses].
A vehicle (*yāna*) means a chariot (*ratha*), a cart (*vayha*), a wagon (*sakaṭa*), or a carriage (*sandamānikā*).
"I shall steal the vehicle," or "for the sake of the vehicle"—if one goes with such intent, a *dukkaṭa* offense is declared; for one who searches for a second [vehicle], there is a *dukkaṭa*;
when there is the effort to move it from its place, if it is found [there], there is a defeat (*parājika*).
One should point out ten instances regarding a carriage yoked with two [oxen]:
for one who drives the carriage while sitting on the pole, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya) when the oxen lift their feet. One should designate this as such.
For wheels, ruin occurs once they have passed beyond their place of stability.
Even for a cart that is improperly yoked, when it stands with its axle supported by a prop,
there are only three positions for its wheels due to the influence of those supporting props.
Likewise, if one moves by the front edge a piece of wood that has been placed on top,
or likewise a piece of wood placed on the ground by its front edge;
or if one causes it to move from its place either forward or backward—
But for all three, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya); however, if one causes them to fall from their position, it is a defeat (pārājika).
Having removed the wheels, one should designate two positions: [one] upon the axle-tops and [the other] upon the wooden parts above.
Dragging it or lifting it up, one who has fallen into a heap of touched space;
or another thing placed upon the ground, whatever it may be—
these five locations for the leader of those not yet purified are thus illuminated.
Or, having grasped it by the spokes, if he moves it from its place, it has fallen.
For a wheel set upon the ground with its hub,
there would be only one location, yet the delimitation is fivefold.
Having touched the ground where it stands, by the rim and the hub—these two positions belong to the wheel; when these are surpassed, it is lost.
Seeing the vehicle unguarded as it proceeds upon the great highway;
Having mounted [a vehicle] without being urged, or having hired it, one may go; this is permitted.
This concludes the Discussion on Vehicles. The burden is fourfold: carried on the head, on the shoulders, suspended from the neck, or as a load.
In that regard, for one who merely touches a burden placed upon the head, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
But for one who, with a mind of theft,
rubs it here and there and causes it to shift even slightly upon the head, there would be a grave offense (thullaccaya).
When the burden has been laid down, it is considered a *pārājika* offense for him;
even one who removes as much as a single hair from the head is defeated.
Having placed whatever burden there was upon the earth, with a mind purified, [he is released].
If he subsequently extracts it with a thieving mind, he is defeated.
522. Here, according to the method already stated, the legal determination regarding the remaining items should be understood in their entirety by one possessing wisdom.
The Commentary on the Burden:
The Sage has declared it an offense of wrong-doing for one who attacks a monastery;
if one who practices defeats another in the Dhamma, he is defeated. 522
For one who gives rise to doubt, there would be a *thullaccaya* offense;
likewise for one who himself violates the Dhamma while practicing it for that person.
When the owner has laid down the burden, having renounced it with the thought, "I will not give [it],"...
It would be a pārājika offense for all those who give false testimony.
This concludes the discussion on the monastery. To seize and take away anything belonging to the Saṅgha from a monastery—
It is not accomplished simply because there is no laying down of the burden for all [beings].
This concludes the commentary on the dwelling.
When one seizes the heads of rice and other crops after having bound them together:
Whether by pulling it out with the mouth, or by cutting it with the hand,
or even if the seed or the base is filled into the fist at the head—
when that [organ] is released from its bond, there is a *pārājika* offense for him.
But even if the stalk is cut—whether it be a mere fragment of bark or a long length of rice straw—as long as it has not been removed, it continues to protect.
If one imagines thus: "Having crushed this, I..."
"Having shaken off [the impurities], I shall take the essence from here"—thinking thus, he guards it.
There is no fault in crushing or extracting, nor even in shaking it off, provided he is making it his own by placing it into his own vessel; for him, there is defeat (parājika).
If, knowing that even as much as a hair’s breadth of earth belongs to another,
one moves it with a thieving mind, there is defeat— provided, however, that the owners have abandoned their responsibility for it.
This ground is indeed priceless; therefore it is declared thus:
if [the object] is to be taken, yet it is secured by two stakes, there is a thullaccaya offense regarding the first, and only at the second is there a pārājika offense.
If a bhikkhu, desiring to make it known, spreads out a rope or lets fall a staff,
thinking, "This is my property," he commits a dukkaṭa offense for each of the two modes of action by which it would become his own.
In the first case among them, there is a serious offense (thullaccaya); in the second, there is a defeat (parājika).
This concludes the Discussion on Fields. The determination of the site (vatthu) is exactly according to the method stated for the field (khettavatthu).
And what should be said regarding the meaning of "village" (*gāma*) is nothing new at all.
This concludes the commentary on the meaning of "village" as a physical site.
Whether it be grass, or leaf, or creeper, or even wood;
It should be treated like the theft of goods: one who takes [wood] is liable for what grows there.
However, in the case of a tree of great value, even when merely cut down, it is lost;
if the tree has been felled and left standing, no one at all may take it.
However, if a tree that has been cut at its base and left half-way up is taken with the thought,
"It has been abandoned by the owners," it is permissible to take it.
There is no fault whatsoever for one who takes [wood] that possesses the characteristics and is covered with bark.
For one who takes what has been inhabited, or even what has been prepared, or what is being destroyed; or for one who,
having reached a place of watchfulness, performed such tasks as meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) and so forth,
or was thinking of something else in his mind— it is indeed a "debt for goods" (bhaṇḍadeyya) for him.
If one who desires to be freed from calamities such as boars, tigers, leopards,
and jackals likewise passes beyond that very place;
There is no fault, however, in the case of "goods-to-be-redeemed" (bhaṇḍadeyyaka).
This is a place of guarding; it is more serious than a customs post.
Therefore, a dukkaṭa offense is prescribed for one who goes there by concealing [the goods].
For one who avoids this with a thieving mind,
even as he travels through the air, the Teacher has declared a *pārājika* offense.
Therefore, in this matter specifically, with a mind endowed with mindfulness—
A monk who is diligent and of lovely virtue should act thus.
The Discourse on the Forest-Dweller.
In a time when water is scarce, water kept in a vessel—
Having pulled it out and inserted it, or likewise having made a hole;
or when taking a vessel from a pond or a tank, having inserted it for oneself— [in these cases], one should be designated [an offense] according to the value of the goods.
But for one who cuts [the boundary] from the side of taking what is not given,
even together with a group of living beings, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is declared.
Whether standing inside or standing outside, while cutting, it is so in both cases.
It should be made with the outer edge [on the outside] and the inner edge [on the inside], starting from the middle.
This concludes the discussion on water. By turn, the novices [should fetch] tooth-sticks from the forest.
If, however, they bring [the robes] even for the teachers,
as long as they do not offer them to the Saṅgha after cutting [the cloth],
all that which has been brought remains the property of those [teachers] alone.
Therefore, for a monk who takes with a thieving mind an article of value belonging to the Saṅgha,
his downfall occurs according to the value of the article.
From the moment it is handed over by those [donors], it then belongs to the Saṅgha.
Even for one who takes it by theft, there is no offense of taking what is not given.
This is because of the lack of a protector, because it is not to be distributed according to seniority, and because it is common to all;
therefore, this is not like anything else.
The Discourse on the Tooth-stick:
One gives fire or uses a blade; one chews it all around;
or one chews "poison," namely that which is called the frog-thorn.
Whether by this or that means, the tree perishes and is consumed by fire;
in every such case, it is declared that the monk must pay for the damage.
Discussion on Trees.
Whether from the head, the ear, the neck, or even the hand—
whether by cutting off or by releasing [the victim]— for one who takes [the property] with a thieving mind,
there is defeat (parājika) at the very moment it is released from the head or other such parts.
For one committing a thullaccaya offense, there is the pulling back and forth;
without even withdrawing the hands, while rubbing the bracelets or the anklets,
he moves them here and there while stroking the upper arms.
If a thief takes that which has gone into the open air, even if he guards it,
it does not remain there, like a bracelet on a conscious arm.
But as for one who steals the garment already worn by another—
But even another person, out of shame, does not release it hastily.
Even a thief drags it away, yet that other person protects it for a while;
only when the cloth has been released from the other's hand is there defeat.
For one who is carrying away goods along with their container, there is a *thullaccaya* offense at the first step;
once he has stepped beyond [the boundary], he becomes fallen [from the training] at the second step.
If, with a thieving intention, he causes the goods to be dropped after having threatened [the owner], [he incurs the same penalty].
When an object has passed from another's hand, defeat occurs at the mere moment of release. Furthermore,
if one causes it to be dropped after having planned it, for that act of causing it to be dropped, a dukkaṭa offense is stated, as is the case even in the act of making [the other] sit down.
If one shakes an object back to its place, or moves it from that spot, there is no fault even if it falls.
Likewise, for one who says "Stay! Stay! while it is being discarded, there is no fault.
However, if someone comes with a thieving intent and later takes it, it would constitute theft.
It is a *pārājika* offense upon the removal [of the object] when the owner has departed with attachment;
however, one is protected from the offense if taking it while perceiving it as one's own, or if taking it while perceiving it as a refuse rag (*paṃsukūla*).
Likewise, there is the offense of "goods to be paid" (*bhaṇḍadeyya*) for one who takes it while perceiving it as a refuse rag.
Even when told, “Stop! Stop! he abandons his goods;
having laid down his burden, the thief flees in fear.
For one who takes with a thieving mind, there is again an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each step taken away.
"When one causes [an item] to be brought that is to be given, there is defeat for one who does not give it.
"Why? Because it was discarded through his effort"—this is stated respectfully in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, though it has not appeared in other [commentaries].
The Story of the Taking. When one speaks a deliberate lie,
saying "I do not take," because of a previous act of taking what was not given, it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense for the bhikkhu.
“However, what will he show me that was placed by me in secret?”—
if such doubt arises, there would be a *thullaccaya* offense for him.
If, while that giving is effortless, another person should deposit the burden;
When both have abandoned their burden, the monk is defeated.
Even if he intends in his mind not to take it back, yet says with his mouth,
"I will give it," when he thus abandons his burden while speaking, there is indeed defeat for the owner.
The Discourse on Deposits:
If one stands inside the customs house and throws [the goods] outside,
or if they certainly fall from the hand, there is defeat at the very moment of release.
If it strikes a tree or a stump and then falls back, or if, though tossed by the wind,
it falls inside [the enclosure], it protects [the goods]. However, if the goods fall upon the ground and subsequently roll away, [they are no longer protected].
If it enters even slightly inside, there would be a *pārājika* offense for him.
If it moves after having repeatedly stopped, and has entered, there is defeat;
however, if it has moved without stopping, he is protected [from the offense].
Thus it has been stated firmly in the Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā and other commentaries;
that should be accepted as the essential meaning, for it appears to be logical.
Whether one winds it oneself or causes another to wind it, [it is the same].
If it rolls while not being stood upon, it would not be one that has been carried.
If, having been stood upon repeatedly inside, it goes outside, it protects [the precept].
When it is placed down with a pure mind, it is valid; it is indeed valid.
If, however, while the vehicle or the elephant is moving, he places it [the bowl] down for the purpose of taking it outside,
there is no offense even when it has been taken out. Or,
if it is placed down while the vehicle is stationary, and it moves away without further effort on his part;
Even if there is a mind of theft, no taking away occurs.
If he drives that vehicle, having set aside the gem from the carriage,
he may incur a Pārājika offense upon crossing the boundary.
If one dies at a customs station, it is permissible to give the duty and then proceed.
The rest of the discussion here is similar to that in the *Araññatthakathā*.
The Discussion on Customs Duties.
One who steals a slave— whether born in the house, purchased with wealth, given by someone,
or brought in as a captive— is defeated. Likewise,
one who steals a human being, even a free person or one’s own mother, is defeated.
Even if it has been placed by the father [the owner], there is no forfeiture.
One who merely wishes to scare it away, or having lifted it with his arms,
moves it even slightly from its standing place— this constitutes defeat.
For one who, having threatened a slave, leads him away by footstep after footstep,
there are stated offenses beginning with a *thullaccaya*.
Even for one who drags him along by seizing him by the hand or other limbs, there is defeat (*parājika*).
This same principle applies even to one who says, “Go! Go away!
Flee! To one who is fleeing in haste while he himself says, “Flee,” there is no offense of defeat (pārājika) for the monk.
But if he speaks while walking slowly, yet walks quickly according to his words, there is defeat for him. If,
having fled, he goes to another village or even a market town;
If, having seen that [snake] has gone away, he then drives it off, there is defeat.
Discussion on Living Beings.
If he touches a snake-basket by way of theft, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
One who moves [the snake] according to its location is defeated when it has fallen from its place.
However, for one who removes a snake after opening its basket,
there is defeat only when the tail has been released from the bottom of the basket.
If, while dragging a snake after having struck it, one pulls it by the tail with the mouth [of the basket],
there is defeat (pārājika) at the very moment the snake-basket is released.
If, having opened the basket, one calls out the name [of the snake];
If a snake emerges [from its hole], there would be a *pārājika* offense for him.
Likewise, even if he merely makes a sound like that of frogs or mice,
or calls out by name to someone who has emerged, there is defeat (*parājaya*).
If one does not open the mouth and acts in this very same way,
and a snake enters by whatever means, there would be a *pārājika* offense.
If the mouth is opened, the snake flees of its own accord.
If he does not call [the owner] forth, it is declared that the goods must be restored.
This concludes the Discourse on Footless Beings. Whoever, with a thieving mind, takes an elephant, a carriage, a seat, or the like;
For him, there are three kinds of offenses, beginning with *dukkaṭa*.
Whether he stands in the hall, inside the building, on the courtyard,
or even in the open space— the hall, the building, and the entire courtyard may constitute the location.
For one who is unbound, for one who is bound, and for the place where he stands—the binding;
therefore, a wise man should have an elephant brought under their control.
But as for an elephant standing outside the city:
A place where an elephant stands is considered a "place"; one should determine this by the length of its footprint.
If, when an elephant is lying down, someone causes it to stand up from that position, then at the very moment it has stood up, there is a *pārājika* offense for that person.
This same method should be understood for horses, buffaloes, and so forth;
there is nothing at all further to be said regarding those with two feet or many feet.
The Discourse on Four-Footed Animals.
If one, having recognized it as belonging to others, moves from its place the wealth of others with a heavy intent to steal, one falls [from the training].
There is no offense for one who perceives it as his own, or in the case of property belonging to animals.
Regarding the taking of items on temporary trust and the possession of property belonging to the departed,
whatever further explanation is to be given here— namely,
the analysis independent of the canonical text— we shall state that in the section on miscellaneous matters from another source.
The second offense of defeat (pārājika) spoken by the Victor, which was declared by the One Free from All Impurities,
has been stated by me in brief as the fourth.
For who indeed is capable of speaking [on this] in its entirety?
Thus ends the discussion on the second *pārājika* in the Vinaya-vinicchaya.
The discussion on the third *pārājika*.
One who, knowing a person’s human birth, should deprive them of life,
or should lay a weapon against them, or speak of the virtues of death,
or teach the means for dying— even such a person is defeated.
That [kamma] should be known as "unintentional," like a rock split in two.
Six modes of application for the taking of life have been taught by the Great Sage:
that which is performed with one's own hand, as well as commanding, relinquishing, fixed, and so forth.
In that regard, when one kills another by means of one's own body or something connected to the body, this is considered "killing with one's own hand" (*sāhatthika*).
And [when one says to a monk]: "Having struck him thus, kill him."
"Causing another to take [something] is the method involving an instruction.
For one wishing to kill at a distance, the discharge of an arrow or similar weapon while bound to the body is the procedure involving relinquishment."
The employment of means such as pits and the like for the purpose of killing another by way of non-moving [mechanisms] is this "static" (thāvara) application.
Furthermore, the chanting of a spell (*vijjā*) by one desiring to kill another [is also included].
This is called "consisting of knowledge" (vijjāmaya); it is considered the fifth application.

And that supernormal power (iddhi) born of the ripening of karma (kammavipākaja), which is capable of causing death—this is proclaimed as the application "consisting of supernormal power" (iddhimaya).
Each one of these is twofold therein, as it is explained:
there is the "specified" (uddesa) and the "unspecified" (anuddesa); this, moreover, is their distinction.
Furthermore, even when many [people] are present, if one deals a blow directed toward a specific individual...
And by that very death, one is bound by that specific action.
Even if a blow is struck against any living being without aiming at them,
if death results from that blow, it is a defeat for the striker.
Whether one kills at the very moment of striking or afterwards, in either case,
the killer is bound by that karma at the moment of the mere striking.
Thus should the "by one's own hand" [killing] be understood, as well as the "by command."
To this extent, in brief, two applications have been shown.
The object, the time, the place, the teacher, and the posture—
these six are the determinants of the specific nature of the act of commanding.
For whoever is to be killed therein is called the "basis" (vatthu);
the time may be forenoon and so forth, as well as the youthfulness and so forth of living beings.
The place is to be understood as a village and so forth; the weapon is that which kills those beings.
For a being who is to be killed, there are various modes of action,
such as the postures of sitting and so forth, as well as piercing, breaking, cutting,
or striking; indeed, there are many such distinctions in the means of killing.
If one who was commanded, "Kill that person," kills someone else instead;
or if, having been told, "Kill [him] after striking from the front," he strikes and kills [the victim] from behind or even while looking back; [in such cases, there is no offense].
The formal authorization regarding the object is not subject to a change of convention, yet the one who was the original instigator is released.
If the person is killed without deviating from that object and in accordance with the authorization,
the bond of kamma for both parties is declared according to the time [of their respective actions].
Furthermore, if one who has been commanded, "Kill him this very morning," should kill him in the evening,
the original perpetrator (mūlaṭṭha) is released from the offense;
he is said to be [only] as one who gave the command.
Bound by his own karma, as the Great Seer has declared,
he suffers the fault of missing the appointment with Death due to his lack of discernment.
When it is not specified as "Kill today at dawn" or "Tomorrow at dawn," since the time is not fixed as dawn,
there is no breach of the agreement regarding the killing.
By this very method, [the same applies] in all cases of differences in time.
The convention and the non-convention must be understood by one who is discerning.
If it is said, "Kill this enemy standing in this village," and he kills him wherever that person happens to be standing, [the offense applies].
There is no ambiguity for him: both are bound by their karma.
Whether it is commanded as "in the village alone," or with the restriction "or in the forest";
or whether it is stated as "only in the forest," yet he kills him in the village.
The conventional designation must be understood, and the meaning of the root is thereby released.
By this very method, through the analysis of all terms,
both the conventional and the non-conventional should be known by the wise.
"Or 'Kill him with a weapon,' even if commanded by someone"—
if one kills with any kind of weapon other than the specific one intended, there is no breach of the agreement.
If it was said, "Kill him with this axe," but he is killed with another axe, [there is no offense].
“If you kill this Āsīsa by means of the [other] stream,”—
if, having been addressed thus, one kills the enemy by means of the other stream,
or even with a sprout or the beak, then, because he was killed outside of the agreement, there is no offense.
By this very method, in all types of weaponry,
both the conventional designation (*saṅketa*) and the non-designation (*visaṅketa*) should be understood in their specific distinctions.
When addressed by another, "Kill him as he goes," he—
If he kills him while he is sitting, there is no discrepancy.
Whether it is said, "Kill him while he is sitting," or "Kill him while he is walking," it kills him as he walks or as he sits, respectively.
"A monk who knows the Vinaya should understand that this is a non-agreement;
and this same principle should be known to apply to all postures.
For he was commanded by another after being pierced with the words, 'Kill him!'"
Having pierced [the victim], he kills him; there is no breach of convention.
For he was commanded by another, "Kill! and having pierced him, he kills;
even if he kills after cutting [the victim's limbs], that remains a breach of convention.
By this very method, the analysis should be understood for all grammatical cases, as well as for the nominative and non-nominative (saṅketa and visaṅketa).
Long, short, thin, thick, black, or even white—
If one is commanded by someone, "Kill him," without specifying who,
and that person kills anyone whatsoever as commanded,
there is no discrepancy in the matter; both are defeated.
If one digs a trench with reference to any human being,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the one digging the pit.
If suffering arises therein, there would be a grave offense (thullaccaya) for him.
If he falls and that person dies, there is a *pārājika* offense for him.
But if he falls and another person dies, no fault exists—
provided, however, that the wound was not aimed at that specific individual.
"For whoever falls here, let them die"— if as many as there are who die after falling, that many faults would belong to him.
Regarding the matter of an immediate offense (*ānantariya*), one should speak of an immediate offense.
Likewise, from [the offenses of] *thullaccaya* and so forth, there arise *thullaccaya* and so forth.
If a pregnant woman, having fallen [into an offense], should die while still with child, there are two acts of taking life;
however, for each single destruction [of life], there is only one [offense].
If one pursues thieves here, and [the victim] falls and dies,
it is said that there is a *pārājika* offense for the one who dug the pit, just as for the digger of the pit itself.
If, having caused an enemy to fall there, the enemies then kill him, [the offense is incurred].
If they kill him there where he has fallen, or if, having carried him outside, they kill him there;
for if he has been reborn in a pit, and being a *opapātika* (spontaneously born being), he dies there;
and if they are unable to get him out—every such case results in defeat.
However, when digging for the sake of yakkhas and others, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) if suffering arises;
if death occurs, it is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) and so forth, depending on the circumstances.
But when digging a pit specifically for a human being, [the penalty is more severe].
There is no offense if [the animals] fall down, even if they are spirits (*yakkha*) or others who have died.
Likewise, when spirits and the like, having been struck by a monk with intent toward living beings,
fall down and die— this same principle applies even in the case of human beings.
“If living beings are caught here, let them die”— without specifying any particular ones—
whosoever sets a snare there, if living beings are caught,
then as soon as they are released from his hand, it shall be a *pārājika* offense for him.
Regarding the cases of immediate retribution (ānantariya) and the nature of immediate retribution itself:
when a snare has been set for a specific purpose, there is no offense in binding others who happen to be caught therein. This is what has been declared.
Whether given for a price or even for nothing, when a snare is set for another, the one who provided the means alone incurs the bond of the deed; this is the established rule.
If the one by whom it was obtained should release it, or if the snare should break loose, [the responsibility remains with the instigator].
In this way, one even makes it firm; thus, there is a bond of karma for both.
If one, having caused the snare to be swallowed, goes away out of fear of evil, another person, seeing that, will indeed set it up there once again.
If those bound repeatedly die, yet the one who set the trap is not released,
then except for the place where it was caught, the animal escapes from the snare.
Even if one guards it, there is no release from a snare that has been self-made.
But if another person takes it up again and restores it,
then among those who die because of that [damage], the original owner is not released from liability; however,
he is released by either completely destroying it or burning it.
Whether one is impaling with a stake or preparing a ploughshare,
the legal determination is the same as for a pitfall or a snare.
There is no offense for a monk who acts unintentionally or unknowingly.
Likewise, even for one whose mind is set on death at the moment of dying, or for one who has become insane after death, there is the perception of a living being in a human life-form,
provided that his mind was intent upon taking life.
The effort and the destruction of that [life] by means of it;
these are the five factors here in the killing of a human being.
Thus ends the discussion on the third *pārājika* in the Vinaya-vinicchaya.
The Discussion of the Fourth Pārājika:
That which consists merely of what is non-existent,
and that which exists by being fixed upon existence.
And one should employ the designation of "other" without overweening pride,
applying it to the distinctions of jhāna and so forth,
whether by way of body or speech, for that purpose.
Just as a palm tree at its crown is incapable of growth once it has been cut off, so too one who has made a declaration within the range of hearing is incapable [of re-entering the order].
He who, immediately after [attaining] jhāna and so forth,
proclaims to another what he himself does not possess—
if he knows it, he has fallen away; if he does not know it, he is a liar.
If he knows [this], it is a thullaccaya for him.
And if it is proclaimed: "The bhikkhu who dwells here in your monastery is an attainer of jhāna."
If he knows it is a *thullaccaya*, it is so;
if he does not know it, it is indeed a *dukkaṭa*. This is the nature of one who possesses a quality that is actually non-existent within himself.
For one who speaks having made the thought "it exists," it is due to overweening pride;
however, this method of non-offense is stated for one who does not wish to speak and is thus the first [of the three].
Having evil desires is his lack of integrity;
the disclosure of it to a human being;
not by means of another pretext, but that very knowledge itself.
The wise declare that there are five factors here.
In the first, the second, and the last, no alternative formulation is found;
in the second and the third alone, there is an injunction, but not in the others.
The first [course of action] has a single origin, possesses two factors, and arises from body and mind;
the remaining ones have three origins, and their factors are seven.
The first is associated with pleasure and equanimity; the third is associated with painful feeling.
The second and the fourth are declared to have three feelings.
For the first, there are eight consciousnesses; for the third, however, there are two;
for the second and the fourth, ten consciousnesses are obtained.
Therefore, it is said to be "with consciousness";
all this fourfold [classification] has been explained as "action," "perception," "liberation," and "worldly offense.
This, however, is appropriate as a rule specifically regarding offenses.
Therefore, only in the case of an offense should it be accepted by one who is discerning.
One with a supple back, one who is pendulous, one who seizes with the mouth, and one who sits [in a hidden place]—
these four are the *pārājika* offenses that follow the sequence.
And for bhikkhunīs there are four; one who has left the order and a bhikkhunī herself;
likewise eleven who are incapable—all these together are twenty-four.
These twenty-four persons are said to be those who have committed a pārājika offense.
Unfit for the state of a monk, like one whose head has been severed, unable to live— so it is with the paṇḍaka, the animal, and the hermaphrodite.
These three are indeed defective in their basis, lacking the causal conditions for rebirth.
The five acts of immediate retribution, living in communion through theft,
one who violates a nun, and one who has gone over to another sect— these are the five who have lost their status through their actions.
As for the essential portion of the legal decision:
This [section] on the Pārājika offenses has been told by me;
by following it, it is possible for the wise one to understand the remainder as well, without exception.
To those who desire the method of the ultimate truth,
[this work] is supreme for producing proficiency in the Piṭaka, which is endowed with manifold methods of the Vinaya.
This must be mastered constantly.
Thus ends the discussion on the fourth *pārājika* in the Vinaya-vinicchaya.
Now begins the discussion on the *saṅghādisesa* offenses.
The intention to emit semen, the exertion, and the emission of semen—
excepting a dream— constitute the offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
Furthermore, having caused another person to exert themselves with one's own generative organ...
If he causes semen to be emitted, a grave offense (garuka) should be designated for him.
However, for one who intentionally makes an effort with his own genitals,
a serious offense (thullaccaya) is declared if the semen is not emitted.
For one who makes a deliberate effort, even by causing a tremor in the air,
there is a grave offense (thullaccaya) if semen is not emitted.
It is not permitted to fill the urethra with water for the sake of play and then urinate.
But for one who plays with the genitals with the hand, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For one who looks at the genitals of three kinds of women with a lustful mind,
whether from the front or from behind, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Even for one who looks at another with a single application of effort throughout the day,
the opening and closing of the eyes do not constitute a factor for an offense;
nor does it constitute an offense for one who lacks the intention to release [the gaze], even though they do not withdraw it.
No offense is declared when one is released during sleep.
This concludes the Discussion on Emission of Semen.
Regarding the touching of a human woman out of lustful desire for physical contact:
If, with the perception that she is a human woman, there occurs an offense involving a Saṅghādisesa;
even if he merely touches a hair of a woman, down to a single hair,
through lust for bodily contact, an offense arises for the bhikkhu.
If, having been touched by a woman, one who intends to indulge in that contact makes an effort and consents to it, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*. Or,
having grasped her with one hand, or with the second...
For one who touches [the body] here and there, a single offense is explained.
For one who touches it without having grasped it— from the feet up to the head—
so long as the hand is not released from the body, it remains a single offense even for an entire day.
But when five fingers are grasped together as one, there would be only a single offense;
for it does not occur according to each individual part.
If, however, one grasps five fingers belonging to different women, [the same applies].
There are five *saṅghādisesa* offenses for a monk in one case:
when he has doubt regarding a woman, or perceives her as a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) or the like,
or even when he touches with his body something connected to the body of a woman.
In the case of a paṇḍaka, a female yakkha, or a female peta, there would be a thullaccaya for him;
in the case of a female animal, there is a dukkaṭa for bodily contact.
Furthermore, [this applies] when a bhikkhu’s body is touched by a woman who is attached to him.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) even for one who touches [an object] attached to the body.
There is an offense of wrong-doing for one who touches women’s female forms made of wood, metal, or other materials, as well as their clothing or ornaments.
Fruit grown there may be eaten, as well as mung beans and the like grown there;
however, for one who touches any kind of grain, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
This applies to all things such as bamboo flutes and the like, as well as the fivefold musical ensemble.
For one who touches any gems, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
All types of weaponry, including the bowstring, the bow, and the staff;
all of these, as well as the net and the arrow-case, are not to be touched.
A golden image and so forth, or a stupa made of precious gems,
is designated as "untouchable" (anāmāsa) in the Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā.
To cover it oneself, or even to cause it to be covered, [is an offense].
To cause [an instrument] to be played, or to play it oneself,
or to play what has already been played, is not permitted. However, when a monk says,
"I shall perform an offering," he who is wise should say that worship of the Buddha must be performed.
When a woman who is a seductress touches him herself,
for the monk who perceives that touch without exerting his own body—
there is no offense for the monk if it was unintentional and he was unaware.
For one whose intention is liberation, as well as for one who is insane and so forth,
the origin and other factors are indeed the same as in the first [offense];
likewise for lustful physical contact and the emission of semen.
The Discussion on Physical Contact:
Through delighting in indecent speech, perceiving a woman as a woman,
and by way of praising or disparaging two paths.
For a monk who makes advances for sexual intercourse and so forth,
even if he merely flashes his light, it constitutes a grave offense (thullaccaya) toward a discerning person,
even by means of a hand gesture. Likewise, [the same applies] if one says, "You are a *sikharaṇī*, you are a *sambhinnā*, you are a *ubhatobyañjanā*."
Even by means of abusive speech, if she hears it as something grave;
whether he utters it again and again, or says it once or many times—
the number of words determines that for women, these offenses are grave.
If she does not acknowledge it, there would be a thullaccaya offense for him;
likewise when speaking of her above the knees and below the collarbone,

Having gone together with four monks at the time of dawn, he should go to that very region where the details of the *parivāsa* (probation) have been determined.
Saying, "I undertake the duty," or "The penance (mānatta)," having undertaken it from them and having declared it with confidence,
one should place it down in their presence, or when they have departed.
Having informed a bhikkhu who has seen it previously, one should deposit [the bowl].
The procedure for its giving, as well as the method regarding the interruption of the night and so forth,
is to be understood by means of the commentary and the canonical text of the *Samuccaya*.
When he has again performed that *mānatta* penance, the Saṅgha consisting of a group of twenty may,
according to the proper procedure, reinstate that bhikkhu who was originally of regular standing but has been suspended.
Even for one who conceals an offense, no *parivāsa* probation exists.
There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who conceals her own [offense]. Whether she has concealed the offense or not,
she must simply practice the *mānatta* penance for a half-month.
This supreme *Vinayavinicchaya* illuminates the wisdom and intelligence regarding the methods of the Vinaya;
those who approach it find it endowed with various systems and principles.
They attain proficiency in the method of the Vinaya.
Thus ends the discussion on the *saṅghādisesa* offenses in the *Vinayavinicchaya*. Now begins the discussion on the *aniyata* (undetermined) offenses.
Out of a desire for the pleasure of sitting in private,
one who wishes to go into the presence of a woman puts on his lower robe, applies collyrium to his eyes, and eats.
For every such action, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in each and every instance.
For one who goes by way of successive steps, and having gone, sits down;
for both the act of sitting and the counting of the preliminary motions,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for him— many offenses even when [the steps] are many.
Even one standing nearby, within twelve cubits, does not incur an offense if he is blind;
however, even for a hundred women, there is no exemption.
Even a sighted man, having lain down and being merely asleep, [incurs an offense].
Even if one is seated inside a room whose door is closed, one does not remain protected.
When a wise person who is not blind is present, there is no fault arising from sitting for one who perceives it as private, provided their mind is not distracted.
For those who are insane and so forth, there is no offense even for the three [types of] transgressions;
their origins and other characteristics are the same as those of the first and last cases. This concludes the Discussion on the First Indeterminate [Rule].
One who is blind but not deaf, or one who is wise— whether a woman or a man—
if standing within twelve cubits [of the offender], shall be free from offense.
Or even one who is blind but not deaf, or one who is deaf but has sight.
One who does not commit [the offense] incurs no offense; this [offense] has three origins.
This concludes the discussion on the second undetermined offense.
Thus ends the discussion on the undetermined offenses in the Vinaya-vinicchaya.
Regarding the Discourse on Forfeiture: Linen, cotton, silk, hemp, and wool—
robe-cloth is said to be of six kinds, and according to its origin, it is permissible.
Dukūla, pattuṇṇa, cīna, and somārapaṭṭaka cloth;
that which is produced by psychic power or given by gods—these are suitable for him.
The three robes, requisites, garments, and a face-cloth;
One should resolve upon a sitting mat and likewise a rug.
A monk should not live even for a single day without his three robes;
nor should he live without having resolved upon a sitting mat for the four-month period.
Having dyed it to the permissible degree and placed the three robes there,
one must indeed determine that which has been produced according to the proper measure.
The outer robe (saṅghāṭi) is five handspans in length at its inner edge.
And across, it is a fist’s breadth; that, moreover, is the maximum limit.
It is declared that even the Teacher’s own robe allowance is permissible;
this very [measure] is illustrated as the standard for the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga).
The five-fist measure is the length;
the width is two and a half cubits or two cubits for the remaining inner robe (antaravāsaka).
For the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), made of new or unwashed cloth, it is considered to be double that size.
The upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) consists of a single layer of cloth, and the inner garment (antaravāsaka) is likewise. However, for robes that have been taken out during the season,
a monk’s outer cloak (saṅghāṭi) may consist of four layers.
Even though the remaining two are said to be double [in size],
a rag-robe (paṃsukūla) is permissible according to one's convenience.
If it is possible, even three, two, or one [strip] may be cut.
If all [the robes] are insufficient, or if there is even more than what is to be given;
or if one wears the three robes that have not been formally relinquished or taken up;
for a bhikkhu who uses them in such a way, a *dukkaṭa* offense is declared due to improper enjoyment.
Having demonstrated the entire procedure for a monk— including the *kusi*, the half-*kusi*, the *maṇḍala*, the half-*maṇḍala*, the *vivaṭṭa*, the *anuvivaṭṭa*,
and even the *bāhanta*— as well as its various divisions beginning with the fivefold [set].
The ascetic’s proper attire has been cut off; however, the triple robe must be made.
[It is forfeited] by giving it away, by taking it back, by receiving it through trust, by returning to the lower life, and by the abandonment of the training.
Through relinquishment, through destruction, through the changing of gender,
and when there is a hole— even if it is only the size of the back of the nail of the little finger— the entire resolve regarding the three robes is broken.
But that which is pierced involves the destruction of the resolution regarding the hole.
Even if a single thread remains uncut, it does not break the resolution,
provided one maintains its whiteness, even if it has been washed by a dyer.
Having first applied the bolt, one cuts it later for protection;
having joined the two ends together, one cuts it later for protection.
Less than four or eight finger-breadths [from the edge], on either side, is the measurement.
The length of all three [robes] has a margin of one span (vidatthi).
For the sitting mat (nisīdana), there are two spans in length and one and a half spans in width, according to the measure of the Sugata.
There is a cloth for covering itches, two spans wide and four spans long according to the measure of the Sugata. In length,
according to the measure of the Sugata, there are six spans.
In detail, a rain-cloak may be [up to] two and a half [vitthas] in length.
For one who makes it exceeding these three [measures],
the Exalted One has declared that there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the cutting down of the excess.
The measurement for a face-cloth or a sheet has not been specified by means of a standard measure. Every kind of bedsheet or robe,
whether with fringes or without fringes, [is subject to this].
Whether large or small, one or many, it is permissible.
Even two face-cleansing cloths are permitted in every respect;
likewise for a sitting mat, whether with or without a fringe, it must have a fringe.
Like those dyed with lac, the circle, and what is taken as permissible;
the kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi (itch-covering cloth) is mentioned, and likewise the vassikasāṭikā (rainy-season robe).
Neither in number nor in measurement are these included among the requisites.
Those who know the tradition say it is "beyond measure and calculation.
A robe called *pacchima* (the last) is four finger-breadths wide and eight finger-breadths long according to the Sugata’s span; it is fit for distribution.
One should determine as requisites and robes for use— the water-strainer,
the bowl, the book-bag, and so forth, as well as the last robe among the set of three robes.
It is also permissible to determine many items together as a single unit.
There is no fault in [keeping] what has been set aside for the sake of one's mother and others.
One may resolve upon a rain-season robe for four months;
having relinquished it again, one may thereafter assign it [to another].
One may determine the itch-covering cloth for as long as the disease does not subside;
thereafter, having removed it, one should assign it [to another].
"This itch-covering cloth, this inner robe..."
One should resolve, saying, "I resolve. This same method applies to the others as well.
Having said, "This itch-covering cloth, this one," while not in the presence [of the recipient], one should relinquish it in this manner;
the wise should understand that this applies to the others as well.
Having formed a mental application, that which is performed by touching with the body,
and that which is established by speech— thus resolution is considered to be twofold.
All this has been stated for the monk who uses only three robes.
Having spoken thus, one should resolve [upon it]; that is the "requisite-cloth" (parikkhāra-coḷika).
It is even permissible to make the three robes into a requisite-cloth;
thus, the exemption stated for one who has been clothed in four [robes] is rendered useless.
No, because the Teacher stated there that it applies specifically to one who uses only three robes (*tecīvarika*);
therefore, everything [regarding requisites] is permitted for one who uses extra robes (*parikkhāracoḷa*). Furthermore, regarding the statement:
