Because there is a rule for the formal assignment (*vikappana*) of exactly that which is to be formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhātabba*),
no fault is found in a monk who acts in this way. If this were not so,
why would there be [a specific rule] regarding face-cloths and the like?
Because they perform the specific functions of face-wiping cloths and so forth, it is appropriate that there be a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for these items that have no other owner.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "This is the opening for storage."
And because it has been stated, one who knows the Vinaya cannot prohibit it.
That "the robe is complete" refers both to the origin of the introductory narrative and to its storage;
this should be understood as the "opening of the storehouse" by the discerning one.
For one who wears robes made of *kusavāka* grass and so forth, or a blanket made of hair,
there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) for wearing [robes] made of bark-fiber,
bird-feathers, or animal-skins. This also applies to robes made of *kadali* fiber, *eraka* grass, *akkha* seeds, or cloth made of paper-bark.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for a tiriṭa, a head-wrap, a bodice, or a jacket.
There is also an offense of wrong-doing for robes that are entirely blue, crimson, black, red, or yellow, as well as those dyed with mahānāma, mahāraṅga, or other red dyes.
In the case of a set of ten [robes] that has not been cut, and in the case of long fruit and flowers remaining;
for one whose robe has not been cut, there is nothing here that is improper.
One resolves it, assigns it, relinquishes it, or it perishes.
No offense is declared when there is trust within the ten-day period.
Regarding that which is called *kathina* by name,
this origin (of the rule) is stated as being without mental intention (*acitta*) and without prior action (*akiriya*), and it possesses three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The Discussion on the First Kathina.

In locations such as villages and the like, having set aside the three robes for even a single night, without the formal authorization of the Saṅgha— provided they are three or five [robes] in number.
But for a bhikkhu, it is not permitted to let that robe go out of his possession;
if he lets it go out of his possession, it becomes an offense of expiation (nissaggiya) at the rising of the dawn.
Having laid aside the robe, even while bathing during the night...
When dawn has risen, what indeed must that bhikkhu do?
The Sage has declared a *dukkaṭa* offense for dwelling [without robes];
out of fear of that, if the bhikkhu goes about naked, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Because the monk remains in the place where his robe was cut,
there is no robe whatsoever that is considered "unallowable" for him.
Having swallowed it and taken it, he then went into the presence of the monk.
Once it has been relinquished, the offense must indeed be confessed by one who is wise.
Having relinquished it to another, for one who uses it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every single act of application, such as wearing it and so forth.
There is no offense if another monk is consuming it;
if he does not take it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who has accepted it.
And when those young monks are walking along the road, both [offenses apply].
If, having taken his bowl and robe, he has departed while still young,
and before he has reached that heavy burden [of the robe], the dawn should rise;
the cloth becomes subject to relinquishment, and the formal support is not suspended.
If, after resting for a moment, one goes while the youth is still departing,
the cloth becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) and the formal support (*nissaya*) is dissolved.
If the dawn rises while he is listening to a discourse on the Dhamma, [the same applies].
There is a robe that must be relinquished, and the formal support (nissaya) is suspended.
There is no offense in the act of renouncing it, even for one who has received formal authorization;
if, before sunrise, he either gives it away or it is destroyed.
In the first [offense], the methods such as origin and so forth are the same;
here, however, it is specified that there is no "non-removal" because of non-performance.
This concludes the discussion on the second *kathina*.
An out-of-season robe may be kept for at most one month;
beyond that, it is not permitted to set it aside if there is an expectation [of receiving another].
It is indeed only the transgression of ten days [that constitutes the offense].
In the first *kathina* ceremony here,
the lapse of a month is prescribed;
the remainder is considered equal to that.
The Third Discussion on the Kathina.
If a monk causes a robe that has been worn by a nun— who is not related to him—
to be washed, dyed, or beaten (to soften it), [he incurs an offense].
For him, a forfeiture offense (nissaggiyāpatti) is proclaimed by the first [clause];
likewise, by the remaining two, two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) are illustrated.
If he gives it into the hand of a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) for the purpose of washing;
Having become [a female], she is ordained later; that is the method for washing.

Even in the description of a novice monk, if the gender changes, having been ordained as a nun, if she washes [the robe], it would be an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
And when a cloth has been handed over into the hands of junior monks,
this same method is considered to apply to those whose gender has been changed.
Likewise, when a robe has been given into the hand of a nun with the instruction, "Wash it," [the same rule applies].
But if the gender has been changed, it is permissible if she washes it.
When the nun is told, "Wash it," if she performs the entire task,
there would be a *nissaggiya* offense for her solely on account of the washing.
"Perform everything that must be done regarding this robe-cloth"— if one says this,
there is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya) as well as two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
[This applies even] when it is a relative and one perceives them as a relative, or in the case of a rug or a sitting mat.
If one causes another’s property to be washed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Likewise, for one who causes a woman ordained on only one side—
that is, by way of the nuns— to wash [her robes], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Whether it be what was not asked for but used, or if one washes something else, there is no fault regarding acting as a matchmaker; the origin and other factors are the same.
This is the Discussion on Washing Old Robes.
If one takes anything that is subject to alteration, or even a final robe,
there is an offense, except for an exchange.
For the effort made with the intent to take, a *dukkaṭa* is prescribed.
For him, there is an offense entailing relinquishment, as indicated by the act of taking.
If he sends a robe into the hand of one who is not fully ordained,
except in exchange for another, it is not permitted to take it.
If one perceives a relative as not being a relative, or if there is doubt,
and one takes [an item] from the hand of one who is ordained on only one side, it is a dukkaṭa offense. Likewise,
if one has made the intention, "I will give," or if it is an exchange;
There is no fault in taking a temporary loan of trust.
However, there is no fault for one who takes other requisites;
this is stated to be an offense originating from acting as a go-between, characterized by both action and non-action.
The Discussion on Receiving Robes. For one who requests a robe from an unrelated person who has not been invited [to do so],
there is an offense entailing relinquishment, except at the proper time.
A *pācittiya* offense is declared for three [factors], likewise two *dukkaṭas* for one who perceives a relative as a non-relative,
or for one who is in doubt regarding that.
Also for one who makes a request at a proper time, or when relatives have already been invited.
Or for the sake of another, or when his relatives have been invited—this should be known as non-offense. Likewise for one who is insane and so forth;
all [factors] such as the origin and so on are considered the same as in the case of matchmaking.
The Discussion on Requesting from an Unfamiliar Person:
If a monk requests more than one robe-cloth from someone who is not related and who has not been invited to do so,
there is an offense entailing relinquishment for that monk.
For one who has lost all three, or two, or even one;
by him not even the slightest thing should be accepted, whether it be two or one.
When bringing what remains, if it is given, there is no cause for it to be considered "cut-off."
It should be understood that there is no offense [if the gift is made] with the wealth of one's own kinsmen and others, or even with one's own wealth; likewise for those who are insane and so forth.
All factors such as the origin and the rest are considered identical to those of the "go-between" offense.
Discourse on That Which Is Beyond:
Out of a desire for what is excellent, one incurs the offense of formal determination (*vikappana*);
furthermore, whatever gain of robes he obtains [thereby] shall be subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
If one who desires to give something of great value asks for something of little value from among the belongings of relatives and others,
it is declared that there is no offense. However, if one perceives a relative as a non-relative,
or if there is doubt, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The methods regarding origin and so forth are stated to be the same as for the case of matchmaking.
This concludes the discussion on the first instance of what was prepared.
Since there is nothing whatsoever that needs to be said regarding the second instance of what was prepared:
Therefore, its determination is exactly like that of the preceding one.
This concludes the discussion on the second alternative.
[Regarding] what has been brought for the sake of a monk by a king or by one belonging to the royal household:
It is not permissible to take what is unallowable,
such as gold and so forth. Whether for oneself or for another,
it is not permissible to accept anything being offered for one's own sake, whether it be silver or gold.
If one accepts [an item] from a monk that was designated for another purpose, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense; this is stated in the Mahāpaccarī.
Furthermore, if someone, having brought an improper article, should speak in this manner:
“‘I give this to the Saṅgha,’ whether to an individual or to a group:
‘Make it an ārāma, or a vihāra, or a cetiya’—
it is not permissible for all of them to accept that site.”
If, without addressing the Saṅgha, a group, or even an individual,
they say, "We give this to the cetiya" or "to the monastery," it is not permissible to refuse that money or gold.
It should be said to the monastery attendants, "They speak thus.
For one who accepts silver or gold on behalf of the Saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya-pācittiya);
and for its use, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Because a pond is considered a field and is the source from which crops arise, it is not permissible for a monk to take [water] from it or to use it. [He may say:
"Let the Sangha or the group enjoy the four requisites."
But if, having spoken thus, he gives it all, it is permissible.
And if he causes [a field] to be made, having had the forest cleared,
he may take even what is in excess within those old fields.
If, regarding a portion that has not yet been demarcated, one says to even those who have planted a new crop, "Give such-and-such a portion," and thereby causes them to produce *kahāpaṇa* coins;
or if, having spoken an improper word such as "Plow! Plant!"—
And for all [monks], everything that has been prepared becomes unallowable.
Whoever establishes a plot of land— without specifying "this much is the portion" or "this much is the ground"— whether by plowing or other means, [commits an offense].
Furthermore, one who measures a field on the ground by himself for the purpose of knowing its extent— whether with a cord, a measuring line, or a staff—
or who stands upon it to guard a threshing floor, and likewise from that threshing floor again;
Or if he has them removed as rice, that is likewise unallowable for him.
And if he says, "Bring this with so much rice," and they bring it when thus told, that too is unallowable for him.
“With this much gold, bring back this [cloth],” he says;
and whatever they bring when so instructed is improper for all.
Whether it be a weaver’s slave or another among dyers and the like—
It is permissible to accept [food] when it is given by the name of the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*).
Even if they say, "We give cows," it is not permissible to accept them;
however, if they say "we give" for the purpose of using the five products of the cow (*pañcagorasa*), it is permissible.
This same method should be understood by the discerning one regarding goats and so forth;
everything may be accepted with words that are allowable (*kappiya*).
An elephant, a buffalo, a horse, an ox, a chicken, or a pig—
Regarding teeth and humans, it is not permissible to take them.
Even though it is forbidden for the Saṅgha, if one goes after giving [the price],
or if some take them after giving the cost to the Saṅgha, it is permissible.
Even when it is said, "We give a field, a building site, or a pond,
as well as cows, goats, and so forth, for the monastery," it is not permissible to refuse.
It is stated that there should be three admonitions and six requests.
If there is only instigation, the offense is double for the instigator.
There is no offense if one does not instigate, or if [the food] is obtained by one who is insane, and so forth.
All factors such as the origin and others are considered the same as in the case of matchmaking.
The Discussion on the Training Rule for Kings.
The First Chapter: On Robes.
Even if mixed with only a single thread of silk, a rug [is considered] made of silk-cotton.
There is an offense entailing relinquishment for a monk who has it made.
For one who makes it for another's sake, or for one who has it made, regarding a blanket;
and for one who uses what has been obtained made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense for one who is a first-time offender while making a canopy,
or a floor-covering, or a mattress, or a pillow.
Discussion on Silk.
If one should have a rug made of pure black wool from the hair of a black sheep, there is an offense for him;
the rest, however, is like the first [offense].
The Discussion on Pure Black Wool.
There is no offense for one who, having taken it, makes it all— whether a small amount, a large amount,
or even the whole thing— either white or brownish-yellow.
These three types of rugs [made] in succession are also [permissible].
Even if they have been forfeited, if one obtains them and uses them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
All factors, beginning with the origin, are considered the same as for the "go-between" offense;
however, among these three, the third is "action-non-action."
The Discussion on the Two-Part [Rug].
For one who makes a rug within six years, there is an offense entailing relinquishment,
except by formal authorization from the Saṅgha of monks.
There is no offense if one has it made or does it for the sake of another;
or if, having obtained what was made by another, one uses it;
or if one makes a sitting rug after six years, or even longer.
Even when made by hanging [the cloth] from a canopy or a curtain-wall.
This concludes the discussion on the six years.
There is no offense if one does not take [the cloth], provided that a rug is not available.
To have it made for another's sake, and to use what has been made.
By way of non-appropriation, according to the Sugata’s span,
and by means of its making, this was spoken by the Teacher regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done.
All [factors] beginning with the origin are considered equal to the conduct of a go-between;
no distinction is found for this [offense] compared to the immediately preceding one.
Discussion on sitting on a spread-out seat.
But if, while a vehicle or elephants, horses, and so forth are moving,
one has hair placed [on them] without the owner’s knowledge,
the offense for the bhikkhu occurs when they have traveled three yojanas.
This same principle applies when those very persons are arriving or have already been stationed there.
However, when a vehicle is approaching— whether it be a horse or the back of an elephant— if one stations [the person] there,
mounts [the vehicle], and then urges it on, it is permissible.
"It is not allowable" is what is indicated;
for in the Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā it says that one who causes another to take it away contradicts the [actual] word.
Even for one who goes after inserting hairs into the ear-holes, [it is not allowed].
It is said that there is indeed an offense at the conclusion of counting the body hairs.
However, it is permissible if they have been tied together with a thread;
for one who carries them after having fashioned them into a braid, the offense has been clearly explained.
If one who has reached a customs station, or is harassed by thieves and the like,
or even one who is otherwise occupied, should go [further], there is an offense.
For one carrying [goods] for three *yojanas*, or less than three *yojanas*.
Likewise, for one who brings it back, [the offense extends] those same three yojanas.
Or, having gone for the purpose of staying there, for one who carries it beyond that point;
or even for one who, having obtained what was stolen or relinquished, carries it away.
For one who causes another to take it away, for one taking a finished article,
and likewise for those who are insane and so forth, non-offense has been declared.
But this origin [of the offense] is from body and from body-and-mind.
Mindless bodily action, the three types of consciousness, and the three types of feeling;
the Discussion on Wool;
together with the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth, as well as the washing of wool.
It is considered equivalent to having an old robe washed.
This concludes the discussion on washing wool.
One should not take, nor cause to be taken, silver or gold.
Having relinquished it, the offense must indeed be confessed by the monk.
Silver, gold, and even a single *māsaka* coin—
these four kinds of objects bring about the necessity of relinquishment.
Pearls, gems, stones, conch shells, coral, rubies, and masāragalla;
grains, the seven types [of livestock] beginning with cows and buffaloes;
fields, land, ponds, and furthermore, female and male slaves.
The bases for an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) have been explained by the Great Seer:
all such things as mung beans, māsas, and so forth; ghee and other products; rice;
thread, cloth, a plow, a ploughshare, and other items that are allowable (kappiya).
If a monk accepts an object for his own sake that is subject to relinquishment, it shall be subject to relinquishment for him.
Likewise, if he takes it for the sake of the Saṅgha or others, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the object itself, and there is also an offense of wrong-doing for every coin.
If one accepts a thousand [coins] such as kahāpaṇas,
the number of offenses shall correspond to the number of objects received.
Likewise, regarding bags and such items that are loosely tied, the number of offenses is stated according to their form in the *Mahāpaccarī*. However,
it is also said that if someone says, "Let this be for the venerable one," [the offense is determined accordingly].
Even if he wishes to take it, it must indeed be refused.
Even when that object has been rejected, if he departs,
it must be guarded in such a way that it does not perish.
“Bring this, take this, give this, deposit this here”—
it is not permissible for a monk to speak thus regarding what is unallowable,
with the exception of accepting money, relinquishing, or exchanging.
Ghee and other such items should be shared and consumed by all.
It is not permitted to take even one's own allotted portion from a receiving monk who has obtained it elsewhere, nor is it permitted to consume it.

[This applies to] fish, raw fish, boars, domestic pigs, porcupines, and rams.
There are five kinds of fat, and oil is likewise fivefold.
All fat and oil— whether allowable or unallowable—

Because it was taken with a specific purpose, and even if seven days have elapsed,

It may be threefold: by way of body, by way of speech, and by way of both body and speech.

But for a monk who confesses a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla-āpatti*) to one who is not fully ordained—

When one speaks of an offense by connecting it with the basis [of the rule], there is indeed fault.

For every single blow, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is proclaimed.
For one who causes [the ground] to be dug, there is one [offense] for the day, and even for one who has it dug repeatedly;

“Dig a lotus pond, dig a reservoir, dig a pit or a well”—
there is no fault whatsoever in one who speaks thus.
“Dig this spot, dig a lotus pond here.”
It is not proper to say, "Dig here at this moment.
It is proper to say, "Dig a bulbous root, or a kurunda, dig a pillar, or a stump;

Having specified, "Dig up this root, this creeper, this palm tree,
this reed," it is not permissible to say,
"If you are able to drain [the water], then with jars [remove] the mud when it has become thin."
A bhikkhu may remove [wood], but it must not be thick.
Having broken off what has fallen near the water of rivers and the like,

If it falls into water, it is permissible even when the rain has fallen;
for if the rain falls while the four months have passed, [the water] is already there.
If they dig a trench on a stone surface, then—
If rain falls first and afterwards the deity rains heavily,
it is permissible to clear or break up the ground within four months;

If dust falls upon water that has already been filled,
it is appropriate to disturb it, for the rain-god pours down into the water.
Dust clings to a smooth, polished back-slab.
At the end of the four-month period, it is not permitted to disturb that [ant-hill] either.
However, if an ant-hill has arisen on a cliff that has not been prepared,

If it is situated in the open air, it is permissible for four months;
the same rule applies to a tree, to clay, and even to the mud of upacikā-ants and the like,

This same method is stated regarding those things on the ground that are not connected [to it]:
they are similar to those very things, such as the clay of a *kasiṇa* circle;

If a dwelling is uncovered or its roof has collapsed,
one should not dismantle what has been repaired after four months have passed.
Therefore, [one should not remove] rafters, walls, pillars, or floor-boards.
If one takes it with the perception, "I shall take it," it is permissible to take it.
While taking it, if bricks and so forth fall and clay falls as well, there is no offense;

If there should be a heap of clay inside a house,

At the end of the four-month period, everything that has been soaked becomes unallowable.
Whatever portion therein has been soaked, that much is unallowable;
however, whatever portion therein has not been soaked, that remains allowable.
If it has been moistened with water and remains joined as one with the ground,

And in an open space, a wall made of clay is established.
At the end of the four-month period, it is said: "The earth has been born.
Therein, the fine dust that clings [to the ground], one may take up a moderate amount as if not rubbing it;

It is not permissible to take [a tree] after disturbing the earth.

and then crosses over it without picking it up or asking permission—
whether it be within the monastery grounds, the precincts, or its surrounding enclosure— [one incurs an offense].
In the first case, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding the foot;

in the second, it may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Due to the destruction of both the lodging and the bedding, for one who goes away after having spread [the bedding] inside a room, an offense of expiation is prescribed.
In the vicinity of a monastery, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding a pavilion and the like;
likewise for one who departs after having spread out bedding, or from the destruction of even a mere bed.
Three offenses entailing confession (pācittiya) are stated in relation to property belonging to the Saṅgha consisting of ten bases.
Likewise, for one who belongs to another, three offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) are explained.
There is no offense for one who departs after having removed [the obstacle], or after having asked permission,
or even when there is an obstruction by another, or when it belongs to oneself.
Having gone there with expectation, even while standing there, he asks about all the factors such as the origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth;
these are considered equal to the immediately preceding [case].
This concludes the second discussion on lodgings.
If one knowingly intrudes upon a monk who has already arrived and prepares a bed in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha,
it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
[This applies even] when a monk enters [the dwelling] where there are stones for washing the feet.
From that bed or chair until one has stepped out,
or from the bed or chair until the place for urination—
this interval is called the "proximate precinct" (upacāra).
In that regard, for a monk who intends to cause annoyance,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) if he spreads out any one of the ten kinds of bedding in the vicinity;
likewise, there is an offense of wrong-doing for him if he sits down or lies down upon it.
Likewise, for one who performs both [acts], there are two *pācittiya* offenses.
For one who performs them repeatedly, at the conclusion of the count of applications,
three *pācittiya*s are stated, and for each individual person, there is a triad of *dukkaṭa*s.
Whether he spreads out a bed beyond the precincts,
or even within the precincts of a monastery, or in the open air; or whether he causes it to be spread there, or sits down upon it—
In all cases, a *dukkaṭa* offense is stated, and wearing [the robe] is prohibited.
There is no offense for one who is ill, or for one oppressed by cold;
likewise for a monk in times of distress, or for one who is insane, and so forth.
All [factors] beginning with the origination (samuṭṭhāna) should be understood as being the same as in the first and last cases; this is painful feeling.
This concludes the Discussion on Intrusion (anupakhajja).
If one should personally eject a monk from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha,
or cause him to be ejected out of anger, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for him.
Even in the case of palaces with many stories, if one [acts] by a single effort—
If he ejects him, one *pācittiya* is explained for that.
For one who ejects [him] repeatedly, in the intervals between each time,
there are as many *pācittiyas* as there are doors counted.
The same principle applies even when one says, "Go forth" with words alone.
For one who issues a command, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) at the very moment of commanding.
If he has been commanded only once, even if there are many doors;
It is a single offense even if one transgresses many times or with many [objects].
This applies from the vicinity of the monastery, such as its assembly hall and so forth,
whether by means of body or speech, and likewise when one is being driven out.
Whether it be the precincts of a monastery or the monastery itself, for one who ejects anyone else from them,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) even regarding their requisites.
A wise person [should know that] in the case of a monk’s requisites that are not attached [to him],...
For one who counts the [number of] requisites, a dukkaṭa offense is declared.
Likewise for one who expels a pupil, a shameless person, or a student;
and for one who is insane, as well as for one who is himself insane.
There is no offense declared for taking from one’s own dwelling place, or from that of someone who trusts them, or their requisites. Likewise,
there is no offense for taking anything from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, as well as from one who causes strife.
But this [offense] has three origins; the feeling is painful.
This is the discourse on expulsion.
[It applies to one who strikes] the middle of the head, or [one who stands] above a hut in the air.
For a monk who sits or lies down upon a bed or chair with detachable legs,
there shall be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each instance of such application.
A *pācittiya* offense is stated for three [cases], and a *dukkaṭa* for three regarding an individual;
or when there is no use below, or when it strikes the head;
or when staying without longing, or even when it belongs to oneself.
Or in a place of trust, nor with one who is ill or insane,
etc.; or standing where a screen has been provided, he causes it to be attached—
this origin is considered the same as that of the *eḷakaloma* (wool) offense.
The Discussion on the Dwelling Hut. Up to one cubit from the door,
a bhikkhu may either plaster it himself or have it plastered by another, for the purpose of fixing the bolt.
This same method applies even to the preliminary work for the light-intervals of what is to be known;
however, regarding the covering, it may be determined after two or three applications while standing on green grass.
Beyond that, if one should nevertheless determine it, [it is invalid].
For him there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya), while for one standing there [on the roof], it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Someone standing on the ridge-pole of the back-rafters at the edge of the roof—
where, standing, he cannot see the monk who is standing below.
But it is not permissible for a bhikkhu to stand in that spot,
for it is the very place where the falling vihāra will collapse.
One who perceives it as "excessive" when it has been used less than two or three times [is at fault].
In that case, even for one who is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no fault in two or three turns [of conversation], or in a shelter, or in grass huts.
All factors, beginning with the origin, are considered the same as in the case of matchmaking (*sañcaritta*).
The Discussion of the Two or Three Methods:
If one who knows the water contains living beings should sprinkle grass, clay,
or even soil with it— or have others do so— it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, however, one interrupts the stream while pouring clay,
even for a single jar, one *pācittiya* offense is explained.
If one interrupts the stream, it is according to the number of applications.
Even for one performing it in the presence [of the accused], regarding a flowing stream as the matrix:
if there were but a single offense, let it flow even for a day;
yet for one binding it here and there, there would be a calculation according to the number of applications.
If one throws even a cartload of clay or grass into the water,
there is one *pācittiya* offense for each [action] taken together.
If one throws them in one by one, it is according to the number of individual acts.
Whether it be for the sake of clearing away [dirt] or for the sake of turbidity, water flows in such a manner.
For one who says, "Sprinkle [it]," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
with a single instruction, even if one sprinkles for an entire day, there is but one offense.
If one perceives water that is free of living beings as containing living beings,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) even for one who is in doubt in every case. In every case,
for one who perceives it as containing living beings, or for one who is unintentional or lacks mindfulness;
There is no offense for one who does not know, nor likewise for one who is insane and so forth.
[The following cases involve] water containing living beings, the perception that it contains living beings,
and the sprinkling of grass and such without the intention to kill.
Four factors have been pointed out by the Great Seer for this [offense]:
the methods beginning with the origin (samuṭṭhāna) are indeed the same as those for taking what is not given.
This is explained as being both a fault according to the formal rule (paṇṇatti-vajja) and consisting of three types of consciousness.
This alone is indicated here, as well as its qualification.
The Discussion on Water with Living Beings.
The Second Chapter: On Lodgings.
The authorization for a monk to instruct a nun was here permitted by the Great Seer through a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (ñatticatuttha) for a monk endowed with eight qualities.
That monk who is authorized by her [the Saṅgha] regarding the eight weighty rules (garudhamma):
Whether to one person, to several, or even to the community of nuns,
if he should exhort them while still reciting those very teachings, at the conclusion of that exhortation,
there shall be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for him.
But for one who instructs by means of another teaching, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
likewise for one who instructs a person ordained on only one side, or by means of the heavy rules (garudhamma).
[This applies] even when a bhikkhunī ordained [in the nuns' order] is in the very presence of the bhikkhus.
Likewise, in the case of a reversal of gender,
it is declared that there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). For a monk who has been duly authorized,
a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is proclaimed when he fails to deliver the exhortation and speaks according to another rule.
Even when it is said, "We are united," or likewise when instructed by another,
and even when it is said, "We are divided," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding the heavy rules (garudhamma).
This applies even to one who does not accept the instruction, or who does not respond to it.
Setting aside the case of one who has committed a *dukkaṭa*, one who is foolish, one who is ill, or one who is about to travel—
But in the case of an illegal formal act (*adhamma-kamma*),
if those in the minority within the community of nuns perceive it as illegal, there may be three *pācittiyas*.
Likewise for one who is doubtful, and for one who perceives it as a legitimate legal act (dhammakamma);
nine offenses of expiation (pācittiya) are stated, and there are just as many even when the Saṅgha is unanimous.
Due to the status of those who are junior, these become eighteen for two [groups].
Even in a formal legal act (*dhammakamma*) that is invalid, there may be seventeen kinds of offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Or, one who is told "Recite [the confession]" or answers a question when asked;
or in the case of a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*), or for one who is insane and so forth—there is no fault.
The two matrices (mātikā) should be made thoroughly mastered by heart;
four recitation-sections (bhāṇavāra) are declared from the Suttanta.
One path of discourse is revealed for the purpose of providing a detailed exposition (parikathā).

For the sake of what is auspicious and inauspicious, there are exactly three kinds of rejoicing (anumodanā). For the sake of the Uposatha and other observances, there is the determination of what constitutes a formal act (kamma) and what does not.
Likewise, there is one meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that leads to the highest goal.
Having mastered this much, one who has been a resident for five years and is well-versed may,
at his own will, release from dependence and live independently.
Both Vibhaṅgas should be recited from memory and made proficient in their phrasing and so forth.
Even if there is only a single manuscript among all four Nikāyas, one must master this much:
what is an action and what is not an action, and the formal procedures (vatta).
However, if one has ten years of seniority, even if it is the very last section.
One who is learned and has mastered the directions may go wherever he wishes;
as a master, he obtains an assembly at his will to attend upon him—
[he] for whom the entire Tipiṭaka, together with its commentaries, is committed to memory.
Thus, he is called "one of great learning" (bahussuta) and may be an instructor of bhikkhunīs.
He should demonstrate the three factors beginning with formal authorization (assāsammatatā);
the methods regarding origin and so forth are indeed equal to those for the recitation of words (padasodhamma).
The Discourse on Exhortation:
It is an offense of expiation for a monk who exhorts a nun after sunset, whether by means of the heavy rules (garudhamma) or by some other teaching.
A *pācittiya* offense is stated for even a monk who has been duly authorized [to exhort];
there is an *dukkaṭa* offense for one who exhorts a person ordained in only one [order].
Likewise, it is an offense if he does so when the sun has not yet set, or if he perceives that it has already set.
In this regard, even for one who is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By way of recitation and so forth, its non-offense has been declared;
the remaining methods, such as the origin (samuṭṭhāna) and others, are similar to the immediately preceding ones.
The Discourse on the Setting Sun.
Having gone to the nuns' quarters to exhort a nun,
except at the proper time and for other than the heavy rules, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If he is not appointed, there are two *pācittiya* offenses;
and if he speaks after the sun has set, there are three.
But for one who speaks by means of another legal point (*dhamma*), there are two *dukkaṭa* offenses.
There is one *pācittiya* offense for a monk on account of the night.
For a monk who has been formally authorized (*sammatassa*), there are two *pācittiya* offenses:
because of the source of the *garudhamma* and because of the absence of formal authorization.
If one advises that same person by means of another teaching, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
because of being duly authorized, there is no offense; for one [night], there is one offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Three offenses of expiation have been stated, and in the other two cases, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
For one who exhorts a single person who has received full ordination, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Likewise, having gone to the nuns’ quarters by means of another rule,
all factors such as the origin and so forth are considered identical to those of the Kathina [Khandhaka].
The Discussion on the Nuns' Quarters: If a monk, when invited, speaks to a nun for the sake of robes and other requisites,
saying, "I am advising you," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for him.
A triple *pācittiya* is stated, and likewise a triple *dukkaṭa*;
for one who speaks to a monk not authorized by the Saṅgha, there is a *dukkaṭa*.
Likewise for one who speaks to a person not fully ordained, whether they are authorized or unauthorized.
There is no offense for one who speaks while giving advice for the sake of material gain.
Likewise, no offense is declared for those who are insane and so forth.
This [offense] has three origins, and its feeling is painful.
Discourse on Material Gifts.
If a monk should give a robe to a nun who is not related to him,
it is an offense entailing expiation, except in exchange for a robe.
The method is the same as for the training rule on receiving robes;
the remainder is considered identical, including the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth.
In that case, it was given by a nun; here, it is by a monk.
Therein, the offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) is indicated here as a simple offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This is the discourse on the giving of robes. For whoever should sew a robe, or have it sewn by another;
For a nun, however, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) [if she accepts] from one who is not a relative.
What is intended here by the Great Seer as "robe" (cīvara) is that which can be worn or that which is suitable for wearing as an upper garment.
For a monk who sews after having inserted the needle himself,
and for him [the donor] when he removes the needle, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is declared.
Even if he has pierced it a hundred times, for one who removes it all at once, [an offense is incurred].
One *pācittiya* offense is stated, though many may arise depending on the application.
However, if one is commanded by a monk without distinction,
saying "sew it," and completes the entire task, there shall be one *pācittiya*.
"If the work regarding the robe here is entirely yours, it is a burden for you"— if,
being thus instructed by the monk, he nevertheless completes everything,
then it is [an offense] for the monk who gave the instruction alone, on account of that single instruction.
There are offenses of expiation (pācittiya) regarding multiple paths on a road.
But for one who causes [the instruction] to be repeated again and again, when there is no single instruction—what indeed can be said? There may be three offenses of expiation.
If one perceives a relative as a non-relative, or if there is doubt,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding a robe for which only one side has been ordained.
Apart from a robe, for one who sews another requisite, [there is likewise an offense].
There is no offense when it has been specifically designated, nor for those such as trainee nuns (sikkhamānā).
The origin of the offense of matchmaking (sañcaritta) is through action (kriya), is a formal rule (paṇṇatti), and excludes what is naturally wrong (vajja);
it consists of bodily action and verbal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The Discussion on Sewing Robes.
If a monk, having made an appointment with a nun,
should travel along a road together, except on an appropriate occasion, [he commits an offense].
Whether crossing from one village boundary to another, or traveling more than half a yojana,
a monk incurs an offense if he does so in a forest where there is no village.
In this regard, whoever makes an arrangement while standing on improper ground [incurs an offense].
However, for one who makes an appointment, a dukkaṭa offense is declared.
But for one who stands on allowable ground while making an appointment and does not speak with the intent of making an appointment, there is no dukkaṭa.
In both cases, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the monk while he is actually walking;
it occurs when he has stepped into the vicinity (upacāra) of the next village.
Even there, for the first step, a wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is declared.
In the second section on the sequence of steps, a *pācittiya* offense is declared.
Even in the case of making an arrangement in between, there may be a *dukkaṭa* for a monk;
when there is a door, a path, or a signpost, an offense is said to occur.
When it is not the time for distribution, if monks perceive that it is the time for distribution,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding that very act of distribution. Or,
if having distributed it at the proper time, they go away without the agreement [to wait].
There is no offense in cases of misfortune, nor for those who are insane and so forth.
This [offense] has four origins: from body, from body and speech, it originates from body and mind, and from the triad of body, speech, and so forth.
A Discourse on Arrangements:
If one should board a single boat that is either void of strength or full of strength together with a bhikkhunī, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Along the bank of a village, or by way of another village;
along the bank of a non-village, when traveling a half-yojana.
Likewise for one traveling through the middle of a river a yojana wide.
Regarding the measurement of one and a half yojanas, these indeed constitute offenses requiring expiation (pācittiya).
For in all the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā), it is discussed that while there is an offense in a river according to one's pleasure, there is no such offense in the ocean.
If they carry it up or down the river for the purpose of constructing a landing place,
and they are engaged in that task, no offense is declared.
Likewise, if they have made an agreement [to do so], or if they are crossing over horizontally.
For in times of adversity, a distinction is indeed considered equal to the immediate offense.
The Discussion on Boarding a Boat.
Having learned that a meal had been prepared for her, a bhikkhunī ate it.
Having abandoned the undertaking of a householder, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for a bhikkhu.
Food is said to be of five kinds; in taking it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
in all instances of swallowing it, there would be offenses of expiation.
If food is prepared for one’s own relatives and so forth, or even if it is prepared by householders,
there is no fault for a monk who eats it, provided it was not cooked specifically for him by a nun.
For a monk who perceives food as being specially prepared when it is not so prepared, [there is an offense].
In both cases, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who is doubtful about anything.
For one who consumes food prepared by someone ordained on only one side,
there is an offense of wrong-doing simply by the act of swallowing it.
Or whatever else besides the five kinds of cooked food— there is no offense for one consuming rice-gruel,
solid foods, fruits, and so forth. The origins and other characteristics are the same as those of the first and last offenses.
This, however, is a fault of formal rule (paṇṇattivajja), involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
This is the discourse on the ripening [of karma].
The tenth [case] is considered similar to the second undetermined [offense].
This entire training rule, according to its origin, method, and so forth,
concludes the discussion on sitting in private.
The third section, the Chapter on Nuns, is finished.
A single alms-meal at one lodging may be eaten by a monk who is not ill;
beyond that, for one who eats, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Even when [a meal] has been prepared for an unspecified [number of monks], a monk may eat as much as he requires.
One may eat there only once; beyond that, it is not permitted.
On the second day, taking food there is considered a *dukkaṭa* offense;
for every act of swallowing it, a *pācittiya* offense is considered incurred.
Whether prescribed by a single clan or together with various clans,
it is permissible only as a single portion among the various divisions of places.
And that which is prescribed in various places or by various clans—
But when eating at all [alms-rounds], there is no fault if one follows the sequence.
For one who has finished the sequence with the remainder and then eats again,
starting from the beginning, it is not permissible for a bhikkhu.
There is no offense for one who is ill, or for one who is coming or going;
nor for one who eats once from what has been specifically set aside and prepared in small quantities.
However, it is always permissible to consume rice-gruel and similar foods.
The sesame-cake incident is the same regarding its origin and other factors.
Discussion on Lodgings.
Eating in a group is declared to be a *pācittiya* offense, except at the appropriate times.
A "group" (gaṇa), however, is defined as four or more than that.
Whatever food is obtained here— whether by invitation or by request—
it must be one of the five [kinds of] staple foods.
If, having taken up even five kinds of food,
one invites monks— whether four or many— by name alone, saying:
"Please accept and take this rice, this food, this meal," [it is an offense].
Thus, either by synonyms or by another language,
those monks, having accepted that invitation,
go— whether together or separately— and receive [the food] from one [place].
For all [of these], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) on account of eating in a group;
here, "on account of eating in a group" refers to taking [food] together.
Whether going together or separately, or even the act of eating itself—this constitutes eating in a group.
The wise do not call that a "cause" (justification) regarding communal feasting.
Even if one has requested from people— whether from one person or from many— by mentioning the names of the rice and other foods;
If, having gone separately from various places, they take [food] together,
it is still considered "group-eating" (*gaṇabhojana*).
This is described as such because of the act of receiving [the food] for both types [of groups].
It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) and a confession-offense (pācittiya),
as explained regarding the act of swallowing. No offense is declared in seven circumstances,
even when two or three people eat together after taking [food] from one [person].
The Sage has invited those who have not received full ordination to partake of alms-food;
even when these four groups are combined into one, a schism in the Saṅgha is declared.
Indeed, this is by no means the case even on account of those who have obtained [their status] through special agreement.
An offense of schism in the community (gaṇabheda) should be understood by the discerning one as occurring through the eating of the five kinds of food in a group; however,
there is no such designation for rice-gruel and the like, though that [designation] may apply to them in certain contexts.
For a monk who perceives it as eating in a group when it is indeed eating in a group,
or for one who is in doubt about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
This applies to the five kinds of food, excluding rice gruel and the like.
It should be understood that there is no offense even in the case of regular meals and the like.
Likewise for those who are insane and so forth. Furthermore, by way of its origin and other factors, this [offense] is declared to be similar to that of the wool of rams.
The Discourse on Eating in a Group.
A bhikkhu who is invited by many people to [partake of] the five kinds of cooked food;
If, having abandoned an earlier invitation,
one accepts a later invitation for almsfood from anyone among the five [classes of persons]—
or likewise in reverse order— this is a transgression.
If he eats even a single grain of rice, it shall be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, having been invited by anyone to any of the five kinds of food,
he eats another kind of food instead of that [invited meal], it is an offense of expiation.
And among those very five kinds of food, this one was designated by the Great Sage as "successive" (*paramparā*),
provided that milk or juice is poured into it.
That by which food is completely saturated becomes entirely of one flavor.
However, it is specified in the *Mahāpaccarī* that there is no offense for one who consumes it after it has been thoroughly mixed, starting from the very edge.
Regarding "succession": in the case of eating what has not been received through succession, even for one who is in doubt about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for consuming it.
This applies even if [the meal] comes from an entire village, a guild, or a market town.
No fault exists for one who has been invited or for one at a regular meal.
All factors such as the origin and so forth are the same as those for the Kathina robe.
This is stated to be both an action and a non-action, involving eating and the non-delegation of the task.
The Discussion on Successive Eating:
If cakes or flour-pastes have been prepared for the purpose of provisions for a journey,
or if there are other items intended as travel rations, a bhikkhu may [take] those from that place.
Two or three bowls may be accepted, filled with cakes and solid foods;
if he accepts more than that, there is an offense of expiation for the one taking them.
When departing after having taken them, [he should say]: "Two or three bowls have been taken by me here."
But when he sees a monk and says, "The cakes have been taken," if he does not say,
"Do not accept them," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
and for the monk who accepts them after having heard that, there is also an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives a bowl as "excessive" when it contains less than twenty-two bowls' worth,
or if one is in doubt about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Furthermore, if three bowlfuls have been received from that [person], then...
Two portions are to be given to the Saṅgha; if there are two [monks], one [portion] each, not together.
Also, the gift for the journey and provisions, or whatever remains from that;
even when giving what belongs to relatives and others, it must be less than that.
There is no offense even for one who accepts [the gift], nor for one who is insane and so forth.
All factors such as the origin (samuṭṭhāna) and others are considered identical to the case of a go-between. The Discourse on the Mother of the One-Eyed Man.
But if one who has been invited to five kinds of staple foods eats again food that is not left over, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). [The factors are:
the food, the staple food itself, and the act of taking it within arm's reach.
The rejection of body and speech, and the invitation ceremony with its five factors.
Rice, parched grain, boiled rice, fish, and meat—
these five kinds of food are taught in their entirety by the one free from conceptual proliferation (nippapañca).
There, "odana" is considered to be the boiled rice of seven kinds of grain;
however, the powder of roasted grains is called "sattu.
"Kummāsa" refers to barley gruel, while "maccha" refers to fish.
Even my own meat is allowable meat; this is the decision in this matter.
Rice, paddy, barley, millet, varaka, wheat, and kudrūsaka—these seven grains have been taught as grain by means of grain.

The other should reply, "Tissa, Tissa.

Having assigned it among those of the same Dhamma— among any of the five [groups]—

Knowing the water contains living beings, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who uses it;

There is bodily action, vocal action, non-action, and painful feeling. This concludes the discussion on indecent speech (*duṭṭhullakathā*).
