Having set aside other requisites, if one speaks in disparagement after giving [the robe], it is a Dukkaṭa offense.
Even for one not authorized by the Saṅgha, [giving] a robe or something else;
likewise toward one who is not fully ordained—in all such cases there is a dukkaṭa offense.
This is because of acting according to one's own will and so forth, and because of the inherent nature of the act.
There is no offense for one who is ceasing [the act], as well as for one who is insane and so forth.
The methods such as the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and others should be known as being the same as those for the groundless charge (*amūlaka*). This concludes the discussion on weak cases.
In this [chapter], the twelfth section is entirely identical to the final section of the Tiṃsakakaṇḍa; this alone is the distinction.
Therein, what was stated as *nissaggiya* (to be relinquished) concerns its dedication to oneself.
Herein, it is a simple offense of expiation (pācittiya) regarding the person, [arising] from the act of diverting [the gift].
This concludes the discussion on diverting. The eighth chapter, the Section on Fellow-Practitioners (sahadhammika-vagga), is finished.
If the king has not yet departed and the queen has not yet departed from his bedchamber,
whoever crosses the threshold commits a dukkaṭa for the first step and a pācittiya for the second.
Whether it belongs to the queen or the king, if one has not learned its provenance,
a dukkaṭa offense is declared for one who, when it has been announced, perceives it as unannounced, or who is in doubt about it.
Neither for one who possesses clear perception, nor for a Kṣatriya,
nor even for one consecrated by the Kṣatriya coronation rite—
when both have departed from each other, or even when they have gone beyond the range of sight.
There is no performance or non-performance of the *kathina* ceremony for those who are insane and so forth.
Discussion on the inner palace.
Regarding silver or gold, for one who takes them for oneself;
For him there is an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya-āpatti), whether he causes it to be acquired or not.
For a group, an individual, a Saṅgha, for building work, or for a shrine—
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who causes it to be acquired or even for one who receives it.
For one who acquires the remaining jewels, such as pearls,
either for oneself or for the sake of the Saṅgha and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
This applies whether the object is a permissible thing or an impermissible thing.
Whether it be a palm-leaf fan or an earring for the mother’s ear—
whatever belongs to a layperson, even if held under the pretext that it is the property of the storekeeper—
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who takes it back [without permission].
If someone says, "Give this back after setting it aside," one should not deposit that item at all after saying, "It is not permitted.
And if a person, having been told "Set it aside," drops it and then departs;
This indeed is called an impediment, yet it is permissible to set it aside. However,
if one has learned [the rules] in a permitted place,
but through negligence does not properly put them down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, in a place where permission has been granted, for one who takes a jewel and deposits it properly,
or for one who receives a commodity considered a jewel on trust, or even for a temporary loan;
It does not apply to those who are insane and so forth, nor to one who acts as a go-between. This concludes the Discourse on the Jewels.
From the time after midday until before the rising of the sun;
In this interval, it is called "time" (kāla) or "non-time" (vikāla).
Without having asked a present bhikkhu for permission, and without the requisite [robe-material], at a non-time,
or upon crossing the boundary of an enclosed village— these are the occasions [for an offense].
In the case of an unenclosed village, even when one has merely stepped into its precincts,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the first step, and it becomes an offense of expiation (pācittiya) at the second.
Furthermore, if many [monks] enter a village at an improper time:
One must depart only after taking leave; not otherwise from one another.
If they go elsewhere than that, it is permissible to say "to another than that";
there is no need for taking leave again, even if it is a hundred villages away.
Having calmed their zeal, they have gone out for the sake of dwelling;
if they enter another [house], they should ask about what is in between.
Having performed the meal-duty at a family home or elsewhere, however—
If one wishes to go out for alms, whether for ghee or other requisites, one must depart only after having requested permission, provided that another monk is available to see [to the task].
However, if no such person is present, it is said there is no need [for permission]; one may then go as one pleases.
If, having descended onto the main road, one sees a bhikkhu, there is no need for formal permission; one may proceed as one pleases.
This applies even when a bhikkhu is traveling along a path through the middle of a village.
When the thought has arisen, "I shall go," for the purpose of seeking oil as alms,
one must depart only after having taken leave, provided that another monk is present.
For one who goes without stepping off [the path], what is the use of taking leave regarding the way?

There is an offense of expiation for three [cases]: when it is the right time, one perceives it as the wrong time; and when it is the right time, one is in doubt. There is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) even for one who is in doubt when it is the right time.
Having asked for permission when [the preceptor] is present, or not asking when he is absent;
When a bhikkhu enters [a village] for some urgent business,
or while walking through a monastery, a nunnery,
a rest-house, or a hermitage of non-Buddhist sectarians;
If the path were through a village, there would be no offense even for minor transgressions;
all [factors] such as the origin and so forth are considered identical to those of the *kathina* robe.
It is not only by failing to ask permission, but also by failing to fasten what ought to be fastened.
There is no offense even when going about without having put on the outer robe (saṅghāṭi).
This concludes the discussion on entering a village at an improper time.
[Regarding needles: they may be made of bone, ivory, or even horn; or they may be housed in a case.
In having [a bowl] made or in making it oneself, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the bhikkhu.
Upon its acquisition, if it is a bowl that causes division, a pācittiya is declared;
the same applies to making it or having it made for the sake of another.
If one obtains and consumes what has been prepared by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense in the case of a water-strainer, a needle-case, or even a thimble;
nor in the case of a water-wiper, a razor-hilt, or for one who is insane, and so forth.
The methods beginning with origination (*samuṭṭhāna*) are considered to be the same as those for the offense of acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*).
The discourse on the needle-case (*sūcighara-kathā*). A monk who has a new bed or bench made:
It should be made with a measurement of eight finger-breadths according to the Sugata’s finger-breadth,
excluding the lower rim; if it is cut short, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya),
and if it exceeds that [measurement], there is likewise an offense.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for making it for another’s sake, likewise for having it made, and for using what has been obtained made by another.
There is no offense for one who makes it according to the proper measure, or for one who uses what exceeds the measure.
Having obtained it, while cutting and consuming it from his feet;
or, if he does not wish to cut it, having buried it to its full extent,
or having tied it up— whether face-up or face-down— while consuming it.
The Discourse on the Couch:
Furthermore, whoever should have a couch or a chair upholstered with cotton down,
for him it is declared that there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) due to impropriety.
There is no offense, however, for a monk in the case of a yoke, a binding, a shoulder-strap, a bolster, a water-strainer, or in bags and such; likewise,
when he obtains something made by another and uses it after having had it unsewn.
The method for this [offense] is the same as that for acting as a go-between.
The Discussion on the Cotton-Filled [Rug].
When making a sitting mat, it must be made according to the prescribed measurement.
If it exceeds the proper measure, there shall be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of undertaking it.
Upon its acquisition, if it is cut down, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is declared.
Having split it into two places, it shall have three fringes.
There is no offense for one who makes it to the proper measure, or for one making it less than that;
for one making a canopy and so forth, the principle is the same as for a go-between.
Discussion on the sitting mat.
A covering for itch-disease must indeed be made according to the prescribed measure.
If it exceeds that measure, there shall be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of making it.
By the mere acquisition [of such a garment], a forfeiture-requiring offense (pācittiya) is declared upon its cutting up.
The method for non-offenses here is considered to be the same as in the immediately preceding case.
The discussion on the itch-covering cloth:
it must be made according to the proper measure, and likewise the rainy-season robe.
Regarding the transgression of its measure, the method is the same as for the preceding case.
This is the discussion on the rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*).
If it is equal in measure to the robe of the Sugata, however—
If a monk should have a robe made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) at the time of making it.
Upon its acquisition, if there is a cutting [of the cloth], an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is declared.
This very sequence of immediate [offenses] is considered the method for non-offense.
In length, its measurement is nine spans of the Sugata’s span;
across, it is prescribed as six.
If one uses what has been made by another and obtained [as a gift], there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
All [factors] beginning with the origins are considered equal to the act of matchmaking.
The Discourse on Nanda.
The Ninth Chapter: The Section on Kings.
Thus ends the discussion on the *pācittiya* offenses in the Vinaya-vinicchaya.
Now, the discussion on the *pāṭidesanīya* offenses:
"If a monk, from the hand of a woman who has entered within the house..."
If a monk should, with his own hand, accept from an unrelated woman anything whatsoever—
whether solid food or soft food— the offense for the act of receiving is *dukkaṭa*; upon consuming it, it becomes a *pāṭidesanīya*.
Whether standing on a street, in a military formation, at a junction or a crossroads,
or in an elephant stable and such places— this same principle applies even to one who takes [the food].
If a bhikkhunī, standing on a street, gives food;
If a monk stands within the monastery grounds and takes [the robe], there is an offense.
For once she has entered the interior of the house,
the standing place of the monk is described as not being the determining factor according to her words.
Therefore, there is no fault for one who receives [food] from a nun standing in a monastery or similar place;
nor is there any fault for the receiver if she is standing on a street or similar public place.
This applies to food that is to be consumed within a watch of the night, within seven days, or throughout life.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in taking [the food] for the purpose of eating, and also in swallowing it.
This was said with reference to that which has not had its flavor mixed with [other] material things;
if the flavor is mixed, there may be an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
For one who receives from the hand of one who is fully ordained,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the sake of food, even regarding all four types of timely food.
This applies also when one perceives a relative as a non-relative, or when one is in doubt.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who perceives the woman as a relative, or likewise for one who gives to a woman who is not a relative.
There is no offense for her who causes [the gift] to be given, or for her who gives herself;
nor is there an offense for her who, having set aside [the object], stands within the monastery or elsewhere and gives it.
If she brings it out from the village and gives it, it is permissible outside;
if she gives it with the thought, "Eat when there is a requisite," it is permissible during the three meal-times.
Likewise, [food] from the hands of female novices (sāmaṇerī) or a trainee nun (sikkhamānā).
This [offense] is considered to have the same origin as that involving sheep’s wool.
The Discussion on the First Pāṭidesanīya.
Regarding the phrase "having spoken, one should depart," it refers even to a single bhikkhu.
If one accepts food for the purpose of consuming it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) at the time of receiving;
upon consuming it, it becomes an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
There is an offense of wrong-doing for one who does not prevent a person fully ordained on only one side [of the Saṅgha] from doing so.
Likewise, for one who perceives as ordained those who are not ordained,
or for one who is in doubt regarding that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is no offense if she causes her own meal to be prepared, provided she does not give it away.
Likewise, if she does not cause another's meal to be given, or if she causes it to be served;
if she causes that which was not given to be given, or wherever it was not given—
therein the bhikkhunī causes that also to be given equally to all.
Whether she is living apart, a trainee nun (sikkhamānā), or a novice nun (sāmaṇerikā);
regarding the five kinds of food, it is declared that [the offense] arises together with the kaṭhina robe, except in cases such as insanity.
This has been stated regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done, as well as the three types of consciousness and the three types of feeling.
This concludes the discussion on the second *pāṭidesanīya* offense.
Regarding the term "one in training" (*sekkha*): it refers to a monk who is so recognized, or to a family that has received formal authorization.
If one who is not ill, having entered the vicinity of a house and not previously invited,
should take and consume food, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the taking, and it shall be an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya) in the consumption.
Regarding [food] kept for a watch of the night, for seven days, or for as long as life lasts:
in both taking it up and in consuming it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
This applies even if one perceives what is approved for those beyond training (asekkha) as being approved for those still in training (sekha).
In that regard, it is explained in the same way for one who is in doubt.
There is no offense for one who is ill, or for one who is slightly ill;
nor is there an offense for one invited [to a meal] who gives alms-food there to others.
If they give it anywhere after having brought it out from the house,
or even in the case of regular meals and so forth, as well as for those who are insane and the like;
for indeed, when the bhikkhu has not yet arrived, first from the house—
If, having brought [the food] out, they give it once the [monk] has arrived at the door, it is permissible.
However, if they bring it out from the house only after seeing the monk and then give it, it is not permissible;
this case arises like the simile of the ewe.
The Discussion of the Third Pāṭidesanīya:
If, however, having entered a monastery or its precincts, whether as a householder or a non-householder, a woman or a man, [one should accept food].
“‘Such-and-such a person’s meal or rice-gruel is being brought for you’—
this is what is called ‘informing’ when it has been stated thus.
It may be brought later, or exactly as it was announced.”
Or, having prepared a large amount of other accompaniments for him,
if they bring rice porridge, cakes, and cooked food after making them known [as such],
this too is called "known" (vidita) and is permitted according to the Kurundi.
If other families or one's own property to be given away are carried along with it, all that is likewise permissible.
This applies even to what has not been announced and what has not been brought from the monastery.
That which is called "unnoticed" is what has been announced according to the rule.
Having made it unnoticed, however, that which has been brought outside,
one should send it back to the monastery and have it brought in after it has been prepared.
Or having gone along the way, it should be accepted by the bhikkhu;
if he does not do so, then from the vicinity of the monastery,
upon taking it and swallowing it, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of taking.
Regarding the modes of swallowing food, this is considered a *pāṭidesanīya* offense.
If one perceives that the food has been announced when it has indeed been announced,
or if one is in doubt about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
When it has been announced to him, or when there is leftover food for the sick;
or when he takes [food] outside the monastery, or while he is eating inside it;
or when he eats fruits and such grown right there—there is no offense.
All [factors] beginning with the origin (samuṭṭhāna) are considered equal to those of the Kathina [robe].
The Discussion on the Fourth Pāṭidesanīya.
Thus ends the Discussion on the Pāṭidesanīyas in the Vinaya-vinicchaya.
Regarding the Discussion on the Training Rules: Whoever, out of disrespect, should wear his lower robe hanging down either in front or behind,
incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
But for one who wears it like an elephant's trunk and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
one who fears transgression should always wear the robe evenly all around.
Below the circle of the knees, it should measure eight finger-breadths.
Having lowered it, it must be worn; less than that is not permitted.
There is no offense for one who acts unintentionally, or for one who is merely absent-minded, or for one who is ill, or for one who is insane, and so forth.
The Discourse on the Circular Fold:
Having made both corners even and having respectfully formed a circular fold, one should indeed wear the robe in this manner;
for one who does not do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
But since these two training rules are stated without distinction,
therefore, whether in a house or in a monastery, one should dress in a perfectly circular manner.
Second.
Having fastened the toggle and made both ends even at the corners,
having covered the wrist and the neck, one should go.
Without doing so for a monk, [one should cover] the navel and the chest as well.
If one opens [the door] and goes away as one pleases, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
This is the third [offense].
Above the throat and above the wrist, the head [is measured].
If one sits having exposed the flesh of the buttocks on the hands, both parts below the feet,
and the rest, while covering [the private parts],
he is well-concealed; there is no fault for one who has approached a dwelling.
The fourth [verse]:
A bhikkhu, not moving either hand or foot, should walk with well-restrained conduct;
there is no distinction in the sixth [verse].
The fifth and sixth [precepts]:
A bhikkhu should walk with mindfulness, looking only a yoke’s length ahead,
well-restrained, and with downcast eyes.
In any place whatsoever, even within a single house or interval,
it is permissible to look about to see whether there are any dangers.
However, he who looks here and there while showing disrespect—
Going into another’s house while naked is likewise the eighth offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
These are the seventh and eighth.
Having been on one side or both sides, with the robe lifted up;
If one goes inside from the boundary marker (indakhīlaka), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Ninth.
Likewise, while sitting, when drawing out the water-pot (kuṇḍikā);
It should be given after having been set aside; there is no fault for one who has entered the rainy-season residence. Tenth.
The First Chapter.
It is not permissible to go about or sit down while laughing;
however, when there is a cause for laughter, merely smiling is permitted.
This concludes the first and second [rules].
One should walk with little noise; this same principle applies to the fourth [offense] as well.
For one who makes a loud noise, there is an *dukkaṭa* offense in both cases.
[These are] the third and fourth.
If one walks shaking the body, shaking the arms, or shaking the head, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); and likewise for one who sits so.
However, having held the body, the arms, and the head straight, [one may walk].
One should walk and sit with a composed posture.
For one who has entered a residence among those engaged in the three types of sitting mats,
it should be understood by the wise who know the Vinaya that there is no offense.
The Second Chapter.
For one who walks leaning on a staff, or with a head-covering, or having wrapped [the robe] around [the head],
or likewise squatting on the heels— the Sage has declared this to be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he sits in a house with his hands folded over his lap,
or with his robe folded over his lap, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
This applies when entering for the second, fourth, or sixth meal.
"Non-offense" means those that are appropriate; twenty-six types have been explained. Sixth.
By a bhikkhu who is careful, endowed with mindfulness, and conscious of his bowl;
Almsfood should be accepted by the wise man with equal curry.
Soup that is one-fourth of the rice is called "equal curry";
soup made of mung beans, black gram, or peas is called "soup."
There is no offense if it was unintentional, if one is ill, if it is for various flavors,
or likewise if it is for the sake of relatives and so forth, or with wealth for another purpose.
These are the seventh, eighth, and ninth [rules].
It should be taken as if filled up to the rim of the bowl's mouth according to the measure of its brim,
provided it is suitable for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
For one who takes it by making it into a heap there, it remains "to be used at the proper time" (*yāvakālika*).
Whatever offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) a monk may have incurred:

in the case of a bowl that has reached the stage of formal determination, as well as the three types of time-bound food, and all the rest when heaped together, it is certainly permissible; of this there is no doubt.
If, having taken food from two bowls,
one fills a single bowl and sends it, it is permissible for the monks.
Whatever— such as pieces of sugarcane or fruit— is being placed into the bowl [is likewise permissible].
If it ascends from below, it would not be "placed like a stupa.
If, setting aside flowers such as *takkola* and the like,
one offers a *vaṭaṃsaka* (ear-ornament) without applying black lacquer, that too would not be "placed like a stupa."
If they give almsfood by placing a flower ornament on top of the rice, this would be "placed like a stupa.
Or if there is a leaf, a bowl, or anything else placed upon the food—
Setting it aside and filling it up, if he takes it, it is permissible.
However, it is not permissible for him to receive all of that at once;
once it has been taken properly, it may afterwards be consumed as he pleases.
The Third Chapter.
Regarding the first and second [sections], the method has already been stated;
however, in the third, after demonstrating that which obstructs, one should eat in successive order.
But when one pours one's own food into the bowl of others, there is no fault provided there is no negligence; the same applies to additional curry.
Third.
Whatever was to be said regarding the fourth [offense] has been stated in its entirety previously;
in the fifth, the fault reaches its peak for one who consumes [food] after having crushed it.
There is no offense for one who is ill, nor when only a small remnant remains.
But for one who eats after having mashed it on one side and gathered it together—
these are the fourth and fifth [offenses].
Whoever, out of a desire for more, [takes] either curry or sauce...
If one should conceal [the offense] by means of food, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for him.
This is the sixth [case].
Regarding the act of requesting, however, nothing new at all needs to be said.
But in the eighth case of complaining, even one who is ill is not exempt.
It should be known that there is no offense for a monk who looks [at the food] thinking, "I will give it" or "I will have it given," provided he does not perceive it as complaining.
Eighth. However, a peacock’s egg is large, while a hen’s egg is small;
a mouthful should be made with a size between those two.
But regarding chewable foods, in all cases— whether they be roots,
hard foods, fruits, or other such items— there is no offense for one who is ill, insane, or otherwise [legitimately exempt]. Ninth.
But it should not be made long; the mouthful should be round.
There is no offense regarding snacks, subsequent food, or fruits.
The tenth [chapter].
The Fourth Chapter.
Regarding food not yet brought to one's mouth, or when the morsel has not yet reached the mouth,
as well as for one who opens his own mouth [before the food arrives], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
First:
For one who thrusts an entire hand into the mouth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
and it is not permitted to speak while having a mouthful of food in the mouth.
If his speech is not complete for as long as it should be,
then while he is speaking with that much remaining in his mouth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For one who speaks after having placed harītakī or other such things in the mouth, [the same applies].
If the statement is complete, it is permissible to speak.
This applies to the second and third [instances].
Also, regarding a monk who throws up his alms-food, or one who cuts off mouthfuls;
Or like a monkey with its cheeks, one commits a *dukkaṭa* offense by eating.
[These are] the fourth, fifth, and sixth [rules].
Having shaken off food from the hand or scattering grains of rice upon the meal;
Whether it be sticking out the tongue or making the sound "capu capū," a *dukkaṭa* offense occurs for one who eats with an attitude of disrespect.
There is no fault in the seventh or eighth [instances] when clearing away refuse.
The Seven Intoxications.
The Fifth Chapter.
Having prepared it thus, one should not eat it while making the sound "suru surū."
Nor is it permissible to eat from a hand-plate. However,
having taken molasses or thick gruel with one's fingers,
it is permissible to place those fingers into the mouth and eat.
The bowl must not be licked, nor with a single finger;
nor even with a single lip, nor must it be licked with the tongue.
Fourth.
One should not grasp it with a hand that has food on it, nor should one grasp the water vessel;
this is prohibited because of its repulsiveness.
This applies to an individual, to the Saṅgha, to a householder, and even to a monastic.
However, if it belongs to another—whether it be a conch shell, a saucer, or even a shallow bowl—it must not be taken;
for one who takes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
But taking it with a hand that is free of food is permitted.
The fifth [offense].
Having lifted it up, or having broken it, or having taken it into a receiving vessel,
there is no offense for one who carries it out and discards it outside the house.
Sixth. If one teaches the Dhamma while another person is holding a sunshade— whether with their hand or with a limb of the body—
it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Seventh.
This same method is stated regarding a person holding a staff:
the staff is four cubits in measure, from the middle of the hand.
The eighth:
Likewise, if one teaches the Dhamma to someone holding a weapon, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"I was not one holding a weapon," [he says], "but I was standing there with my sword girded."
The ninth:
Having taken a bow together with an arrow, or a bow alone,
or even an arrow alone, or likewise a strung or unstrung bow-staff.
Whether standing, sitting, or likewise lying down,
if one teaches the True Dhamma, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Even if a bow is fastened around one's neck, as long as it is held by the hand...
A person does not grasp [the teaching] as long as [he is so situated]; it is permissible to teach the Dhamma.
The sixth chapter.
Even for one who has put on sandals, teaching the Dhamma is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The same rule applies whether one has stepped upon it and remains there, or has already put it on.
First.
This same analysis also applies to footwear.
In all cases for one who is not ill—whether in a vehicle or on a bed;
for one who is not ill while lying down on a straw mat or on the bare ground;
or while sitting on a high stool or couch, or while standing.
It is not permissible to teach while standing on high ground,
