If one takes anything whatsoever belonging to a human being,
in that taking of material goods,
a grave offense (thullaccaya) is declared.
If one swallows [it], it is a *saṅghādisesa*; the others [offenses] arise from the preliminary effort (*payoga*).
If one accepts anything while it is raining from one side, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
In the acts of swallowing, there may be an accumulation of grave offenses (thullaccaya) [if the food is not properly prepared].
[This applies] when receiving from the hands of yakkhas, petas, animals, or paṇḍakas;
likewise, when receiving from those with human form, or from those who are hermaphrodites.

In this case, regarding one who is lustful on one side, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the taking of water, tooth-sticks, the grasping [of the woman], and the enjoyment [of the act]— in all these instances.
If he takes [the woman] when both are free from lust, there is no fault.
"But she who takes [it] knowing, 'He is not lustful'— for her,
no offense is declared for those such as one who is insane.
The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other factors are the same as for the first and last cases."
Fifth. In the case of one woman’s incitement and the other’s acceptance,
there are offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding the enjoyments, and the group [of monks] would incur a grave offense (thullaccaya).
At the conclusion of a meal, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* for all four types of non-human beings,
such as *yakkhas*, and likewise for a human male.
Furthermore, this applies when one provides or encourages the use of tooth-sticks and water.
For using those [items], a dukkaṭa offense is proclaimed.
But for the remaining items belonging to yakkhas and others,
there is a dukkaṭa for taking them or employing them, and a thullaccaya is declared for consuming them.
Whether she knows him to be "not lustful," or does not accept [the proposal] because he is angry,
or even out of compassion for the family— yet she sends him away; for her,
no offense is declared, provided she is insane or otherwise [exempt].
The methods regarding origin and so forth are similar to those for taking what is not given.
This is the sixth [offense]. The seventh and eighth are considered similar to the schism of the Saṅgha.
In terms of their origination and so forth, there is no difference whatsoever.
[This applies to] the seventh and eighth [rules].
Regarding the ninth or even the tenth, there is nothing at all that needs to be said.
The methods beginning with origination (samuṭṭhāna) apply only to the immediately preceding [offenses].
[These are] the ninth and tenth [rules].
Also by the two faults of being corrupt and the fault of being a go-between—by that, there are six.
The eight [offenses] involving a third admonition, and the four [offenses] here and there:
this is the Discussion on the Saṅghādisesa [Offenses]. The Discussion on the Nissaggiya [Pācittiya Offenses].
If a bhikkhunī should keep a bowl that requires formal determination for even a single day—
without having determined it or made a formal assignment of it—
then simultaneously with the rising of the dawn, she would incur an offense.
For this [offense], there is a *nissaggiya* offense due to the act of storing a bowl.
As for the rest of the procedure, the entire method of exposition regarding the training rule on bowls here is to be understood according to the very same principle already stated.
When there is an exceeding of ten days in that case, and an exceeding of one day here;
this indeed is the distinction between these two.
First.
If a robe is given out of season, or even if it is given at the proper time by someone,
yet it is specifically designated with the instruction, "When [the monks] have assembled,
let them divide it," then that out-of-season robe is considered a "robe for the proper time. However, if...
And she should cause it to be shared out; for the act of so doing, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Whatever she has obtained for herself, that indeed shall be subject to relinquishment (nissaggiya);
having received it, once it has been relinquished, she should employ it according to the manner of its distribution.
But having performed the disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*), even if that [robe] is obtained again,
it is not permitted for him to make use of it. If there is a perception that it is the wrong time regarding a robe that is actually timely,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
It is demonstrated in both cases, as is the case for one who is doubtful.
Regarding the perception of it being the right time or a robe, in both instances concerning the robe, there is no fault;
for those such as the insane, it is considered to have three origins.
The second [offense].
Even when many robes have been tied together and set aside,
there would be only a single offense if one takes them away oneself.
Likewise, in the case of having [something] cut, there is one offense under one formal injunction (*āṇatti*);
in the other cases, it depends on the application (*payoga*) of the various bases.
There is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses for another [object], but for requisites (*parikkhāra*), it is an *dukkaṭa*.
The threefold *dukkaṭa* has been indicated; however, regarding the robe of the other [nun], there is no offense for one who receives it when it is being given by her, or when it is on loan to her.
This is considered to have three origins.
The third [offense].
If, after having requested one thing, she requests something else instead;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for her due to the act of requesting, and upon acquisition, it becomes an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya).
A triple offense of expiation (pācittiya) is stated [for the first case];

for those other than these, there are two offenses of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Furthermore, there is an offense when one perceives another as not another, or when it is insufficient; or again, when that very thing is another, or when another is used even though the purpose is served by that other.
When one points out the benefits and persuades another [to commit misconduct], it should be known that there is no offense; the same applies to one who is insane.
The methods regarding their origin and so forth are stated to be identical to those for a go-between.
The fourth [case]:
Having caused one thing to be bartered for, he should later cause another thing to be bartered for, thinking:
"He brings and gives me grain that was bartered for something else."
Through the act of causing [an object] to be obtained, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the one who is the basis [of the transaction];
upon acquisition, it becomes an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), whether brought by that person or by another.
One should designate the remainder as being similar to the immediately preceding case.
There is nothing new whatsoever regarding the origins and so forth.
Fifth. [The offense] which occurs through the use of requisites given for another purpose...
If a nun here should have something made by others using property belonging to the Saṅgha,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort, and upon acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya) for her.
In this case, regarding that which is not intended for another, two offenses of wrong-doing are specified.
The remainder [of the training rules] are for other purposes; there is no offense for one who returns [the robe];
having asked the owner, or even for one who has fallen ill, or for one who is insane.
They are said to be equal to the rule on matchmaking (sañcaritta) regarding their origin (samuṭṭhāna) and other methods.
The seventh is similar to the sixth, except for the absence of "one's own" and "borrowed.
These are the sixth and seventh.
Regarding the eighth or the ninth, there is nothing whatsoever to be said.
“By one who has the perception that it is a group [of people]” is the heading for the section.
In the tenth [offense], all the discourse is considered identical to the immediately preceding one;
there is no difference whatsoever regarding its origin and other such factors.
The eighth, ninth, and tenth [offenses].
The first chapter.
[The offenses concerning] more than four *kaṃsa* measures, and heavy outer garments;
If she should cause it to be made by that [nun], an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated for the undertaking; upon acquisition, it is considered a forfeiture (nissaggiya).
A quantity of four kahāpaṇas, however, is called "brass" (kaṃsa).
But for one who [exchanges] less than four kaṃsas, two dukkaṭas are prescribed;
however, there is no offense for exchanging up to four kaṃsas, even if it is a heavy [offense].
If she causes [it] to be exchanged for less than that, or if it belongs to her relatives, [there is no offense].
Whether for the sake of another, or for one's own wealth,
or for a nun who is intoxicated with self-importance; whether she procures [the robe] at a high price, or even if she is merely procuring it—
regarding its origin and all other factors, it is considered identical to the offense of acting as a go-between.
Eleventh. However, a light cloak worth two and a half *kaṃsa*s;
if a bhikkhunī causes one to be procured for more than that, [she commits an offense].
For this [offense], there is a *nissaggiya* offense, followed by a *pācittiya*;
the remainder is identical to the immediately preceding [rule], with no distinction whatsoever.
The twelfth.
The remaining ones are common;
those eighteen as well as these twelve indeed total thirty.
The Discussion on Forfeiture.
Regarding the discussion on the *pācittiya* offenses:
garlic is said to be a "bundle," not that which consists of one, two, or three cloves;
it must be raw Magadhan garlic that one takes up with the intention, "I shall eat it."
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for her upon taking it; if she eats it, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One should explain that it is an offense of expiation specifically by way of swallowing.
However, if she chews two or three morsels together, [it is an offense].
If she swallows one [kernel] of it, there shall be one *pācittiya*.
But for her who eats the kernels after breaking them up one by one,
there shall be a number of *pācittis* according to the number of kernels.
The onion (*palaṇḍuka*), the *bhañjanaka*, the green one (*harita*), and the *cāpalopi*;
furthermore, the four types of garlic (*lasuṇa*)—these are indeed permissible by their very nature.
The onion is pale in color, and the *bhañjanaka* is red.
The *harita* is green in color, as is the *cāpala*, though the latter is also white.
There is one seed-pulp (*miñjā*) in an onion, there may be two in a *bhañjana*, and three in a *haritaka*; the *cāpala*, however, is without a seed-pulp.

In the case of the cooking of meat with broth and so forth, and in the case of *sāḷava* and *uttaribhaṅga*, there is no fault regarding the origin [of the offense] for those such as *ummattika*; it is like the simile of the ewe.
First.
If she causes even a single hair to be removed from the cramped areas of the armpits or from the pubic region, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Likewise, if she causes many hairs to be removed, it is the same.
This is by way of the application [of the hair], not by way of counting every single hair.
There is no fault for one who gathers the hair when there is an affliction;
its origin and other characteristics are considered identical to those of the preparation for the Path.
The second [offense].
There is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) even for striking the glans penis with one's hand,
or through passion for the hair, or for a lotus.
If there is a boil or a wound there, there is no offense for the one who strikes.
The origin and other factors are the same as in the first and last cases.
Third.
But if a nun, overcome by sensual lust, inserts even a lotus leaf into her own anus, it is not permitted.
This case of the "eightfold wax" was stated specifically by way of the physical object.
Whether it be with a stick, a melāḷuka fruit, or even by means of urine,
if she consents to the contact and he inserts it,
or if he causes it to be inserted therein, there shall be a *pācittiya* offense for her.
There is an offense due to the condition of illness, or for one who is insane;
the origin and other factors are considered identical to those of the *talaghātaka* (slapping with the palm).
The fourth [section].
However, for one who inserts more than two finger-joints of two fingers into [the anus] while performing a cleansing with water, it is a *pācittiya* offense.
There are three joints in length on a single finger.
If she causes it to enter [the vagina] by inserting even a single joint of four or three fingers— whether from the width or the depth—
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her.
Thus, in every respect, this meaning has been elucidated, having been made even more distinct by the Mahāpaccarī.
There is no fault in [a toothpick] being two finger-breadths long, as it does not cause any affliction.
Even when inserting more [fingers] while performing purification with water,
likewise for those who are insane and so forth, it is declared that there is no offense.
All factors such as the origin (samuṭṭhāna) and the rest are considered identical to the "striking the palm" (talaghāta) rule.
Fifth: If one should stand before a monk who is eating, holding either drinking water or a fan,
there is an offense of expiation for her.
Flavors such as milk, buttermilk, and so forth, are apprehended by water alone.
And whatever is called a "fan"—such as the corner of a cloth and the like—is also included.
Here, the offense consisting of the condition of being within arm's reach is illustrated.
The offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) mentioned in the Khandhaka regarding striking is distinct.
Furthermore, for one who stands up after leaving the reach of the hand,
or while [the other] is eating, there is an offense of wrong-doing for eating [what has been left behind].
There is no offense if she gives [the robe] herself or causes it to be given; likewise for one who is insane.
This origin is considered the same as that of the *eḷakaloma* (wool) rule.
The sixth.
If a bhikkhunī, having recognized raw grain, roasts it, pounds it,
and cooks it, she incurs a *pācittiya* offense when she consumes it.
It is not only for the taking of grain that there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Also in the carrying away of grain, as well as in its drying;
in the preparation of the pan and the hearth for the roasting of grain;
in the kindling of the fire and the preparation of the ladle and the pan.
In the placing of grain there, the stirring and scraping with a ladle,
and all such actions as the shaking [of the bowl], constitute a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Indeed, in this case, the measure consists of both the food and the solicitation.
Whether she herself has learned [the method] from another regarding frying and so forth, or having had another learn it, or having had it done by another,
or having done it herself— whosoever then consumes [the food].
In the various methods of swallowing food, there would be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her;
even if she has requested it from her mother, there is an offense of expiation when she consumes it.
Whether she herself performs the roasting and so forth, or causes them to be done, [there is an offense].
If she eats what she has obtained herself without having requested it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
But if she has obtained it through another request, or by her own request,
or even if she has had it made or prepared for her, there is likewise an offense for her when she consumes it.
For the purpose of begging for work and so forth, or for the solicitation of grain—
excluding the seven types of grain— and also for the solicitation of anything else:
it should be known that there is no offense, as well as in the case of one who is insane.
Furthermore, raw grain from one's own kinsmen is not permitted.
What is obtained without prior solicitation is permitted for use in new construction projects.
All factors, beginning with the origin, are considered to be the same as those for the [prohibition on] long-distance travel.
Seventh: One should not discard feces, urine, rubbish,
or food scraps over a wall, nor cause others to discard them there.

For her, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); this same method applies even regarding a wall. However, for one who discards [the robe], it is shown that there is a single offense for each act, or multiple offenses.
Furthermore, these four bases [of offenses] in their entirety—
It may be [an offense] for one who discards [a tooth-stick] with a single act of application.
This same method should be understood by the discerning one even in the case of an instruction;
thus is the Pācittiya regarding the discarding of a tooth-stick clearly explained.
In all such cases, however, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the bhikkhunī,
whether she is in a place where there is no danger of falling, or even after looking around.
There is no offense for one who is discarding [the robe], nor likewise for one who is insane.
The origin of the offense of acting as a go-between may be either intentional or unintentional. This is the eighth [offense].
Furthermore, whether it be in a field or in a grove such as a coconut plantation;
If a bhikkhunī plants [seeds] in a green area anywhere at all,
these are the four bases [for offense]. If she herself discards them,
or causes them to be discarded, the determination of the offense is according to the method already stated.
If one sits down while eating, or likewise in a green field;
or if one goes there while chewing sugarcane and such things;
or if one discards waste, water, or scraps of food—[one incurs an offense].
For her there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya), and for the monk there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
There may be an offense for one who discards [water] even in a place where there is but a little water;
likewise for one who drinks coconut water that has been cut at the top.
But when the site has been ploughed and the seed has been sown,
as long as the sprout has not yet emerged, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for all [involved].
Even if the field has been harvested, if people guard it again...
For the sake of its growth there, it remains exactly as it was in its original place.
There is no fault in discarding [the seed] once the field has been cleared;
however, for one who discards everything, all factors—starting from the origin and so forth—are considered identical to those of the eighth [offense].
Nine: Should a bhikkhunī go for the purpose of seeing dancing, singing, or even instrumental music,
it shall be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her.
For one who goes for the purpose of seeing a dance or for hearing a song,
there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each step taken.
If she looks and sees [the performance] with a single effort, [she incurs the full offense].
If she hears their singing, one *pācittiya* is explained.
But if she sees a dance in another direction and hears singing from elsewhere, there would be separate *pācittiyas*.
In this case, the counting of the offense is according to the number of performances;
a bhikkhunī herself may not dance or sing.
It is not permitted to say, "Tell someone else to dance or sing."
When it is said, “Let us attend upon [the Buddha],” to accept [this] constitutes an offense.
In all such cases, there is a *pācittiya* for the nun, and a *dukkaṭa* for the monk;
however, when it is said, “Let us attend upon [the Buddha],” there is an offense for the nun.
“Attendance is praised”— this may indeed be said thus:
whether one stands right within the monastery and sees or hears [the teaching],
or whether one comes from one’s own place of residence and applies oneself [to it].
Whether she goes and sees [him], or for such reasons as those;
likewise when she sees him on the road, or at a dance, or even on the opposite path;
and likewise in cases where there is no offense for women who are insane and so forth.
This [offense] is considered to have the same origin as the preceding one;
it is a worldly transgression, involves an evil mind, and is associated with three feelings.
The tenth.
The First Chapter on Garlic.
Just as if, in the thick darkness of night, when there is no lamp,
a nun should stay together with a man while alone.
For her, a *pācittiya* offense is declared when she converses with him,
or when she comes within arm’s reach for the purpose of secret intimacy.
Or, if she should leave the range of arm’s reach from a man—
Even if she does not leave behind yakkhas, petas, and so forth,
if a bhikkhunī remains standing with such a person, a dukkaṭa offense is declared for her;
there is no offense, however, if some wise companion is present.
Likewise, for one who is insane and so forth, or for one who has acted otherwise than prescribed,
there is the offense of theft arising from a caravan, which is a formal act (kiriya) characterized by release through perception.
First.
In the second [offense], however, the phrase "in a concealed place" is additional;
all else is considered the same as the first.
This is the second.
In the third and in the fourth [cases], there is nothing whatsoever that is unprecedented;
they are identical with the first case regarding their origin and other such factors.
These are the third and fourth [cases].
If one sits down where there is no shelter from the rain,
or if one sits out in the open air, or even within the precincts [of a monastery],
the offense that occurs at the first step taken beyond [the boundary] is a *dukkaṭa*.
In the second phrase, the offense for her is a *pācittiya*.
For [spreading] on a place other than a couch, a *dukkaṭa* is proclaimed.
Likewise, when asked, if one perceives it as not asked, or if one is in doubt.
The offense is not removable, or it occurs when one is ill or in unavoidable circumstances;
all [factors] such as the origin and so forth are considered the same as those for the *kaṭhina* robe. Fifth.
For one who walks while sitting, there is one offense; for one who walks without sitting, there is likewise one.
For one who walks while lying down, there is one offense.
For one who walks after having both sat and lain down, there are two offenses.
The remainder is the same as the immediately preceding [case] regarding origin and so forth.
This is the sixth.
The seventh is equal to the sixth; in the eighth, there is nothing at all.
It should be stated that these two [offenses] have three origins, are associated with one’s own mind, and result in painful feeling.
Regarding the seventh and eighth [offenses]:
whether it be oneself or another, [one should refrain from] hell and the holy life.
To curse [another] is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) for every single word spoken—
provided one excludes the hells and the holy life (brahmacariya)— using such terms as:
“You are a female dog, a female pig, a female crow, one-eyed, or crooked,” and so forth.
If she reviles with speech, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for that speech;
for the [other] three [types of speech], a pācittiya is stated, and for the remaining [speech], a triad of dukkaṭas.
This applies when she speaks while being preceded by others who are giving instruction on the higher Dhamma.
There is no offense by reason of the eighth [ground]; the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same. Ninth.
Having killed one who is weeping, a Pācittiya is explained.
If one commits even one of these two offenses, there is indeed a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).

The rest here is exactly as explained in the *Uttara-vibhaṅga*; however, regarding the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth, they are identical to those for the *Dhurānikkhepa* (abandoning the task), with the only distinction being the specific action involved.
The tenth.
The second chapter, the Chapter on Darkness.
[And she who, having become naked, bathes...]
For every preliminary effort,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); at its conclusion,
the nun incurs the fault spoken of by the Conqueror.
[The offense applies] when robes have been torn away, or lost, or in times of distress;
it does not apply [if done] with a motive of malice, or for the sake of wool or hair. The origin and other factors are the same.
The first [offense].
But regarding the second [offense], nothing new need be said;
all its origins and so forth are considered identical to those of the Sañcaritta [offense].
This is the second.
Having undone a robe that was poorly sewn for the purpose of sewing it again,
if a bhikkhunī does not sew it afterwards without delay— thinking,
"I will not sew it," while setting aside four or five days— [she commits an offense].
As soon as the task is undertaken, there is a *pācittiya* offense for her.
If she sews afterwards after having set aside the task, it is a *pācittiya*;
three *pācittiya*s are stated [for this], and for the remainder, there is a triple *dukkaṭa*.
It is stated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for either of the two [monks] regarding the requisites of the other;
however, there is no offense for one who is ill, or when an obstacle exists.
There is also no offense for one who exceeds five days, or while making a robe.
This is considered the origin (samuṭṭhāna) known as "laying down the burden.
Third.
Now, if one should exceed the five-day limit for the distribution of the outer robe (saṅghāṭī);
There is an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*); at dawn on the sixth day, there is [an offense] for that.
For one robe, there is one [offense]; five are explained for five [robes].
However, there are five: the three robes, the *saṃkakṣikā*, and the water-strain cloth.
For the *tikkapācittiya*, there is a double *dukkaṭa* when five days have not yet elapsed;
on the fifth day, one incurs five [offenses] regarding the use of robes.
There is no offense even in the cases where one dries them for the sake of one who is ill.
All [factors] beginning with the origin (samuṭṭhāna) are considered equal to the Kathina [rules].
Fourth.
Having taken [the robe], that which is to be transferred as a robe without having informed [the owner]—
If she enjoys it for another, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her.
A triad of pācittiyas has been stated; for the remaining cases, there is a triad of wrong-doings (dukkaṭa):
when one's robe has been stolen, when one's robe has been lost, or in times of distress.
Likewise, it is declared that there is no offense for those who are insane and so forth;
this origin [of the offense] through the kaṭhina is the same as [the previous case], consisting of both action and non-action. Fifth.
If a nun prevents a robe that ought to be received by the Saṅgha from reaching her,
it is declared to be a Pācittiya offense. In the case of a group or an individual, if she prevents them from receiving their share, it is an offense of Dukkaṭa.
Likewise, if one prevents another from using requisites,
provided one does so by pointing out the benefits, there is no fault; [in such a case],
the origins and other factors are considered identical to those of taking what is not given.
Sixth: She who should prohibit a lawful distribution of robes incurs a *pācittiya*;
for her, a *dukkaṭa* is also declared.
When one perceives what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, or when both parties are in doubt,
yet she forbids [the act] by pointing out the benefit [of restraint],
there is likewise no offense for those who are insane and so forth; this has been declared.
All [factors] beginning with origination (samuṭṭhāna) are considered to be identical to the immediately preceding ones.
Seventh. Likewise, that which is suitable for the lower robe (nivāsana), as well as that which is suitable for the upper robe (pārupana);
Having set aside something that has been marked with a boundary for one's fellow practitioners of the Dhamma,
if one should give a robe to anyone else—
even to one’s own father or another— there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for that person as well.
In this case, according to the method of counting, those [robes] for robes are to be counted as *pācittiya* offenses for a monk; there would be a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If he gives them on loan to another, there is no offense.
The methods regarding the origin and so forth are stated to be the same as for the Sañcaritta [offense]. Eighth.
Having prohibited [the use of] robes, this is the analysis (vibhaṅga) concerning robes.
If she should let the time pass due to the fault of having weak hope, or if,
regarding a robe that is not weak, she thinks in her mind "it is very weak," or if she is in doubt about both—
regarding these, the Victor declared an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Having pointed out the benefit, he restrains [others] out of kindness, not out of malice.
The origins and other factors are considered to be identical to those of taking what is not given. Ninth.
If a bhikkhunī should obstruct the lawful dismantling of the kaṭhina,
the Lord of Sages has declared that she incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Great is the benefit for one whose purpose is rooted in the spreading of the kaṭhina.
That which is based on removal is small and should not be given in such a manner.
There is great merit for one whose [gift] is based on removal.
That which is based on spreading is small, but such a kind should be given.
Likewise, even when there is an equal benefit,
it is permissible to prohibit [an action] by first demonstrating the benefit for the sake of preserving faith.
However, the remainder is considered entirely the same as the seventh [case].
There is nothing new whatsoever regarding the origins and so forth.
The tenth [chapter]. The third section, the Chapter on the Naked (Naggavagga).
When one has already lain down, another may lie down;
two may lie down together, and for the two of them there would be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
It should be known that there are many offenses when lying down again and again.
If one [nun] is lying down and another sits,
or if both sit together, or with one who is insane—
the origin of the offense is non-existent; this is considered the same as the case of the ram.
First: If, however,
having spread out a cloak, a rug, or the like, one alone, and then,
among those things that may be rolled up, puts on [the robe] with that very same thing;
If two lie down together, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for both;
if they lie down with one [person], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the two—thus it is called "two offenses of wrong-doing.
However, if they lie down after having established a boundary [between them], [there is no offense].
There is no offense for those who are insane and so forth; the remainder is equal to the first case.
Second.
And if, without having asked permission beforehand, one performs walking meditation and other such acts;
But if she should do so for the sake of another's comfort,
it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The number of offenses of expiation is to be known by counting her turns back.
Faults arise precisely from the preparation itself regarding the places for lying down and sitting. Regarding the recitation and so forth,
it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) at the conclusion of counting the words.
A pācittiya offense is stated for the first [offense], while for the remaining two there is a dukkaṭa offense.
There is no offense, however, for one who asks permission beforehand and performs walking meditation or other such activities for her when she does not desire comfort.
The methods regarding its origin and so forth are the same as for taking what is not given.
This evil mental action is both performed and unperformed, and it results in painful feeling.
Third.
If she herself, being free from obstacles, does not have another sister living with her who is suffering attended to, or if she does not attend to her herself,
then as soon as she has abandoned that responsibility, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her.
Whether for the resident pupil or for the other [the teacher], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense if she is ill, or if she has sought [food] but could not obtain it;
nor is there an offense in cases of emergency, insanity, and so forth, or when the burden has been set down.
The fourth [offense]:
Having given one's own private property,
if she then personally ejects him from that dwelling which has its own door.
Even by a single act, though there be many doors and so forth,
for her who is ejecting him, there shall be one *pācittiya*. In this case,
the number of *pācittiyas* is considered according to the number of acts.
The same method applies to a command as well; this was stated by the Great Sage:
"These many doors—throw him out! If one issues such a command, there may be offenses according to the number of doors.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for [opening] that which lacks a door-panel; for the rest, there is a triple wrong-doing.
However, for both [cases], in all instances regarding requisites, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
The remainder here, together with the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth, is explained in its entirety.
For it is considered equivalent to being expelled from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha.
This is the fifth [offense].
As for what must be said here regarding the sixth, there is nothing new whatsoever.
The determination for one who has committed an offense under this training rule is identical [to that of the previous]. Sixth.
Furthermore, within a country considered dangerous, for a bhikkhunī...
For a nun traveling on a journey without a caravan, there may be an offense.
Upon entering another village, or traveling half a yojana in the forest,
the method for the *pācittiya* offense should be known by a monk who is learned in the Vinaya.
There is no offense when traveling with a caravan, or when seeking a place of safety.
This [offense] is the same as that involving wool from sheep (*eḷakaloma*) in terms of its origin and other factors.
The seventh [chapter].
In the eighth or even the ninth [offense], nothing is found that is not explained;
they are identical with the seventh in terms of their origin and so forth.
These are the eighth and ninth.
It is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for abandoning one's responsibility, saying,
"I will not go," and likewise for one who has abandoned her responsibility and then goes later.
It is permissible to travel five yojanas after having invited [the Sangha] to the Pavāraṇā ceremony.
In all six cases, this very point must be stated: why indeed should it not be so here?
Having gone by three [paths] and returning by that same one is not permitted;
however, it is permitted to return later by another path.
There is no offense in ten cases: when there is an obstacle, when she is ill, in times of misfortune, when a companion cannot be found, or when there is no second person available.
[The obstacles are: kings, thieves, humans, fire, water, wild beasts, and reptiles.
These are obstacles to the holy life and to human existence.
They are equal in terms of their origination and so forth, as well as regarding the first and last bases;
for this alone is the distinction: [the former] is non-action, while [the latter] is painful feeling.
The Tenth.
The Fourth Chapter on Tuvaṭṭa.
A royal palace, a painted hall, a monastery, or a pleasure grove;
For those women going to see the various forms of the pleasure pond,
the Sage has prescribed a *dukkaṭa* offense at every step;
even if all five see it, they incur the offense without having lifted their feet.
However, only one offense is indicated as a *pācittiya*:
if they go and see that [person], there would be separate offenses for each.
Even due to the multiplicity of the acts, there would be a multiplicity of *pācittis*.
For a bhikkhu, however, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in all cases.
The remainder— the analytical exposition of the path of discourse regarding non-offenses—
is equal to that of watching dancing, together with its origins and so forth.
First:
The Teacher has declared that for those who make use of a high couch or a luxurious couch,
or one adorned with animal figures, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
It occurs by way of the abundance of application even for sitting and lying down;
thus it is described as being absolutely constant.
The enumeration of the Pācittiya rules is as follows:
Having cut off the legs of a chair, and having broken the frame of a couch—there is no offense;
this origin is considered identical to the immediately preceding one.
The second [offense].
If a bhikkhunī weaves any one of the six types of cloth,
for as much as she has woven with her hands while that [cloth] is being wound upon the distaff.
One *pācittiya* offense is specified for spinning thread; however, for all prior preparatory acts, there is a *dukkaṭa* for each manual operation.
There is no fault in spinning thread that has already been spun, but for one who spins it again, [there is an offense].
This is the same as the offense regarding wool from sheep (*eḷakaloma*) in terms of its origin and other factors.
This is the third [offense]. However, starting with the threshing of rice, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
In all prior preparations, for one who performs service,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each vessel counted when [distributing] rice-gruel and so forth;
indeed, for snacks and the like, it should be explained by counting the portions (rūpa).
If one's mother and father have come to one,
it is not permissible to do nothing at all without having them perform some task.
Likewise, whether it be at a rice-gruel offering for the Sangha or at a meal provided for the Sangha, [one must attend].
In the case of making an offering to a cetiya, or for one who is performing a service, there is no offense for oneself; likewise for one who is insane.
All factors, beginning with the origin, are considered identical to the third [offense].
The fourth [case]:
In the case of abandoning the task, just as in the instance of sewing a robe,
so here too, no exemption is granted for even a single day.
The remainder is exactly as previously stated;
therein, regarding the sewing of robes, it should be understood by one who discerns it along with its origin and other factors. This is the fifth [offense].
Whether by means of the body, or with something attached to the body, or likewise with something relinquished;
whatever for householders there may be, other than tooth-sticks or water—
any other thing intended for swallowing— that she gives to others.
For her, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya), except in the case of those who share the same Dhamma.

Regarding tooth-sticks and water, the Sage has declared here an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who neither gives nor causes them to be given, even when she has gone out and is giving them herself.
One gives either an external ointment or [a substance] from a pool of pus;
all factors such as the origin and so forth are considered identical to the third [offense].
The sixth [chapter].
If one should consume [food] without having first offered it,
or if there is a dwelling and a robe— on the fourth day, having washed that robe again—
if it belongs to a novice or even to a woman in her courses;
For her, a *pācittiya* is stated; it may be a triple *pācittiya*.
When that [article] has been forfeited by her, two *dukkaṭas* are stated;
but in the absence of those who are in their season, there is again a turn for others.
Even in cases where there is no offense— such as when robes have been lost or stolen— all factors, beginning with the origin, are considered identical to those of the Kathina ceremony. Seventh.
If she departs on a journey without having given [the key] for the sake of protection,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her as she sets out on the tour.
However, for one going from her own village to another village—
For a monastery that has an enclosure, or likewise for its enclosure itself;
or for another [monastery], it is the precincts.
By the first phrase, there is a dukkaṭa offense upon crossing that boundary; by the second, however, it is a pācittiya.
In the case of locking the door, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is revealed;
there is no offense if there is an obstacle, or if she does not obtain a watchman.
Likewise, there is no offense for one who is ill during times of misfortune, or for one who is insane.
All [factors] beginning with the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) are considered equal to those of the Kathina [robe-making ceremony]. Eighth.
[The offense] connected with elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth, or indeed with a craft;
If she should learn anything that destroys others, such as spells or various medical applications, from anyone whatsoever,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her here, by way of each word and so forth.
There is no offense in the case of writing, for the purpose of memorization or protection;
nor in the case of all protective charms (paritta), or for one who is insane. Ninth.
In the tenth [offense], there is nothing to be said; this is the same as the ninth.
The origin and other factors for these two are identical, as are their classification and legal status.
The tenth.
The fifth section, on the Hall of Paintings.
For one who enters a monastery containing monks, having recognized it as such,
whatever she does without first asking permission, is comprised within the offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If a bhikkhunī, however, without having asked permission, crosses the enclosure— even if it be only the root of a tree—
or even crosses the precincts of that which is unenclosed;
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the first foot [of the verse], and there may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the second.
If one perceives it as "with monks" when it is actually "without monks," or if one has doubt regarding that perception,
there is an offense of wrong-doing for both cases.
For those entering first, she who looks after their heads [leads];
wherever they have gathered, she goes into their presence.
Furthermore, without asking a monk present, [she may cross] the road or through the middle of a street.
For one who goes [to another village] by means of that [robe], or for one who enters it during times of misfortune,
as well as for those such as the insane and so forth, no offense is declared;
the methods regarding origin and the rest are indeed equivalent to the case of relinquishing the responsibility.
First:
If a woman should revile or even abuse a bhikkhu, for her there is a pācittiya offense of the threefold type,
and for the remaining cases, a dukkaṭa offense of the threefold type.
Placing before them the instruction on the supreme Dhamma as they speak,
one should not [speak] with words of fault-finding or envy.
The remaining method is considered to be the same.
Second.
For one who reviles the Saṅgha, there shall be a pācittiya offense.
Whether one person or many, or likewise with the other [type of speech],
for her who reviles, a *dukkaṭa* offense is declared;
the remainder is the same as in the immediately preceding case regarding its origin and so forth.
Third.
Whether one has been invited or whether one has already finished the meal-offering:
both "invitation" (*nimantana*) and "meal-offering" (*pavāraṇā*) possess the characteristics as previously described.
If one accepts, at the time before the meal, rice-gruel—
excluding the three types of food that may be taken at any time— as well as any other kind of edible food intended for consumption,
there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of accepting it.
In this context, a Pācittiya offense is explained by way of swallowing.
If one takes the three types of food that are restricted to specific times for the purpose of eating,
a Dukkaṭa is stated for the act of taking, and likewise for one who swallows it.
But she who has been invited and not refused further [food],
it is permissible for her to drink rice-gruel here;
likewise, having spoken thus, [she may do so] again with the permission of the host.
Even if she eats other food, provided that she eats only the three types of timely food when the requisites are available;
likewise, for those who are insane and so forth, no offense is declared.
The origin of this offense is the same as that for traveling [on foot]; it is an act of non-action regarding the journey.
If one who has been invited eats without asking permission from the owner, it is an offense.
However, whether one has had something made allowable (*kappiya*) or not, if...
If she consumes it, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This is the fourth [offense].
To speak dispraise of bhikkhunīs in the presence of a family is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Whether one speaks in disparagement of a family, or speaks of bhikkhunīs,
or speaks of existing faults, or speaks out of madness—
these cases are identical to the offense of abusive speech (omasavāda) in their origin and other formal characteristics.
The fifth [case]:
If the path is less than half a yojana away, or if it is not safe, a monk who is to give the exhortation should not stay there.
This is what is called "without monks";
however, if there is a residence there, for one who enters it for the rains, an offense occurs at the rising of the dawn.
Whether she has departed, gone over to another faction, left the Order, or even died;
Bhikkhus who have entered the rains residence are not subject to offenses even for minor matters.
The remainder of the course of discourse should be understood accordingly;
however, as for the instructor of the bhikkhunīs:
This [offense] is like that involving wool from a sheep (*eḷakaloma*) in terms of its origination and other factors.
The sixth [section].
If a nun who has completed the rains residence in both Saṅghas subsequently says,
"I will not perform the Pavāraṇā," and she thus relinquishes her responsibility,
at the mere moment that responsibility is relinquished, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her.
If there is an obstacle, or if she is ill, or in times of distress,
even if she has sought out a monk and failed to find one, there is no fault for her; this, however,
is declared to be the origin of the offense of "laying down the burden."
Seventh: "I will not go for the sake of exhortation and so forth"— if one has merely set aside this duty,
it is declared to be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The origin is the same as for the first and last offenses;
they are non-intentional, worldly transgressions, bodily, and associated with painful feeling.
The eighth.
“I will not request instruction, nor will I inquire about the Uposatha”—
if one thus relinquishes the duty, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
However, if there is an obstacle, or if one is ill, or in cases of distress;
There is no offense for one who, having sought a second [person], does not find one.
Even in the eighth case, there is likewise no offense; this has been declared in the same way.
However, this is proclaimed as the origin arising from the laying down of the burden.
The ninth [offense]:
If a boil has arisen in the groin, or if it is merely a pimple,
she may go alone with one man, even without having asked permission from the Saṅgha or a group.
“‘Split it! Break it! Wash it!’—all these are for one who causes [the robe] to be made.
When [the robes] are finished, there are offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); for her, there are six offenses of expiation (pācittiya). ‘Whatever is to be done here, you do all of that.’”
If she gives the command and he carries it all out,
then for that single utterance there would be six *dukkaṭas* and six *pācittiyas*; thus, there would be twelve offenses.
If, among acts such as causing a schism, one person gives the order and that person carries out all of them, there shall be a single *pācittiya* offense. Or,
even if he has informed a wise person or taken a companion with him, [the same applies].
If she causes all [acts], such as causing a schism and so forth, to be committed,
it is declared that there is no offense for her if she is insane and so on;
all [factors] beginning with the origin (samuṭṭhāna) are considered to be the same as those for the Kathina [offense].
The tenth.
The sixth chapter, the Chapter on Monasteries (Ārāmavagga).
[It concerns] seeking a group, and one who ordains a pregnant woman.
Through the motion and the formal proclamations, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the preceptor.
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation, a Pācittiya offense is incurred;
likewise when one perceives her as pregnant, even though she is not actually pregnant.
If both have doubts that she has given birth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
this is declared for her who acts accordingly, as well as for the Saṅgha.
If one perceives two [women] as not pregnant, or if she is insane, there is no fault.
The methods regarding origin and so forth are the same as those for taking what is not given.
First [offense].
In the second [offense], there is nothing further to be said; it is considered equal to the first.
In terms of origin and so forth, there is no difference whatsoever.
Second.
However, a *sikkhamānā* who has completed the six-year training should indeed be ordained as a *bhikkhunī*.
If she were to give the full admission (vutthāpeyya) for two years, there would be an offense;
the Teacher has stated that in the case of a legitimate legal act (dhammakamma), there is a triad of pācittiyas,
whereas in the case of an illegitimate legal act (adhammakamma), a triad of dukkaṭas is explained.
If she ordains one who has trained in these six trainings for two years without breach, there is no offense;
likewise for one who is insane.
For these six trainings, even if [the candidate] were sixty years old, [she must still train].
The going-forth should be granted; one should not cause it to be performed without having given [permission].
Third.
Regarding the fourth, there is nothing further to be said: here, it must be authorized by the Saṅgha.
There is no offense for the one who ordains her as a trainee (sikkhamānā).
If she has not [previously] been given the initial permission to ordain,
that too must be granted there in the ordination hall.
The third and the fourth [offenses] should be understood as being the same as the first in terms of their origin and other characteristics; however, the fourth is both with and without formal action.
The fourth.
If one who has not yet reached twelve years of age, though she is a married woman,
is ordained by one who perceives her as being of full age,
there is no offense for the one ordaining her. Yet she remains unordained, even though she has been ordained.

If it is done, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), but it does not invalidate [the act].
Some say that it invalidates it; however, that should not be accepted.
This same principle should be understood by the wise in all other cases as well.
There are twenty-five who are incapable of the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*);
even if one is ordained without knowing [this], such an admission is subject to expulsion.
There are thirty-two [defects] beginning with "hand-cut" (*hatthacchinna*), and thirteen beginning with "leper" (*kuṭṭhin*).
If the essence of their agreement has been reached and it takes root,
there is one upajjhāya and there are three teachers.
And there are two or even three who desire full ordination.
By means of three preceptors alone, there is a single proclamation together.
A formal act performed after one has been reinstated is neither invalid nor permissible.
He has a single preceptor;
likewise, he has a single teacher.
And those seeking full ordination—
whether there be two or three—
having announced them in due order, he [the preceptor] should state their names and his own.
Having announced [the motion] from one side, even if it is performed, it does not become invalid.
Even by one who does not have a preceptor and one who does not have a teacher,
having announced to each other, the formal act (kamma) that is performed is valid.
Sumanā instructs his pupil to Tissatthera;
Tissatthera instructs his pupil to Sumanatthera.
Here, it is not by having no preceptor at all, nor by having only one teacher.
Full ordination was rejected by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
The Discourse on the Mahākhandhaka.
The Discourse on the Uposathakkhandhaka.
The boundary is considered to be of two kinds, according to whether it is fixed or unfixed;
however, it is formally established by connecting one boundary marker with another.
This [boundary] is free from the eleven defects of boundaries.
There may be a boundary that is "bound" (*baddhā*), which is endowed with threefold perfection.
Due to the divisions of broken [boundary], common residence, separation, and so forth, the bound is thus said to be of three kinds;
the unbound (*abaddhā*) is likewise considered to be of three kinds.
From the village to the throwing of water, and even within seven [leagues] from it;
therein, the boundary of the village is called the "village precinct.
Around a lake, the ocean, or a river—
The "middle water-splash" is known as the water-splash boundary.
However, in a forest that is not a village, there are seven *abbhantara*s within;
this boundary on all sides is called the "seven-*abbhantara*" boundary.
One internal boundary is said to be twenty-eight cubits;
those who splash water are considered to be by way of throwing a clod of earth.
These two boundaries, moreover, increase according to the size of the assembly.
There may be those with water thrown inside, or those beyond the standing space.
One who stands within the boundary, either leaving a hand’s reach [of the door],
or not exceeding that distance, or even beyond the boundary itself.
"One who stands still violates the ritual action"—this is the method of the Aṭṭhakathā.
Therefore, it should be performed either within arm's reach or outside.
The configuration of the bound boundary, the sign, and the description of the directions [are required].
Having ascertained the measurements and cleared the area, the wise man should establish the boundary.
It may be triangular, square, circular, or like a drum;
it may be shaped like a canopy, like a bow, like a small drum, or like a cart.
One should illustrate eight signs: a mountain, a forest, a rock, a tree, a path, and an anthill;
as well as water and a river.
Among these, beginning with the first three signs, one should [visualize them] all around.
However, it is permissible to bind [the boundary] even with a hundred signs.
A boundary extending up to three yojanas is declared to be the maximum;
that which takes in twenty-one monks is considered the minimum.
The superior is for the superior, and the inferior for the inferior;
these two are said by the Kinsman of the Sun to be without boundaries.
However, having designated the sign on all sides, [one should meditate] upon everything.

Subsequently, it is fit to bind the boundary by means of a motion followed by a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*). Immediately after having bound it, one should appoint the [boundary] that prevents separation from one's robes;
once bound, it is called "the non-separation [boundary]."
"If one were to establish a boundary within rivers, lakes, or oceans, it would not be submerged by that very [water];
thus the Victor declared: 'It is without a boundary. The Discussion on Boundaries.
Furthermore, by virtue of the duties to be performed by the maker of the day (the sun),
nine Uposatha days were taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:
the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the Uposatha of concord.
These three Uposatha observances have been explained by the day itself:
the Uposatha in the Sangha, and the Uposatha for a group and for an individual;
these three Uposathas are stated according to the agents who perform them.
The Uposatha consisting of the recitation of the Suttas, the Uposatha of purity,
and the formal resolution— these three types of Uposatha are specified as formal acts (kamma).
There is the Pātimokkha for the Saṅgha and the purity for the group.
The Teacher has indeed specified the purpose for one [recitation]:
five recitations of the Pātimokkha have been declared by the Great Sage.
Having recited the Nidāna, the remainder should then be announced.
This same method should be understood by the wise for the remaining cases as well;
furthermore, there are these nine recitations for the bhikkhunīs.
On the Uposatha day, the recitation of the Pātimokkha must indeed be performed.
Even without an obstacle, the assignment was prevented;
and the Elder was its master,
according to the reading "the domain of the Elder."
If he is requested by one who is performing [the recitation], it is valid for him. Or,
while the recitation is being performed, if those who are equal [in status] arrive;
That which has been recited is well-recited; the remainder must be announced.
If the assembly has risen while only a portion of the monks has been recited, then purification (pārisuddhi) must be performed at the root of those [remaining] monks, provided they are numerous.
To sweep, to light a lamp, and to prepare a water-seat—these were prescribed by the Elder.
For one who does not do them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Having performed the sweeping, having lit the lamp, and having set out the water-seat;
The Uposatha should be performed by three [monks] even without establishing a formal motion (*gaṇañatti*).
Having completed the preliminary duties, one who is alone should then make the formal determination (*adhiṭṭheyya*);
if he does not make the determination, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
By an illegal procedure with an incomplete assembly; by an illegal procedure with a complete assembly;
likewise, by a legal procedure with an incomplete assembly;
and by a legal procedure with a complete assembly—these, the Conqueror declared, are the formal acts of the Uposatha.
Among these four, the fourth is considered the legitimate (dhammika).
For what kind of Uposatha here is performed by a faction through illegality (adhamma),
when four monks are dwelling within a single boundary?
If three persons, having brought about the purity of one,
perform the purity [ceremony], it is an unrighteous *pārisuddhi-uposatha* of a faction.
For even if it is by an unrighteous method, it is a concordant assembly when four monks are gathered together.
If they perform the purification while being in concord,
it is legitimate. But what kind of Uposatha is that which is performed by a faction,
even though four monks are dwelling within a single boundary?
If three people, having brought about the purity of one person,
recite the Pātimokkha, that Uposatha is valid according to the Dhamma; for it is both in accordance with the Dhamma and complete.
Four monks gathered together here recite the Pātimokkha;
this is considered a complete assembly according to the Dhamma.
For one who performs the Uposatha while perceiving a united Saṅgha as divided, or while being in doubt,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, for one who intends to cause a schism, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
An offense occurs when a group is united, even though they perceive themselves as being united. [This applies] with one who has been suspended,
with a householder, with the remaining [monks] who follow the Dhamma,
or with eleven [monks] including those whose training has lapsed or been suspended.

The Uposatha should not be performed by one who has committed an offense similar to that of the others, nor by one who has been excluded from the consent; for one who does so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Furthermore, it should not be performed without having confessed the offense or without having cleared away doubt.
The Uposatha should not be performed on a day that is not the Uposatha.
Furthermore, a monk should never go from a residence where there are monks to a residence that is not a residence, nor to a place where there are no monks, on the Uposatha day.
On whatever Uposatha day there is a duty to be performed in a residence,
if that residence is said to have monks present;
The "residence" has been explained.
For what purpose is the Uposatha? For what purpose is the Pavāraṇā?
The Uposatha is for the sake of concord; the Pavāraṇā is for the sake of purification.
To protest against a legitimate formal act (dhammakamma) is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
likewise, it is an offense of wrong-doing for one who does not give consent or bodily presence.
There are five kinds of Saṅgha, distinguished by the fourfold assembly and so forth.
And this is illustrated by way of the actions that ought to be performed:
apart from the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), the formal confession (*abbhāna*), legal acts (*kamma*), and ordination (*upasampadā*),
there is nothing that cannot be performed by a quorum of four.
Rehabilitation by a group of five, full ordination in the Middle Country by a group of ten,
and rehabilitation by a group of ten— all these are permissible even without [the required quorum].
No formal act whatsoever should be performed by a group of twenty.
It is to make known that there is a fault when [the quorum] is deficient, not that there is excess when it is more than required.
Only four regular members are indicated as being eligible for the formal act;
this same principle applies to those acts that must be performed by a quorum of four and to the remaining cases.

Having performed what is to be done by a quorum of four or more, if one makes a person who does not share the same residence complete the quorum, the act that was performed becomes invalid, and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) arises.
This applies even in the case of formal acts such as probation (parivāsa); in those instances, the person remaining there serves to complete the quorum.
But for those who perform [the ritual] after having first performed it, the rest is likewise permissible.
The Discussion on the Uposatha Khandhaka.
The Discussion on the Vassūpanāyika Khandhaka.
There are two occasions for entering the rains residence: the earlier and the later.
One who enters must either manifest attachment or utter words [of intent].
Or else, for one who knows [the time] but does not enter the rains residence, there is the offense of *vassūpagamana* (non-entry).
Whether having stayed for the three months of the rains, or even while wandering about, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
It is not permitted to enter the rains residence in the hollow of a tree, under a canopy, in a barrel-vaulted hut, in a thatched hut, or even in the open air.
There is no offense if the rains-retreat is interrupted, provided there should be an obstacle;
for a monk whose rains-retreat has been cut short, the invitation ceremony is indeed considered as already performed.
However, [it may be done] for the sake of seeing one's mother and father.
It is for the purpose of seeing five types of persons who are in accordance with the Dhamma—
those who are ill and those who attend to them—
and for the sake of seeking food and other requisites for them.
"Having gone to one who is thus dissatisfied, we shall cause him who has arisen [from his state] to withdraw; or we shall dispel his wrong view or his remorse.
Thus, by means of this seven-day business, a monk who is knowledgeable in the Vinaya—
One should go even if not invited, let alone when sent for. However,
for a monk who has entered the rains residence there,
it is not permitted to go for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma unless he has been invited.
“If on such-and-such a day there will be a gathering”—
if an agreement has been made in this way beforehand, it is permissible. However,
it is not permissible [to say], “I will wash and dye my belongings.”
If one's teachers or preceptors send for him, it is permissible.
However, it is not at all permissible to go for the sake of recitation and so forth;
a person may go for the purpose of seeing his elders.
If the teacher says, "Do not go today," it is explained that there is no offense if the night is cut short.
This applies whether it concerns any relative or a family of supporters.
If one goes for the purpose of seeing [the preceptor], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) if the night is cut short.
If one thinks, "I will go to the village today and return this very day," it is permissible provided that one is indeed able to reach [the destination] and return.
In three situations for a bhikkhu— on foot, on a carriage, or on a boat—
if the rains retreat is interrupted, there is no offense, and it is permissible to perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony.
This applies when there is a deficiency of requisites or when the body is unwell.

"Thinking, 'This very thing is an obstacle,' one may depart even after cutting short the rains residence. For whoever has not entered the rains residence due to some obstacle whatsoever, a second [rains residence] should be undertaken,
or else [one who has] cut short the rains residence [may enter it]."
Whether he does not enter the rains residence at all, or departs on that very same day, or even after having entered it,
if he spends more than seven days outside, then for him,
even the previous [rains-residence] is no longer valid.
And for a monk who gives his consent, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Furthermore, having entered the rains residence and then departed before dawn has broken,
the monk incurs [an offense] simply by the act of leaving for seven days.
And even during those very seven days while he was returning,
there would be no offense— what need to mention one who stays [there] and then goes outside?
If there is a sense of attachment, thinking, "I will dwell here for the rains retreat," [then it is an offense].
If one has not completed the rains-residence due to a lack of mindfulness, yet the lodging has been taken up, that taking is considered well-taken; he is not one whose rains-residence is broken.
He may indeed perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony, and no fault whatsoever exists.
“I enter this residence for three months; I enter this rains retreat.
Once these words have been uttered three times, one has entered the rains retreat.
However, it is permissible for a bhikkhu to go [elsewhere] starting from the ninth day.
And let him come later; there is no fault in that.
The Discussion on the Chapter on Entering the Rainy Season Retreat (Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka). The Discussion on the Chapter on the Invitation (Pavāraṇakkhandhaka).
The fourteenth, the fifteenth, the invitation for concord,
and the invitation for the three-fold, two-fold, and one-fold [confession];
these nine invitations were spoken by the Lord of Sages for the Saṅgha, the group, and the individual.
Having set aside the three types of formal acts, one should perform the invitation by means of the motion itself.
Having completed the preliminary duties and having assembled those who are present and fit,
the invitation should indeed be performed by the Saṅgha after the formal motion has been established.
While the elders are performing the invitation ceremony, the junior monk should remain seated;
however, he must remain in the *ukkuṭika* (squatting) posture until he himself has invited.
Having made the formal motion (*ñatti*), four or three [monks] may perform the invitation.
Having completed their prior duties, if they dwell in a single residence,
two persons may invite one another without a formal motion (*ñatti*);
however, if even one person resolves [to do so], the rest is a communal invitation (*saṅghapavāraṇā*).
If the Saṅgha has already invited [for the meal], but one who has not yet arrived—
whether because he is staying elsewhere or his rains-residence is cut short— performs the Uposatha of purity;
or if in a certain residence there are five, or four, or even three [monks];
Having carried [the invitation] to each one individually, those ascetics perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony among themselves;
if there is an offense, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The wise one should understand the method here according to the method already stated for the Uposatha.
By the offering of complete purity, one achieves personal purification;
by the giving of one’s consent to the Saṅgha, one accomplishes everything for oneself.
Therefore, in this case, for the sake of fulfilling the duties of both, [one should act].
The declaration of purity must also be given by the monk who gives his consent.
Even when many give their consent, the declaration of purity may be omitted by one who holds the consent alone; for consent brought through a succession does not convey purity.
The one who takes away [the robe] may take it by means of a formal motion (*chanda*), or by means of a declaration of purity (*pārisuddhi*), or by means of an invitation to the end of the *pavāraṇā*;
or he may acknowledge himself as a novice (*sāmaṇera*) or some other status. If, before reaching the Saṅgha, he should become insane or die;
If one has not brought all of it, yet after reaching [the Sangha] it becomes something that was brought;
or if, having reached the Sangha, one is negligent, asleep,
or deranged in mind and does not report it— there is no offense, though there is an intentional *dukkaṭa*.
Those who are devoted to insight, untiring by day and night,
intent on insight during the first and last watches of the night—
for those who dwell in comfort, there can be no decline.
The inclusion of the Pavāraṇā [Khandhaka] is stated in the Kattika month.
This concludes the discourse on the Pavāraṇā-khandhaka.
Now follows the discourse on the Camma-khandhaka.
However, for a bhikkhu, the hides of sheep, goats, and deer are permissible—
namely, those of the rohitā, eṇī, kuraṅga, pasada, and migamātā.
Apart from the hides of these, any other [animal hide] constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding bags and sandals, all leather is permitted, provided it is not made from human skin.
In the Middle Country, sandals with multiple layers of soles are not permitted;
however, they are permitted within the monastery precincts, and for one who is ill, they are permitted everywhere.
Those bound with a cloth-sack, likewise those covered with hair,
those filled with cotton, and all those that are entirely blue and so forth, are not permitted.
Colorful sandals with heels shaped like the horns of a ram are also not allowed.
It is not permitted for it to be sewn with peacock feathers.
It is not permitted to be trimmed with the skins of cats, black raccoons, owls, lions,
tigers, leopards, or panthers, nor with any other animal hide.
Whether by removing the lining and so forth, or by cutting it away entirely,
or likewise by altering its color, sandals may be worn.
However, it is not permitted to wear any kind of wooden shoe (pāduka) at all.
Excepting there the footstools for urination, defecation, and rinsing,
as well as the high bed or the luxurious couch known as a *āsandi* or *pallaṅka*;
for one who uses such things that exceed the prescribed measure, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Gonaka wool, cut-cloth, mind-patterned, and likewise paṭika and paṭalika;
single-sided wool, variegated, stuffed with cotton, and with the fleece on the outside.
Furthermore, hair-cloth, silk, and rugs for elephants, horses, and chariots.
Even a coverlet made of excellent kadali-deer skin,
or a double-layered red pillow beneath a red canopy— all this is unallowable;
for one who uses it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If there is an improper underlay beneath, it is not permitted;
even if there is a white canopy above, it is not permitted when that [underlay] is present.
However, setting aside the high seat (āsandi), the couch (pallaṅka), and the stuffed mattress (tūlika);
Furthermore, he may take all that remains belonging to the householder.
There is no offense in sitting on a Dhamma-seat, nor even in the midst of the meal;
it is also permissible to lie down there upon a ground-covering.
The Discussion on the Chapter on Leather;
the Discussion on the Chapter on Medicines.
It has been stated that [the formal acts] for householders also consist of those based on consent and those based on proclamation.
There are four types of allowable grounds (kappiyabhūmi):
namely, a house belonging to the Sangha, or a house belonging to a nun;
it must be made allowable and sufficient for one to sleep in.
Except for what has been given by others into a permissible enclosure (kappiyabhūmi) by a monk,
this house belongs to those [donors] as their own property, O householder.
For that which is authorized by the Saṅgha is indeed called a "conventional" (sammutikā) enclosure.
Either by reciting the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*) or by making a formal announcement (*āpattiparikathā*),
it is permissible. However, when first establishing bricks,
stones, pillars, and so forth, those on all sides should say, "We are building a kitchen (*kappiyakuṭī*)."
When others have lifted it up and set it down, or when others have touched it, or when he himself has lifted it up,
he may perform the *ussāvanantika* (the formal proclamation) for its placement.
However, regarding the laying of bricks and so forth, one must speak to the monks.
The conclusion [of the recitation] must coincide with the end of the speech.
A monastery that is unenclosed, whether it be entirely so or even mostly so—
both these types are called "gonisādi" by the wise.
These four, moreover, are grounds for what is allowable (kappiya-bhūmi);
here, all food—whether cooked or grown—is permitted.
That which is "defined by proclamation" is established upon pillars and the like.
When the pillars and so forth have been removed, it remains even when other parts are gone.
When all [parts] have been removed, it may be considered as having abandoned its physical basis;
the *gonisādī* is enclosed by a fence, while the rest [are lost] through the destruction of the covering.
Except for a bhikkhu, receiving from the hands of others,
and their storage— these are permitted for a bhikkhu as stated within [the rules].
Whether it belongs to a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, or the Saṅgha;
That which has been stored overnight and that which is cooked [overnight]: neither of these two is permitted.
That which was stored in an unauthorised hut, or mixed with ghee and so forth—this is designated as "stored overnight";
this refers to the first two types of seasonal food.
With those same substances such as ghee and so forth, a monk may use [medicines] for as long as life lasts;
however, that which has been cooked is permitted for only seven days, provided it is not mixed with non-medicinal food.
If he consumes that which has been cooked while mixed with non-medicinal food, [it is not permitted].
He eats food grown within the monastery, as well as food grown by himself.
There is food to be consumed at the proper time, drink to be consumed during the watch of the day,
that which is called "to be consumed for seven days," and the group of five beginning with ghee.
The remainder, beginning with turmeric, is medicinal tonics for life-long use.
These are declared to be of four time-periods; water is "not-time-bound" (akālika).
By way of formal acceptance alone, those that have passed their time are "three-time-bound" (tikālika).
When eaten, these cause harm, as does not eating at all,
and even a third time. Mango, rose-apple, citron, plantain, honey,
grape, salu, and phārusaka— thus drink is considered to be of eight kinds.
The use of beverages was permitted, as were fruits, both ripe and unripe;
however, receiving them for the purpose of making a drink was prohibited, provided they had a physical base.
Mangoes, having been well-pounded and crushed in water—
After having strained it, it is permissible to drink the beverage.
However, while that which is cooked by the sun is permissible, that which is cooked by fire is not.
This same principle is illustrated for the remaining types of beverages as well.
These four flavors—of flowers, leaves, fruits, and sugar-cane—are permitted;
these eight drinks were authorized by the one who allowed them.
All the flavors of flowers are stated [as permitted], with the exception of the flavor of *madhuka*.
All juice from leaves is permitted, except for that of the *pakkaṭṭhaka* plant.
With the exception of the juice produced from the fruit of the seven grains along with their corresponding plants,
all juice produced from fruit is allowed at improper times.
Even for bowls of *yāvakālika* (food to be consumed within the day),

if they have been placed in cold water and then crushed, even if they are cooked by the sun, it is permissible at an improper time (*vikāla*). This includes the *tāla*, the coconut, the jackfruit, and the breadfruit as well.
Tipu, sālābu, kumbhaṇḍa, as well as puṣphaphala, and likewise eḷāluka—
these nine fruits indeed, and all other secondary foodstuffs,
are compatible with the seven grains.
The jujube, the *timbaru*, the *selu*, the *kosamba*, the *karamaddaka*,
the citron, the wood-apple, the *vetta*, and the tamarind fruit—
such are the juices of these and other small fruits.
Because it conforms to the eight kinds of drinks, it is designated as "conformable" (*anulomika*).
Aside from the juice derived from fruit,
there is no other juice of fruit here that is not subject to the time-restriction of the night.
The Discussion on the Chapter on Medicines.
The Discussion on the Chapter on the Kathina:
He spoke of the spreading of the Kathina for monks who have completed their rains residence.
For the sake of five benefits, the Bull among Sages did not permit a monk to take up a robe—
excluding the twenty-four types such as the "merely scraped" and so forth— and to set aside an old one.
Having made the resolution, one should further speak with the words:
"By means of this inner robe, I shall spread the Kathina.
When this has been said three times, the Kathina is considered spread.
But having approached the Saṅgha and taken up the kaṭhina, that monk should say:
"Venerable sirs, the kaṭhina has been spread for the Saṅgha; please give your approval.
This is the lawful spreading of the kaṭhina."
“Venerable sir, you have properly spread the *kaṭhina* for the Saṅgha once again;
this is a legitimate *kaṭhina*-spreading—may I express my appreciation.
And what is the root of the *kaṭhina*, what is its substance, and what are its grounds?
How many qualities must a bhikkhu know to be worthy of performing the Kathina-spreading ceremony?
One root, there may be three kinds of material, and six grounds;
a bhikkhu who knows these eight qualities is worthy of performing the Kathina-spreading ceremony.
The Sangha is designated as the "root"; the material basis is the three robes.
The six types of cloth, beginning with linen, are mentioned; there are six grounds for the robes.
Prior setting aside, subsequent setting aside, formal determination, distribution, and the summary table (mātikā) as well.
The obstacles and the removal thereof, as well as these eight benefits:
washing, stretching, cutting, sewing, binding, dyeing,
and making it allowable— this is called "the preliminary task."
The outer robe, the upper robe, and also the inner robe;
relinquishment, formal determination, as well as the laying down [of the robes],
