departure, completion, formal resolution, and forfeiture.
The *savanā-sīmā* (boundary for hearing) and the *sīmā* (formal boundary); these eight are the "simultaneous removals.
Having taken the robe that has been finished, being indifferent toward one's residence, when the boundary has been crossed, there is the offense of "departing" (*pakkamanantika*).
Taking up the benefits of tranquility, having no regard for his monastery,
he goes instead to another monastery where there is a pleasant dwelling.
While staying there, if he should make a robe;
When the robe is finished, it is called "completion" (*niṭṭhānantika*).
However, if one thinks, "I will not make the robe; I will not return to that monastery," such a relinquishing of the task is considered "decision" (*sanniṭṭhānantika*).

If, having received the Kathina robe-offering, one has gone away with the thought, "I will not return," then even while he is making [the robe], it is subject to loss if it is destroyed or burnt; this is the rule regarding its disappearance.
However, if he has gone outside the boundary while still desiring the benefit he has obtained, [it is lost].
If she hears of the distribution within the boundary, she becomes one who has heard of it.
Having set out with the expectation of a robe, but having gone outside the boundary, she is told by someone:
"I will give you a robe. This is one who has been told.
If, when asked again, one says, "I cannot give you your robe," she is considered an "expectation-breaker" because her expectation has been cut off at its root. Or,
having stayed in a monastery where she completed the rains retreat, she might go to another monastery.
While coming on the way, he passes beyond the limit for its suspension.
For him, that suspension of the *kaṭhina* is considered to be "beyond the boundary.
If he has departed while still having regard [for the robe] and having accepted the benefits of the *kaṭhina*, [the suspension occurs].
If he returns and causes the Kathina to be dismantled again, that dismantling of the Kathina for him is called "dismantling together. [The grounds for the dismantling of the Kathina are:
departure, completion, reaching a decision, and [leaving] the boundary.
Four persons are dependent [on others], and the suspension of the *kaṭhina* depends on the Saṅgha.
Suspension, hearing [of the announcement], and the cutting off of hope—these three are suspensions of the *kaṭhina*;
but it is neither by the Saṅgha alone nor from an individual monk.
The impediment of the residence and the impediment regarding robes—
these two impediments were spoken by the one who teaches the meaning of the joined and the unjoined. Or,
[they are spoken] regarding the eight matrices (mātikā), or even regarding the internal robe-offering.
Two types of "lifting" (ubbhāra) have been declared for the kaṭhina by the Great Seer:
the lifting by not taking leave and the lifting by the group for as long as needed.
Regarding that, there is the arising of robes and these five benefits.
The Discussion on the Kathina Section.
The Discussion on the Cīvara Section:
Regarding the arising of robes, there are eight matrices for robes.
Giving to a boundary, to a formal agreement, to a designated alms-residence, and likewise;
giving to the Sangha, to both Sanghas, and to one who has completed the rains-retreat;
giving to a specific [object] and to an individual—these, moreover, are the eight headings.
In that regard, "he gives within the boundary" means:
it has been praised by the One of Excellent Complexion that [the gift] should be divided among the monks who have entered within the boundary.
And as for what is given by agreement (*katikā*) to those monasteries that share a single profit (*ekalābhaka*):
In this regard, it is said that what is given by all must be shared out.
For wherever permanent services are performed for the Saṅgha,
and whatever is given through the provision of alms-food— this is declared by the Great Seer to be "given."
But whatever has been given to the Saṅgha with a mind of straightforwardness,
that indeed is said to be distributable in their presence.
When one gives a robe out of faith, designating it for both Saṅghas;
Whether there be few or many monks, an equal distribution is appropriate.
It is praised that whatever robe-cloth is given to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence,
it should be divided among those who have completed the rains residence.
But if, regarding a meal of rice-gruel or cooked food,
one gives a robe to such a person, the wise one should apply that very robe to that specific occasion.
However, as for whatever robe is given specifically intended for a particular individual:
That indeed is called a gift designated for a specific person (*puggalodissaka*).
It is when one says to anyone among one's fellow practitioners within the five [groups]:
"Upon my passing, this requisite belongs to me, or to my mother, or even to my father."
“Let it belong to the preceptor,” if he says this very thing, it does not belong to them; rather, it is the property of the Saṅgha alone.
A gift given after the passing away of five [monks] does not bear fruit at all.
That belongs to the Saṅgha alone, yet it bears fruit for laypeople.
Whether it be a bhikkhu or a sāmaṇera who dies in a bhikkhunī’s residence,
his requisites belong solely to the bhikkhus.
If a bhikkhunī or a sāmaṇerī dies in a monastery,
whatever personal requisites belong to her are the property of the bhikkhunīs. If [someone] says,
"Take this and give it to so-and-so," that which has been given belongs to the former [recipient].
"What is given with the words 'I give this' belongs to the last person [to whom it was given].
Having understood this rule for what is given, whether [the donor] is dead or has passed away,
one may take it as a trust, or one may take the deceased's robe."
Dyeing is said to be of six kinds—distinguished by root, leaf, fruit, trunk, bark, and flower—by the Tathāgata, who has vomited out all faults.
Regarding the roots: turmeric; regarding the trunks: madder and tungahāraka.
A robe that has been stained with *allī* dye, as well as one with *nīlī*,
*kusumbha*, or *kiṃsuka* flowers, or with *lodda* bark or *kaṇḍula*—
with the exception of all such dyes, every kind of fruit dye is permitted.
Whether it be a soiled robe or even a discolored *cīvara*,
it is permissible to wash it by rubbing it against the bowl.
The remaining discussion regarding robes belongs to the first *kathina* [section].
In this regard, it should be understood by one who discerns according to the method already stated.
The Discourse on the Chapter on Robes is finished. The Mahāvagga is concluded.
The Minor Section:
Discussion on the Chapter on Those Undergoing Probation;
Reprimand, Demotion, Expulsion, and Reconciliation;
Including the threefold suspension, these reveal seven formal acts (*kamma*).
There are forty-three procedures (*vatta*) designated as formal acts in the Khandhaka;
and thirty-nine more in the Khandhaka that follows it.
Thus all the observances (vattas), numbering eighty-two, were established by the Great Seer through the inclusion of both those already undertaken and those yet to be taken up.
These include both the probationary period (pārivāsa) and the observances for a monk who has formally accepted them.
How is the breaking of the night defined, and how does the breach of formal conduct occur?
Living together, living apart, and failing to announce [one's status];
for a monk who is on probation, these constitute a breach of the night and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

In a residence covered by only one roof, a regular monk is prohibited from dwelling with one who has been suspended, even if it is merely for the duration of pouring water. For a monk undergoing probation,
dwelling within the same boundary is likewise not permitted.
However, it is explained in this way [in the *Mahāpaccarī*];
for in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* and other texts, it is stated without distinction:
"By the pouring out of water from both, dwelling [there] is prohibited."
In a residence where no monks are present, or even in some places that are not residences,
for one staying apart from his community, there is a breach of the night and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Upon seeing a monk at that very moment, a monk who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika) [must inform him].
For one who does not announce it, there is a breach of the night and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Furthermore, one on probation receives exactly five [privileges] according to seniority:
remaining right there, he may perform the Uposatha and the Pavāraṇā ceremony.
If donors to the Saṅgha provide food and alms according to seniority up to one hundred years of age,
then these five [monks] receive them as well.
The Discussion on the Khandhaka on Those Undergoing Probation (Pārivāsika-kkhandhaka).
The discussion on the Samathakkhandhaka:
the basis for disputes and the legal issue of accusation;
the basis for offenses and the legal issue of business.
These four, as well as those spoken of by the Great Sage, are the grounds for causing schism; therein dispute is based.
There are likewise four failures, and accusation has arrived.
The "basis for offenses" refers to the seven categories of offenses.
The "legal issue concerning business" arises in dependence upon the duties of the Saṅgha.
The settling of these four [issues] is considered their resolution.
Resolution face-to-face, and resolution for one who is not confused, and also resolution by admission;
likewise, the procedure for the worse-offender and the majority decision;
and the covering over as with grass—this is considered the seventh method of settling disputes.
These seven methods for settling disputes were taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:
a dispute is settled by two [methods], an accusation by four,
an offense by three, and a formal act by one.
By the sixth and by the first as well, a dispute is settled here;
by means of the three beginning with *sammukhā-vinaya*, in successive order.
Likewise, even by the fifth, a formal accusation (*anuvāda*) is indeed settled.
Through face-to-face confrontation, through admission, and through the "covering over as with grass"—
by these three methods of settlement, the resolution of an offense occurs; indeed,
the matter is settled by the single method of face-to-face discipline alone.
In a formal act by majority decision (*yebhuyyasika-kamma*), the wise one should have voting tickets (*salāka*) distributed—
whether secretly, openly, or by whispering into the ear.
[The method] is secret for those who are shameless and arrogant, but open for those who possess a sense of shame.
A wise person may, by whispering in the ears of fools, have them cast lots.
But how can one distinguish who is modest and who is shameless, or who is a fool?
Only by their own actions can they be known.
One who intentionally commits an offense and conceals that offense,
who follows the wrong course out of favoritism and the like— such a person is one who lacks a sense of shame.
One who does not intentionally commit an offense and does not conceal that offense...
Such a person of integrity does not even go toward a state of rebirth.
But one who thinks ill, speaks ill, and likewise acts wickedly—
such a person is known as a "fool" by his very characteristics.
By taking voting sticks in three ways, many speak according to the Dhamma;
the Victor declared that the decision should be made by a majority vote.
One who is shameless, one who speaks in opposition, and one who is impure in their actions [should be excluded].
That person is fit for the formal act of further penalty when there has arisen brawling and quarreling, in a dispute that is not slight,
when much that is unbecoming to a recluse has been practiced, and even when the talk has not yet ceased.
For one who seeks the very root, there arises what is fierce and harsh;
it is declared that [the dispute] must be settled by the "covering over as with grass" (tiṇavatthāraka) method.
And just as excrement and urine are covered over with grass and leaves, so too [should the dispute be settled].
And it does not emit a foul odor; it subsides at that very moment.

With the exception of a grave offense (*thullavajja*), that which is connected with householders, and that which involves the disclosure of what has been seen—if one is not present therein [at the time of the offense]—[it is not an immediate offense].
For any remaining offense, until the ordination hall,
one is pure and free from offense through the "covering over as with grass" (tiṇavatthāraka) method. Thus ends the discussion on the Khandhaka on Settlement (Samathakkhandhaka).
In the Discussion on the Section on Miscellaneous Matters (Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka):
If, while bathing, one should rub one's own body against a tree,
a wall, an uneven place, or pillars, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
One should not rub the body with a perfumed hand, nor with a kuruvindaka thread, nor with a bowl;
nor should one rub one part of the body against another.
What is called an "unmade bowl" is permitted only for one who is ill.
That which is called a "bowl" (mallaka) is not permitted for anyone at all.
Fragments of skull or brick, a broad-bristled brush for everyone—
whether sick or healthy— and a cloth-wick are permitted.
Lumps of foam, stones, and pebbles are mentioned for rubbing the feet;
whether round or square, a soap-nut scrubber is not permitted.
Even for one wearing any kind of ornament, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If a monk should, even as much as a palm-leaf,
brush his own hair with his hand, or with a comb,
or with a brush— his offense is declared to be a *dukkaṭa*.
It is not permitted for a bhikkhu with hair growing upwards to use oil or ghee for the purpose of adornment, even if it is for the sake of smoothing the skin.
Having moistened his hand with oil, he may wipe his hair.
For one who is tormented by the heat of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and wishes to wipe it away with the hand of moisture—
looking at the reflection of one's own face in a mirror, a water bowl, or anywhere else—
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), provided there is no other reason for doing so.
“[Is it permissible] to see one with raw flesh on the face?”—no, except for the purpose of diagnosing a disease.
“Is he old?”—it is permissible to ask this for the sake of knowing the life-faculty (*āyu-saṅkhāra*).
As for dancing, singing, or instrumental music, [these are not permitted] for a bhikkhu.
For one who goes in order to see or to hear, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Even to see as little as a peacock’s dance is not permitted;
even to hear as little as a song accompanied by clapping of teeth is not permitted.
For one who dances oneself, or causes another to dance, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense if one hears or sees [the performance] while standing within another monastery,
thinking, "I shall see" a dance, a song, or instrumental music.
Whether moving from one dwelling to another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who goes.
Even while staying within the monastery, there is an offense for one who rises up and goes,
or even for one who stands on the path and looks about with the neck extended.
One should not wear long hair; for one who wears it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
It should be [kept] at two finger-breadths or two months' growth; beyond that is not permitted.
One should not wear long nails or long nose-hair.
It is not permissible for a bhikkhu to have [hair] shaved more than twenty times.
If he should have his facial hair or beard trimmed separately,
or if he should have the hair in the private parts removed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for him.
It is said that for one who cuts [hair] with scissors, or causes another to cut it for oneself when not ill, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Likewise,
for one who cuts his own private parts, there would be a grave offense (thullaccaya).
In the case of cutting off remaining limbs or killing oneself, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, there is no fault in cutting off a limb or letting out blood for one bitten by a snake, insect, or the like, when it is for the sake of such a disease.
If one goes along a path that is not open to public use, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
the same applies to one who asks for such a path, or likewise to one who does not yield it.
One should not eat, nor drink, nor go naked, nor chew, nor taste [food] [in such a place].
One should neither give nor receive, nor should one even walk on a direct path [with the body uncovered].
One should not pay homage to one who is naked, nor should one cause such a person to be paid homage.
One should not perform services for a naked person, nor should one have such services performed by a naked person.
The preparation, the covering, and the three [types of] sauna and so forth have been mentioned;
however, the covering of the cloth is permitted in all cases.
It is not permitted to eat from a box anywhere at all.
There is an offense of wrong-doing for one who eats from the same [dish], or from a single vessel.
If they lie down with a single upper covering or a single bedspread,
or even on a single couch, there is an offense of wrong-doing for them.
One should not sit with one’s outer robe folded over the knees;
one should not engage in any kind of play, nor should one scratch the grey hair.
One should not scratch the eyebrows, the forehead, or even the beard.
It is permissible even to have such a bald-headed person carry it.
If a monk who is not ill should hold an umbrella, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
however, it is permissible for the purpose of protecting one's own robes and other belongings.
For one wearing an elephant-trunk [robe], a four-cornered robe, a fish-scale robe, a lattice-work robe, or a palm-leaf fan,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Likewise,
for one wearing a robe that has been taken up [in the air], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
In the matter of wearing and draping [the robes], the circular shape is prescribed.
A monk should not teach Lokāyata, nor should he master it;
nor should he teach secular sciences (tiracchānavijjā); indeed, these must not be taught by a monk.
It is not permissible to carry any yak-tail fan;
nor should one polish a gift, nor even one’s own face.
One should not pull a double-yoke cart, but it is permissible to pull a cart with a single yoke between two poles.
There is no fault in using a tooth-stick with a head-piece, a handle, or a loop.
For a monk, one measuring eight finger-breadths or more is the minimum, while the maximum is four finger-breadths;
if he chews a tooth-stick beyond these limits, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
One should not climb a tree, even when there is human business to be done;
yet in times of distress, it is permissible to climb one as desired.
One should not eat garlic, unless one is ill.
The Buddha’s word must not be addressed otherwise than this:
when one is told "Live! by a layperson, one should reply "I live";
and when told "Live long!", it is appropriate to say "May you live long."
For one who strikes a novice or a householder, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
It is not permissible to lie down on a bed strewn with flowers.
One should not take up shaving equipment, even if one has been a barber in the past.
A hair-turban is not permitted; all [hair-cloths] must have the nap outside.
For one who applies body-paint, a dukkaṭa offense is declared;
this applies even to one who enters a village without a waistband.
All things made of metal, wood, or clay that are allowable,
except for the knife, the bowl, the *kataka* fruit, and the potter’s ware.
The Discussion on the Minor Section on Requisites.
The Discussion on the Chapter on Lodgings:
A chair, even if it exceeds the prescribed measure, is permissible;
likewise, a five-legged stool and a seven-legged stool are also permissible.
Cotton-wadded beds and chairs are permitted for one who is not ill to sit upon even within the house;
likewise, a pillow made of sissoo wood is allowed for one who is not ill.
However, for one who is ill, it is permissible to spread out pillows there as well.
Having given a bedspread, it is permissible for one who lies down [upon it].
A pillow is measured at one fist-span in width;
in length, it is one and a half [spans] or two cubits, according to the Kurundi.
And filled with five kinds—cloth, leaves, grass, and bark;
five types of mattresses were spoken of, ending with the enumeration of cotton.
There are exactly five types of mattresses and cotton, and likewise three types of cotton.
The fur of wild animals and birds, and the womb—these are for the purpose of a bolster.
Among furs, human hair is [prohibited]; among flowers, the *bakula* and so forth;
and among leaves, the pure *tamāla* leaf—these are not permitted.
The five kinds of wool and cotton which were prescribed by the Great Sage for the mattress—
those are indeed permitted for the bolster.
This is stated in the Kurundi commentary on the Aṭṭhakathā:
"Whatever three kinds of cotton there are, they are not allowable for a mattress;
however, that which is mixed with *tālapatta* leaves is permitted in all cases."
But for one who has images of men, women, or animals made,
or causes them to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Furthermore, regarding having a birth-story or a scene made by others...
Flower-gathering and creeper-work may be done by oneself.
One who is a "fellow-seated" (samānāsanika) is one who is senior by two years,
or whether senior or junior, by even a single year.
The same should be said for one who has rained for seven years; what difference is there here?
One who has rained for five years sits down together with those who have rained for seven or twenty years.
As for the long seat below, it is for three [monks], provided it is sufficient for them to sit upon.
It is permissible for two people to sit on a single bed or bench.
However, with the exception of a hermaphrodite and a paṇḍaka,
it is permitted for everyone to sit together on long benches.
The first, the last, and likewise the intermediate;
these three ways of taking up lodgings were proclaimed by the Fully Awakened One.
From dawn on the previous day until the dawn of the first day of the fortnight;
The dawn does not break again for him;
for this is called "the field" by one who takes up a dwelling when entering the rains retreat.
If another monk comes and requests a lodging that was already taken early in the morning, he should be told, "It has been taken.
If it was taken as a rain-season residence after obtaining the consent of the Sangha, [it should be told: "It has been taken."
Even if one has left the rains residence, if one obtains something produced there,
and if the monk who has completed the rains residence takes some allowable article from the hand of the resident and gives it back to him; then [the former] may keep it.
“‘In such-and-such a family, my rainy-season robe was taken;
go and receive it’—having spoken thus, he departs for that direction.
If he should disrobe there, at the place he went, [the robe] is not obtained.”
If he receives it there, it shall belong to the Saṅgha alone.
But if he causes people to accept it there in his presence,
he receives the entire vassāvāsika robe-cloth that has arrived.
A monastery garden and a dwelling—these are the sites for both types [of property].
Furthermore, the third category consists of: a mattress, a bolster, a bed, and a bench.
Also: an iron pot, a cauldron, a water-pot, and an iron vessel.
The axe, the hatchet, the spade, the adze, and the pick;
the creeper, the bamboo, the grass, the leaf, as well as the muñja-grass and the pabbaja-grass;
the clay and the wooden vessel—these are the five, according to what has been said.
“Two are comprised of two [factors], the third is comprised of four;
the fourth has nine divisions, and the fifth is considered eightfold.
Thus, with these five groups, he whose eyes are the fivefold stainless vision—”
“The Lord has declared twenty-five kinds of heavy goods.
Indeed, if a monk disposes of or distributes property belonging to the Saṅgha that is classified as heavy goods, he incurs a thullaccaya offense.”
If heavy property has been relinquished by the Saṅgha or by a group,
yet not formally released, divided but not distributed—
among these three [categories] mentioned first, there is no offense regarding heavy property.
The iron cauldron, the iron pot, and the iron vessel— these three types, whether small or large, are considered heavy articles; however,
an iron water-pot used for washing the feet is regarded as a divisible article.
But above that, the copper vessel is a heavy article;
indeed, all items such as the *bhiṅkāra* and so forth are heavy articles.
The iron pot, however, is to be distributed.
Copper, iron, and earthenware vessels, as well as smoke-tubes and the like,
are indicated as not to be shared.
Whatever metal utensils a bhikkhunī has acquired for herself,
she must not use them as personal property.
This includes all vessels made of bronze, brass, and iron.
They may not be used with the enjoyment of private property.
This same principle should be understood by the discerning person regarding even the three types of goods:
there is no fault in regard to what belongs to the Saṅgha or to the possessions of laypeople.

That which is produced from milk-stone (khīrapāsāṇa), such as heavy trays and the like, is a "heavy vessel" (garubhaṇḍaka) from the point of being held by the feet upwards. A jar (ghaṭaka) is also a heavy vessel.
[Vessels] made of horn, bamboo, gold, silver, copper, bronze, crystal, and stone;
Vessels are not permitted, even those belonging to householders.
A small adze is for sharing, but a large one is heavy equipment;
likewise is an axe, and even a physician’s blood-letting lancet.
An axe, a adze, a spade, heavy tools, and a pickaxe— by that very [measure],
it is declared that even a pinnacle is included.
Furthermore, among those [measures], there are the four-cornered-mouthed, the trough-mouthed, and the curved.
Everything small that is subject to a fine, as well as heavy property such as a chisel,
a mortar, a pair of tongs, a scale, and so forth—
if anything has been given to the Saṅgha, all of that is heavy property.
A barber’s pair of shears and his large scissors, as well as a large needle-case, are the heavy property of tailors.
A creeper, whether given to the Saṅgha or grown there, is protected [as their property].
Even items such as heavy rattan creepers measuring half an arm-span in length,
or ropes and cords produced from thread, bark, and so forth,
become "heavy goods" (garubhaṇḍa) at the moment they are given to the Saṅgha.
Whether it be the pith or the bark of a coconut,
if even a single coil has been made by anyone after twisting it, it is a heavy object (garubhaṇḍa).
Likewise, a bamboo given to the Saṅgha, or one grown there that has been protected [by them], is also such.
An object eight finger-breadths long, even if as thin as a needle-shaft,
may be heavy. An umbrella handle, tally-sticks, a walking stick,
a crutch, a foot-hold, an oil tube, and a vessel— these are the items to be shared.
Even among items such as muñja grass, anything that might weigh a single handful is a heavy object;
likewise, even a single palm leaf or the like, whether given there or grown in that place, is so considered.
Even a blank book measuring only eight finger-breadths in size is a heavy object.
Whether it be natural clay, the five-colored plaster,
or anything such as resin given among other materials, or whatever grows there [upon it],
if it is the size of a palm fruit, it is declared to be "heavy property."
Any item such as a bamboo mat or a broom that is neither guarded nor protected does not constitute "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa) and may be taken at will. However,
when taking something that is guarded or protected, one must take it [only with permission].
Whether equal or more, or even after giving it away as a service,
the wise one who knows the Vinaya should understand that the collyrium, yellow orpiment, asafoetida, and realgar are to be shared out.
Regarding wooden articles as well, any wooden article measuring the size of a needle-handle,
or eight finger-breadths in length, is a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍaka*).
However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, this is shown by making a distinction.
The seven-limbed chair (āsandi), the bhaddapīṭha, and the small stool (pīṭhikā);
the bench with carved legs, as well as the maṇḍaka and the round seat (vaṭṭaka);
the rush mat (koccha), the straw mat (palālapīṭha), and the wooden board for washing.
A basket, a mallet, and a mallet for striking cloth;
a bowl and a casket, a boat, and a dye-vat.
A scoop, a small box, a chest, and a ladle.
All such items as these belong to the Saṅgha and are heavy goods.
All wooden components of a house are considered heavy property.
Permissible leather should be distributed; impermissible leather should not be distributed.
A hide is said to be heavy, as are a mortar and so forth;
likewise, the wares of weavers and the like, and the tools of a ploughman belonging to the Saṅgha.
Similarly, a stand, a bowl-cover, and a palm-leaf fan [are heavy].
A fan, a basket, and a broom— all these are heavy goods.
Any kind of floor-covering, any kind of mattress,
and a vehicle equipped with wheels— all of these are heavy goods.
An umbrella, a leaf-fan, a horn, a gourd-vessel, sandals, a fire-drill,
a water-strainer, and so forth— these are light [weights].
An elephant tusk or a horn, trimmed according to its natural form;
Whatever there may be, such as bed-legs and so forth, that is to be used and is unfinished;
or that which is finished or even carved, such as a container for asafoetida,
a cosmetic box, applicator sticks, a vessel, and a water-squeegee.
All pottery vessels are indeed fit for use:
the alms-bowl, the charcoal pan, the smoke-offering bowl, the potsherd, the stupa-shaped vessel,
the lamp-stand, the brick for building, and the roof-tile.
Moreover, everything belonging to the Saṅgha is declared to be "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa).
A bowl, a golden vessel, a platter, a water-pot,
and even a small jar— even among ironware, a small jar is to be distributed.
Having exchanged heavy goods for heavy items and stable goods for stable items with the Sangha, it is permissible to take them. Furthermore,
one should not step upon bedding or seating with unwashed feet.
A monk [commits an offense] by spitting with his foot, or likewise while wearing sandals;
for one who spits on prepared ground,
or for one who does not see that a wall has been prepared, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
On ground that has been prepared, or on a bed or chair belonging to the Saṅgha,
having spread it out with something that belongs to oneself—
if one should lie down there suddenly while falling asleep;
If any part of the body touches a bed, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding the body hairs, however, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each individual hair;
but it is permissible to step on the soles of the feet.
Someone offered almsfood worth a thousand coins,
together with robes and a bowl, having inscribed it for a monk who was about to die; yet even such almsfood,
after sixty years had passed, [remained as it was].
If a learned one gives [the robe] for the duration of its wearing to a sixty-year-old who has been ordained,
and that person, having eaten the meal offered at the recitation,
becomes a novice (sāmaṇera), he may subsequently take possession of it according to the rule for a novice.
If one who has completed twenty years of age is to receive the formal recitation tomorrow, he is considered ordained today; the period of waiting has passed.
However, if the voting tally is obtained but the meal is not received on that day—
If it is obtained, on the following day it must be distributed; of this there is no doubt.
For a meal consisting of successive portions taken by one who eats alone, the distribution of voting tickets (salākā) should indeed be given after establishing a separate standing procedure for each.
If only the meal was obtained, but not the subsequent portion;
or if the subsequent portion was obtained, but the meal itself was not;
or indeed, whatever specific thing was not obtained by whomsoever it may be.
It is further illustrated that on each successive day, that [food] must also be distributed.
This sevenfold meal, beginning with that designated for the Saṅgha,
as well as the fourfold meal beginning with that for guests, have been proclaimed.
The meal for the monastery’s turn, and the constant meal for the hut;
these fifteen kinds of meals have all been specified here.
Having repeatedly consulted both the Canon and the Commentary, [this has been set forth].
A wise person should properly distribute the requisites belonging to the Saṅgha.
The Discussion on the Chapter on Lodgings (Senāsanakkhandhaka). The Discussion on the Chapter on Duties (Vattakkhandhaka).
[The duties] for guests, residents, and those on alms-round; [the duties] regarding lodgings, the forest, and expressions of appreciation;
the duties concerning meals and for one who is departing.
Regarding returning home and entering a privy,
as well as the conduct toward teachers, preceptors, and students,
one should observe all the rules for dwelling in a monastery.
These fourteen duties have been declared by the Leader whose mind is purified.
When a visiting monk enters a monastery, [he must observe these].
The sunshade must be put away, and sandals must be removed.
One should not cover the head with a robe or even a cloak;
for one must not wash the feet with water from the drinking-water vessel.
Having paid homage, one should ask the senior monk in the monastery about the lodging at the proper time;
and the monk should also inquire about the place for excrement, the place for urine, and drinking water.
The requisites for use, such as those belonging to the Saṅgha,
the kathina-cloth, and the alms-bowl, should be received by the resident monk upon seeing an elder visitor;
having gone out to meet him, he should receive his bowl and his robe.
A seat should be prepared, and water for washing his feet should also be set out;
he should be asked whether he requires water.
One should pay homage and prepare a lodging for him as well.
Whether one has stayed there before or not, whether it is a suitable or unsuitable place for alms-gathering,
the location for defecation and the location for urination, families of those in training (sekha),
the time for entering and leaving, and matters such as drinking water— these must be discussed.
If he is a novice, he should be seated just as one who has newly arrived or is a visitor.
By him [the senior] sitting there, [he should be instructed].
The resident monk must do everything.
However, he should speak thus: "Place your bowl here," or "Please sit on this seat"; and he should also provide a lodging.
Wooden and clay vessels: a monk who wishes to go should depart after having put them away, as well as having secured the lodging.
A monk should also depart after taking leave regarding his bedding and seats.
Even when there is no one to be questioned, or having carefully concealed [the bowl],
the alms-collector should not enter hastily, nor should he depart hastily;
he should stand neither too far away nor too near.
Having lifted the outer robe with his left hand and raised the bowl with his right,
the wise one should receive almsfood after bowing.
He should wait for a moment, observing whether [the donor] intends to give curry or not.
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu should not look at the face of the woman who gives almsfood.
However, he may bring water and such things; by means of that, he should know the lunar mansion, the conjunction, and the directions.
The places for excrement and urine become arranged in succession;
for one who acts according to seniority, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Or, having opened [the door] hastily, one must not enter the latrine.
Having coughed, one should stand outside and then enter slowly.
A monk must not defecate while sneezing;
there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who does so while eating or using a tooth-stick.
One should not defecate outside the latrine pit;
nor should one urinate outside the urinal pit.
One should not scrape oneself with a rough object, nor should one throw a wooden stick into the cesspool.
One should discard it but not throw it away—spittle into a spittoon.
Standing right there on one's sandals, the wise person should lift it up;
but having stood there, one should cover it upon departing.
If one should step out into the water after having defecated while it is present,
a dukkaṭa offense has been declared for him by the Sage, the destroyer of delusion.
One should not step out making a sound, nor "pu-pu" or "capu-capū" sounds after having defecated.
Having rinsed one's mouth, not even a drop of water should be left in the basin.
Even if it has been swept out, if one leaves it without washing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the one departing.
If it is soiled, it must be cleaned thoroughly without exception.
If a water-pot is full because of the scraping of the surface, one should discard it;
if the jar is empty, one should fill the jar with water.
Indeed, one should not recite the Pātimokkha unless requested by an elder.
One should not speak the Dhamma, nor ask a question, nor provide an answer.
It is demonstrated that for one who speaks after having requested permission— when elders and those even more senior have arrived—
there is no further need to request permission again.
Furthermore, when living together with one who is senior in a single monastery,
one must never engage in recitation without having first requested permission;
nor should one give an exposition, so what need is there to mention formal questioning?
A monk should not preach the Dhamma with his "Dhamma-eye.
He should not extinguish a lamp, nor should he light one.
He should close the window shutters; he should not open them.
While walking back and forth on the cloister, one should turn away from those who are senior;
even that [turning] should be done with the hem of the robe, and one should not strike the body [with it].
One should not bathe in front of the elders, nor above them.
To those descending from above, one should yield the way and not strike them.
One who does not fulfill the duties does not fulfill virtue;
with impure virtue and poor wisdom, one finds no one-pointedness of mind.
One whose mind is distracted and not one-pointed does not see the true Dhamma;
not seeing the true Dhamma, one is not released from suffering.
Therefore, the wise son of the Conqueror should fulfill his duty.
Having given the exhortation of the Best of Buddhas, he will go to Nibbāna.
The Discussion on the Khandhaka on the Observances (Vatta-khandhaka). The Discussion on the Khandhaka on the Bhikkhunīs (Bhikkhunī-khandhaka).
A bhikkhunī, having uncovered her body, her thigh, or even her breast,
must not show her private parts to a bhikkhu.
Nor should she engage in any kind of physical contact with a bhikkhu.
Then, for speaking [to a man], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the bhikkhunī.
And a bhikkhunī should not wear a long waistband,
nor indeed that same waistband, nor even a breast-cloth.
With a strip of bark, or likewise with a cloth-strip, or with a leather-strip,
or with a strip of fine cloth, a braid of cloth, or a roll of cloth—
the ribs must not be bent. For one who bends them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
A female ascetic must not have her private parts rubbed with bones or similar objects.
If she has her hand, hand-glove, foot, face, or thigh rubbed,
there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
One must not smear the face, nor indeed apply powder;
there would be an offense for one who adorns the face with red arsenic (*manosilā*).
One must not apply body-unguents, nor likewise facial cosmetics.
One should not apply collyrium, nor should one apply decorative makeup.
Out of lust for looking, it is not permitted to gaze [lustfully];
one should not stand where there is mutual visibility, nor should one cause dancing to be performed.
The Sage has declared an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who ordains a courtesan,
or for one who sells liquor, meat, or vegetables.
It is not permitted to engage in usury or trade.
If one wears a *tirīṭa* cloth or a bodice, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Furthermore, a male slave, a female slave, a laborer,
or even an animal must not be employed as an attendant.
A bhikkhunī must not wear a robe that is entirely blue or any other such color;
she should not wear one, nor should she wear one made entirely of felt.
Whether it be concealed or unconcealed, cut or uncut—[she must not wear it].
It is not permitted to look at any male sexual organ.
However, having seen a monk from afar, a nun should give way to him by stepping aside well before he has reached her.
But having seen a bhikkhu, while she is walking for alms,
she should take out her bowl and show it to the bhikkhu with its opening turned downward.
She may either wrap herself in a shawl or wear a waistband.
At the appropriate time, the Great Sage permitted for women a vehicle joined with a female animal,
or even one turned by hand; and for one who is ill, it is allowed to mount a palanquin.
Even for one who stands firm in the eight *garudhammas* while undergoing the *mānatta* penance,
a second nun must be appointed and given [the formal act].
But for that woman who, at the time of her going forth, gives birth to a fetus—
If she too has a son, a second [woman] should likewise be given to her.
The mother obtains the right to suckle and feed her own son;
moreover, she obtains the right to adorn him by holding him to her breast.
Except for sleeping in the same bed with him,
she must indeed behave toward that second man exactly as she would toward other men.
For by this very act of leaving the community, she ceases to be a bhikkhunī here.
Therefore, for a bhikkhunī, there is no renunciation of the training.
Just as there is no re-ordination for one who has left the order,
so too there is no re-ordination for one who has gone over to another sectarian fold.
Cutting the nails and hair, being saluted by men,
and even the dressing of a wound— these are permitted to be accepted. However,
excrement must not be deposited in a latrine by anyone whatsoever.
It is permissible even when it is open below and covered above, or even when it is covered below and open above.
However, it is not permissible to sit cross-legged in all cases;
it is declared that for one who is ill, sitting on half a cross-legged seat is permissible.
A bhikkhunī must never, under any circumstances, dwell in the forest;
nor is it permissible for her to bathe at a fordless river or at a place where men bathe.
A female ascetic must not use scented powders or perfumed clay.
If she bathes against the current, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for her.
If, thinking "you yourself use it," she gives what was intended solely for her own use to another without having consumed it herself, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Having had everything accepted, it is for the monks to consume;
however, for the nuns, it is permissible even when [the food] has not been formally accepted by one who is fully ordained.
This concludes the discussion on the Bhikkhunikkhandhaka.
Thus ends the discussion on the Khandhakas in the Vinaya-vinicchaya.
The Discussion on the Fourfold Formal Acts:
There are these four formal acts, known as the *apalokana* (motion);
The motion (ñatti), the motion followed by one proclamation (ñattidutiya), and the formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (ñatticatutthaka);
the act of mere notification (apalokanakamma) proceeds in five instances;
the motion-based act (ñattikamma) proceeds in nine instances, and the second [type] proceeds in seven.
Likewise, even a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*) proceeds through seven stages:
the act of suspension (*nissāraṇa*), the act of reinstatement (*osāra*), the *bhaṇḍuka* penalty, the *brahmadaṇḍaka* penalty,
the act of obtaining permission (*apalokanakamma*), and the formal act characterized by the five [factors].
Declare the exclusion and the readmission from a novice monk.
When one who has been expelled ordains a *bhaṇḍuka*, he should be given the *brahmadaṇḍaka* penance; and this should also be done for any other such bhikkhu.
Having assembled everyone and having requested their consent in every way,
whatever requisites such as robes the Saṅgha gives to that person—
having indeed sought permission three times and with the approval of the monks.
Thus, giving to the Saṅgha indeed possesses the characteristic of kamma:
ejection, reinstatement, the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā,
formal authorization, giving, and receiving as the seventh.
Postponement and the eighth, the proclamation,
and the characteristic of the formal act— these are the nine points of a motion (*ñatti*).
When the legal decision has not yet been reached, for an elder who knows the discipline...
Its removal has been stated as that which is called "removal. For one who desires full ordination, there is the "coming and removal";
this also applies by way of the Uposatha and by way of the Pavāraṇā.
Because they are established by a motion (ñatti), these two are formal acts consisting of a motion:
"One should instruct the one seeking full ordination," and "I,
the monk so-and-so, would question [him] regarding the Vinaya."
For such a formal motion (ñatti) proceeding in this manner is called "convention" (sammuti).
The giving away of robes and other items that have been relinquished is called "giving" (dāna);
the acceptance of offenses is called "acceptance" (paṭiggāha).
Postponement is known as the postponement of the invitation (*pavāraṇā*);
[it occurs when one thinks], "Having performed this Uposatha, I shall invite at the proper time.
In the *Tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over with grass), the motion (*ñatti*) is the very first, and so too are the others.
"This is the characteristic of formal acts": there are nine matters for a motion (*ñatti*).
A formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) proceeds through seven matters:
namely, sending away, bringing back, authorization, and giving.
Furthermore, the seventh [category] consists of the extraction, the instruction, and the characteristic of the formal act;
the overturning of the bowl and so forth are considered the removal of support and the expulsion.
What is called "convention" refers to the boundary and so on; it is considered to be of fifteen kinds.
The gift of cloth for the kaṭhina, the gift of a shroud for the deceased;
the spreading of the inner layer of the kaṭhina—this is called "spreading" (ubbhāra).
There is the teaching on the site for a hut, and the site for a monastery.
In the case of the "covering over as with grass" (tiṇavatthāraka) procedure, and in cases such as the imposition of delusion,
the characteristic of the formal act (kamma) here is considered to be established by means of the formal proclamation (kammavācā).
Thus, these seven [factors] for the motion-and-second (ñattidutiya) procedure have been explained.
Likewise, even a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations proceeds toward seven points:
removal, restoration, authorization, giving, censure, admonition,
and the seventh is the characteristic of the formal act itself.
Furthermore, the performance of the seven formal acts, beginning with the act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*), is considered their "expulsion" (*nissāraṇā*);
the act of reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīya-kamma*) is considered their "appeasement" (*passaddhi*); and the act of reinstatement (*osāraṇā*) is considered their "rehabilitation.
The exhortation of the nuns (*ovāda*) and the various formal permissions (*sammuti*) are thus proclaimed.
The granting of the *mānatta* and *parivāsa* penances is called "granting" (*dāna*).
Furthermore, the revocation of the root offense is called "restraint" (*niggaha*);
there are eight [cases] of following one who has been suspended, each requiring a formal motion three times (*yāvatatīyaka*).
Ariṭṭha and Caṇḍakāḷī—these are the eleven [cases];
their authority should be known as ten and one.
The formal act of ordination and the formal act known as rehabilitation;
This, however, is the seventh characteristic of a formal act (*kamma*) consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*).
A formal act of notification (*apalokanakamma*) should be performed by means of notification alone;
it should not be performed by means of a motion followed by a second or a fourth proclamation.
There are no formal acts consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma) that are light;
all formal acts of authorization (sammuti) must be performed after seeking permission.
However, it is not permitted to perform the remaining [formal acts] by merely seeking permission.
In the very manner already described, one should have it performed by this or that person.
The Discussion on the Fourfold Types of Formal Acts (Kamma). The Discussion on the Failure of Formal Acts (Kamma-vipatti).
The five faults of formal acts (*kamma-dosa*) have been explained: by way of the subject matter, the motion (*ñatti*), the proclamation (*anussāvana*), the limits [of the act], and the assembly.
That which is to be performed in the presence [of the Sangha] (*sammukhākaraṇīya*), he performs in their absence.
An action that fails in its basis is called "unrighteous" (adhamma).
There are indeed eight matters not to be done in the absence of the assembly:
the overturning of the bowl, and likewise the righting of the bowl.
The act of making public, the authorization for a trainee or one who is insane,
the one not to be saluted, the brahmadanda, and ordination by messenger—
having set aside these eight, all the remaining [procedures] are entirely [valid].
The Blessed One has declared that formal acts (kamma) are to be performed in the presence [of the accused].
They are considered to be fivefold according to the method of failure [in procedure],
provided that one does not misapprehend either the subject matter, the Saṅgha, or the individual.
One does not attend to the motion, or one sets aside the motion after it has been made;
for these five reasons, formal acts fail precisely because of the motion.
Five faults of formal acts arising from the proclamation have been declared.
One does not grasp the subject matter, nor the Saṅgha, nor the individual alone;
one omits the proclamation, or even the occasion for proclaiming;
thus they fail, as well as through the failure of the formal announcement itself.
The defects of an act regarding the boundary have been explained by me in their entirety within the Khandhaka on the Uposatha, in relation to the eleven kinds of boundaries.
When an act that ought to be performed by a quorum of four is undertaken, those who are eligible to participate but have not arrived [render it defective].
The consent has not been brought, and they protest in his presence.
Thus there may be a fault consisting of three factors due to the influence of the assembly:
those who have arrived and reached for the formal act, yet the consent has not been brought.
They reject it in the presence [of the accused]; in the second fourfold assembly, those who have arrived and reached the formal act are present, and their consent is also brought together.
In the third fourfold assembly, there is indeed an objection.
Thus, in the groups of five and so forth, and in all three types of Saṅghas,
there may be faults of the fourth kind; at the end of the ten and two assemblies,
the formal acts (kamma) here indeed fail in twelve ways.
The Discourse on the Failure of Karma.
The Discourse on the Shedding of Sweat. Ka.
O you who respectfully attend upon the retinue of the sixteen-fold assembly,
listen to my subtle questions as I speak on their hidden meanings.
(Kha)
He approaches by day but not at night, and indeed at night but not by day;
how then does he accept, and how, moreover, does he not accept?
Ga.
There may be an offense for one who cuts, and likewise for one who does not cut;
there is an offense for one who conceals, but for a bhikkhu who does not conceal, there is no offense.
Gha.
And what offense would there be for a monk who has attained meditative absorption?
For one who has not attained absorption, how could such an offense even exist?
(Na)
For one speaking a grave truth, there may be [an offense]; for one speaking a trivial falsehood, there may be [an offense].
For one speaking a trivial truth, and for one speaking a grave lie, [the offenses are likewise distinguished].
Ca.
Entering the monastery, one does not incur [an offense] upon exiting;
while exiting, one incurs an offense, but not while entering.
Six.
One who undertakes [a precept] while not undertaking it, or one who does not undertake it while undertaking it; one who gives while not giving,
or one who does not give while giving— such a person may be possessed of fault.
Even while acting thus, he is not acting;
he incurs [the offense] by retaining it, and likewise even by not retaining it. (Ja.)
Tell me, how can one be the mother and father of two [fathers]?
(Jha) A woman who possesses both sexual organs conceives a child by herself.
She causes another to conceive a fetus; therefore she is both mother and father.
Whether in the village or in the forest, whatever belongs to others as their own;
If one does not actually take it by theft, how could one be defeated?
This is one who lives in communion through theft, a thief regarding the wearing of the outward signs.
By not accepting the other's gift, he is defeated by that [charge].
(Stanza 8) A bhikkhu with a lustful mind and unrestrained, seeing a beautiful woman... (Stanza 9)
Even after having engaged in sexual intercourse with her, how is it that he is not one who has committed a *pārājika* offense?
[Answer:
It is because he sees a woman resembling a finger-snap (*accharā*) even in a dream.
Even if sexual intercourse were performed with her, it would not have occurred.
Dhā.
A bhikkhu was outside the house, while a woman had gone inside the womb.
There is no hole in the house; how could one who has desisted from sexual intercourse [be there]?
Not by means of a woman staying within a small tent.
By means of the *santhatādi* (the group beginning with "santhatā") alone, having performed [the act], one becomes defeated (*parājita*).
That is found in the *Sutta*, in the *Vinaya* itself, in the *Khandhaka*, and in its concordant [sections].
The wise ones, skilled in all respects, speak these questions.
In the Khandhaka, in the Parivāra, and in the Vinaya with its concordant sections;
Respect must indeed be shown by one who desires proficiency.
The Discussion on the Sweating-Inducing Story. The Discussion on Miscellaneous Determinations.
Any leaf-made umbrella, both inside and out in every respect,
may not be sewn with thread of five colors.
Nor may one cut a half-moon shape or a "makara-tooth" pattern on the leaf.
A handle or a claw-shaped ornament, or lines on the staff, are not permitted.
It is permissible to sew a parasol with thread of a single color for the sake of strength,
or to weave a lattice-work using threads of five colors.
Whether it be a jar, a wild beast, or even a mere line,
it is permissible to wear [the mark] after either breaking or grinding it.
The shape of a snake’s hood is permitted on the end of a staff.
A line drawn by scratching [the ground] is permissible for the purpose of marking boundaries. However,
it is not permissible to sew a robe with various colored threads for the sake of ornamentation,
nor is it permissible to sew it so that it is uniform with the hundred-patch robe and others.
Whether at the edge of the bowl or likewise at the mouth of the bowl,
for one who makes a braid or even a chain-link pattern, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
This applies also to making a band, a knotted stone, or patterns such as eight-sided corners and the like.
In that place, they fashion forms such as clubs and the like from clay.
Furthermore, it is not permissible to insert crab-eyes there;
moreover, the sutures and pustules in that location are described as being difficult to discern.
They may be square or round, with knots, loops, or strips;
threads at the corners and edges should be cut when the robe is dyed.
Whether it be needlework or any other kind of decoration—
It is not permissible for a monk to make or have made a robe himself.
And if a monk inserts a robe into a bag of fermented rice-water,
flour-dough, or similar substances;
One who aspires to supreme beauty of complexion has no liberation from misdeeds. This applies to the making of needles,
hand-fans, and so forth, as well as to the making of robes.
Likewise, when it is soiled, it is permissible for the purpose of washing.
However, it is not permissible for a bhikkhu to put anything such as perfume, oil, or lac into it for the sake of dyeing.
One should not strike the robe with a conch shell, a gem, or anything else whatsoever;
nor should it be struck against a wooden trough. Having placed the robe in a wooden trough, one should not strike it with the fist.
It is permissible to strike at anything with the hands so as to leave a red mark.
However, on a knot, neither a line nor a pustule is permitted;
nor is any modification of a "permissible dot" (kappa-bindu) allowed, due to the distinctions between the *pāḷi* and the *kaṇṇikā*.
Whether on the rim or the bowl, on the outside or even the inside,
no line whatsoever made with a needle is permitted.
If, having mounted the rim and polished the bowl, they cook it [with such lines], it is not allowed.
"It is not permissible to do it thinking, 'We shall make it the color of a jewel.
Nothing at all is permitted on the bowl-rim;
however, there is no fault whatsoever in making *makaradantaka* (tooth-motifs) there."
On the sunshade used for religious purposes (dhammakaraṇacchatte), not even a single line is permitted;
however, one may place that inscription either on the interior or on the rim of the sunshade.
Alternatively, having doubled a cord, they carve [the letters] here and there upon it.
For the sake of the beauty of a waistband, that is not permitted for a bhikkhu.
It is permitted at the two ends for the sake of securing the fringe;
however, it is not permitted to have designs of floral work, creeper work, or painting.
Having shown eyes there, what need is there to mention them when they are carved?
It is not permitted to make crab-eyes or the like appear there,
nor a jar, a water-snake’s head, or even the mouth of a makara.
Whatever has a modified form is not permitted at the edge of the fringe.
However, it is permissible to grind [the cloth] into a straight shape, or like a fish-bone,
or smooth like a tablet, or in the shape of a date-palm leaf.
The waistband and the "pig's snout" (*sūkaranta*)—these two types of waist-belt (*kāyabandhana*);
ropes, cloth strips, and so forth—all such things are suitable for it.
The *muraja* drum, the soft lute (*maddavīṇā*), the *deḍḍubha* lute, and the *kalābu* lute.
Strings are not permitted; there may be twelve at the front.
Strands shaped like a *pāmaṅga* flower are prescribed for the waist-band;
one, two, three, or four are permitted, but not more than that.
The waistband made of a single cord was taught by the Sage;
it should be shaped like a *pāmaṅga* (a looped cord), and even a single one is not permitted.
Having joined many cords together into one, [one may use] a single cord.
Having wrapped it continuously, it is permissible to tie it as a loop.
Tooth-sticks, horn, bone, metal, bamboo, reed, and grass;
resin, conch-shell, thread, and fruit—these are considered suitable materials for the loop.
Even in the case of the waistband (kāyabandhana), any alteration is not permitted; however, a mere line marking the boundaries here and there is allowed.
Decorations such as floral designs, vine patterns, or various other forms are likewise not permitted.
It is not permissible for monks to use a collyrium box that delights people.
However, for a monk who uses such a thing after having crushed it and wrapped it with a thread, no fault whatsoever exists.
Whether circular, square, or even octagonal—the ointment-stick (*añjanī*) is defined as being only circular;
it is not permitted if it is merely colored or polished.
The same applies to the ointment-applicator (*añjanisalākā*) and the ointment-box (*añjanithavikā*).
Embroidery with threads of various colors is not permitted.
However, it is permissible for one who uses a needle-case made of any single-colored thread,
or anything else that has been sewn together, provided it is used as a tool.
It is not permitted for a bhikkhu to place anything at all— a jar, a lump, a pippala fruit, or an iron thorn— [on the ground]. However,
it is permissible [to place] even a staff, provided it is merely a line marking the boundary.
It is permissible to twist [the hair] and then trim the nails. However,
it is not permissible to polish the surface with a fire-drill, a bow, a pressing-stick,
or anything else used for decorative smoothing, such as floral designs and the like.
It is permissible to bind tooth-sticks with a pair of tongs, as well as a chisel for cutting;
