But regarding a non-existent superhuman state, there is defeat.
When a monk is accused of a grave offense based on a ground that is not established,
and it is known that the statement was made figuratively, a thullaccaya is declared.
If one does not understand this, a *dukkaṭa* offense is declared;
for a conscious lie, a *pācittiya* is elucidated.
Two offenses are stated for a monk who is lacking mindfulness.
For one who is fully ordained, it is a *pācittiya*; for another, it may be a *dukkaṭa*.
In the case of inciting slander, there are two [offenses]: a *pācittiya* indeed;
but for slandering one who is fully ordained, the offense for the remainder is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one causes two persons who have not received full ordination to recite the Dhamma, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each instance;
for every line, there shall be an offense of expiation.
For sleeping more than three nights together with one who has not received full ordination, [there is an offense of expiation].
For using [the robe], a *dukkaṭa* is stated; for [using] a mat, it may be a *pācittiya*.
If, however, he makes a bed with a woman, he incurs two offenses:
during the night, they are *dukkaṭa* and so forth.
If one teaches the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six words, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
for every step, there may be an offense entailing expiation.
[This applies to] speaking of what is real to one not fully ordained, concerning superhuman states.
If he reports it to such a person, there are two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) and so forth.

When speaking to one who is not fully ordained, if he perceives it as a grave offense (duṭṭhulla-āpatti), there is an offense of wrong-doing for the preliminary effort; once it has been reported, it becomes an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
For one digging the earth, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is considered to occur in the act of preparation;
for each blow struck, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is fully established.
The first section: On False Speech.
But for one who destroys a grove of living plants, two offenses are incurred:
for the preliminary effort there is an *dukkaṭa*, and for the act of destroying it, a *pācittiya* is declared.
For one who speaks of one thing while intending another, there are two [offenses] for the speaker of what is otherwise.
When [the charge] is brought forward, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); when it has been brought forward, it becomes an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If a monk reproaches another monk, he incurs two offenses:
for the preliminary effort there is an offense of wrong-doing, and once the reproach has been made, there is an offense entailing expiation.
But having spread out a bed or other furniture belonging to the Saṅgha in the open air,
one who departs without asking permission incurs a twofold offense when the range of a clod has been exceeded by the first step.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); by the second [time], it should be shown as an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Having spread out a bed in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, if one departs without putting it away and without informing [the residents], one incurs two kinds of offenses.
When the enclosure has been crossed, however, with the first step, a dukkaṭa is indeed declared; with the second step, it is a pācittiya.
[This applies] when one knows that a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha already has monks who have arrived beforehand.
For one who prepares a bed, there are offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for each stage of the action.

When a monk, being angry, ejects a monk belonging to the Saṅgha from the monastery, wrong-doing is said to apply to the stages of the action; the remainder [of the offense] occurs once he has been ejected.
In a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha,
if a monk sits upon a lofted upper chamber with legs that touch the ground below, he incurs two offenses,
beginning with dukkaṭa. Even if he has determined [the space] for two or three turns, if he determines it further than that...
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of preparation, but a confession-offense (pācittiya) once it has been determined.
Furthermore, for one who knowingly sprinkles water containing living beings upon grass,
there is an offense of wrong-doing for the act of preparation, and it becomes a confession-offense once it has been sprinkled.
The second section: The Chapter on the Village of Bhūta.
If a monk, not being authorized, exhorts the nuns, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort; once the exhortation has been delivered, it becomes an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
In the second, the third, and also in the fourth [offenses],
the classification of the offenses is entirely the same as in the first.
A bhikkhu, giving a robe while intending it for someone else, incurs two [offenses].
It is said that for the act of beginning, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); once it has been given, there may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If a monk sews a robe for a nun who is not related to him, there is an offense of wrong-doing for him during the preparation, but an offense of expiation once he has sewn it.
If a bhikkhu travels together with a bhikkhunī on a journey, except at the appropriate times,
having made an arrangement to do so, he incurs two offenses, beginning with *dukkaṭa*.
A bhikkhu does not incur an offense by boarding a boat alone with a bhikkhunī.
Having made an arrangement, even for two touches, there are offenses such as *dukkaṭa* for the preliminary acts.
But knowing that alms-food has been prepared specifically for a nun, one who eats it incurs two kinds of offenses; of this there is no doubt.
If one accepts food with the thought, "I shall eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for each act of swallowing, an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) is declared.
Furthermore, if a monk sits in private together with a nun...
For one who makes [the robe], both [the preparation and the wearing] are touched by offenses such as *dukkaṭa*.
The third section is on Exhortation.
But for one who consumes alms-food from a lodging beyond that limit;
The method for the ninth [offense] of the next section is the same.
In the second and third as well, there is no distinction whatsoever;
the classification of the offenses is indeed identical to that of the preceding one.
Having taken two or three bowls, if one takes more than that,
it is stated that for the preliminary effort there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and once they have been taken, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Regarding the fifth [offense], the determination of the offense is the same as for the first.
In the sixth [offense], regarding one who has finished eating and refused further food with what is not left over:
if one offers it while he is refusing, he incurs two offenses—
by the very act of speaking and by taking it with the thought, "I shall eat."
For taking it up, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is proclaimed for him in the Piṭaka;
but at the conclusion of eating the food, a formal confession (pācittiya) is fully set forth.
This applies to the seventh, the eighth, the ninth, and also the tenth.
By the first [offense], there is equality in the classification of the transgressions.
The fourth section is on Food.
Giving food and so forth with one’s own hand to those who go naked and the like;
When the action is undertaken, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*; once it is given, one touches upon a *pācittiya*.
Whether having caused it to be given or not having caused it to be given, one who dismisses [the person] incurs two offenses:
for that action there is a *dukkaṭa*, and when he has been dismissed, there is a *pācittiya*.
When a bhikkhu takes a seat in a family where food is being served, he incurs two offenses: the preliminary acts are *dukkaṭa* and so forth.
Whether it be the fourth or the fifth [offense], there is no difference whatsoever.
When combined with the third [offense], the counting of the transgressions may be as follows:
if a monk, without having asked permission from a monk who is present,
goes on a meal invitation or visits families, he incurs two offenses.
With the first step, however, upon crossing the threshold, a *dukkaṭa* is stated in the Piṭaka; with the second, it is a *pācittiya*.
But if one requests medicine beyond that amount, one incurs two [offenses].
In the preparation there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); once it has been requested, it may be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
One going to see an army on active service incurs two offenses:
for going, a *dukkaṭa* is declared; for looking [at it], there is an offense of expiation.
If one stays with an army for more than two nights,
it is said that there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for each instance of preparation, and a *pācittiya* offense for actually staying.
Furthermore, if one goes to a military parade, one incurs two offenses.
Walking, it is said, is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); for one who sees [while walking], it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The fifth chapter on Naked Ascetics (Acelaka-vagga) is concluded.
Furthermore, regarding liquor or spirits, the Sage says that one drinking them incurs two offenses.
For one who takes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for drinking;
once drunk, it becomes an offense of expiation (pācittiya). By poking a bhikkhu with a finger, making him laugh, he incurs two offenses:
for the act itself there is wrong-doing, and for the laughter, there is an offense of expiation.
A monk playing in the water incurs two offenses:
a *dukkaṭa* for [submerging] below the ankles, and a *pācittiya* for [submerging] above the ankles.
Furthermore, a monk acting out of disrespect indeed incurs two [offenses].
For the mere attempt, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated; once it is done, there may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Indeed, a monk who causes [another] to be terrified incurs two offenses:
for the attempt, an offense of wrong-doing; once the terror has been caused, there may be an offense of expiation.
Having kindled a flame, if one fans it and touches it twice,
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated for the preliminary effort, and an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) for fanning it.
If one bathes every half-month and touches it twice, that indeed [is likewise].
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for using [the robe];
at the conclusion of the bath, there may be another.
However, for those who make [robes] discolored, if one uses a robe without taking even one of the three [dyes], one incurs two offenses, beginning with wrong-doing.
Having assigned a robe to a monk or others, if one uses it without relinquishing that assignment,
one incurs two *dukkaṭa* offenses for each instance of use.
Furthermore, if one intends [to assign] a bowl or other requisites to a monk, one incurs two [offenses].
In its application, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); in the remaining cases, it may be when [the object] is not specified.
The sixth chapter on drinking fermented liquor.
One who possesses the wealth of asceticism, intentionally depriving a living being of life;
One incurs exactly four offenses, without a doubt.
For digging an unspecified pit, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense at the moment of digging;
if a human dies after falling into it, there is a *parājika*.
Whether it be a yakkha or an animal in human form,
if one falls and dies as a peta, there would be a thullaccaya offense for him.
But if that animal, having fallen, subsequently dies—
For him, an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) was prescribed by the one of keen intelligence.
If he knowingly consumes water containing living beings, he incurs two [offenses]:
for the act, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); once it has been consumed, it becomes an offense entailing confession.
Knowing a legal matter has been settled, if one reopens it, one incurs two offenses:
it is said that for the preliminary effort there is a *dukkaṭa*, and once reopened, it becomes a *pācittiya*.
Furthermore, knowingly concealing a monk’s grave offense (*vajja*) is likewise [an offense].
It is explained that one incurs a *pācittiya* offense for committing one [of these] transgressions.

However, for one who confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon a person less than twenty years of age, an act of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is incurred at the mere attempt; the remaining offenses would apply once the act is completed.
But for one who, knowing [the danger], sets out on the road together with a band of thieves by prior arrangement, or likewise with a woman—
there are two offenses: the preliminary effort is considered a *dukkaṭa*.
But for one who has entered upon the practice, the offense immediately following is a *pācittiya*.
If he persists in a wicked view, a *dukkaṭa* is incurred by means of the motion (*ñatti*);
at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), it becomes a *pācittiya* for the monk.
Likewise, by eating together with one who has acted contrary to the Dhamma, he incurs two offenses:
there is a *dukkaṭa* for the act of preparing [the food], and a *pācittiya* once it has been eaten.
If he encourages a suspended novice to talk [with others], he incurs two offenses.
A *dukkaṭa* offense is stated for using [water with living beings]; a *pācittiya* for encouraging [another to do so].
The seventh section, on Water with Living Beings, is concluded.
When a monk is being addressed by other monks in accordance with the Dhamma...
For one who says, "I will not be able," there are offenses such as *dukkaṭa*.
But for one who disparages the Vinaya, two offenses are incurred:
a *dukkaṭa* for the preliminary effort, and a *pācittiya* once it has been disparaged.
If one touches two [monks] while being deluded, but the offense of delusion has not been formally charged, there is an *dukkaṭa*;
however, once the delusion has been charged, a *pācittiya* is declared.
When giving a blow in anger, one indeed touches two monks.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated for the preparation; it becomes an offense of expiation (pācittiya) when struck.

When a monk, being angry at another monk, brandishes a palm-leaf fan, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each of the two contacts during the preparation; it becomes an offense of expiation when it is actually brandished.

If a bhikkhu accuses another bhikkhu of a *saṅghādisesa* offense on a ground that is entirely baseless, he incurs two *dukkaṭa* offenses for the preliminary effort; there would be a *pācittiya* offense when the accusation is raised.
Indeed, if a bhikkhu intentionally causes remorse in another bhikkhu...
If a monk stands eavesdropping on a discussion regarding training, he incurs two offenses: a *dukkaṭa* for the act of standing and a *pācittiya* when the discussion is raised.
If he goes to listen, he incurs a *dukkaṭa*; if he actually hears it, a *pācittiya* offense arises.
But having given one's consent for legal acts that are in accordance with the Dhamma,
and then subsequently falling into a state of censure, one incurs two offenses, such as *dukkaṭa*.
When the Sangha has not yet reached a final decision in its deliberation, [one incurs an offense] regarding one's own consent.
For one who departs without having given [the robe], there may be two offenses:
for abandoning the reach of the Saṅgha’s hand, there is a dukkaṭa;
once the reach of the hand has been abandoned, there is a pācittiya for the bhikkhu.
When the Saṅgha is complete and has given away the robe together,
if one enjoys it while the two [periods] are still to elapse, there are offenses such as dukkaṭa for the act.
Indeed, knowing that the gain is dedicated to the Saṅgha, [to divert it] to an individual—
When one causes two [robes] to be dyed, there are offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) and so forth for the preparatory effort.
This is the eighth section, on those of the same Dhamma.
Having previously been unknown, [he entered] the king’s inner palace.
For a monk entering [the village], there may be two offenses:
for crossing the threshold with the first foot, a dukkaṭa is prescribed; but with the second foot, it is a pācittiya.
But one who takes a jewel incurs two offenses:
for the preliminary effort there is a *dukkaṭa*, and once it is taken, there is a *pācittiya*.
Furthermore, entering a village at an improper time without having asked a monk who is present—
When a monk enters a dwelling, he incurs two offenses:
by the first step, as he crosses the enclosure, a *dukkaṭa* is prescribed for him;
but by the second step, it is a *pācittiya*.
One who has a house built with needles made from bone, ivory, or horn incurs two offenses: a *dukkaṭa* for each stage of the undertaking.
One who has a bed or similar furniture built exceeding the prescribed dimensions incurs two offenses.
For the act of using [an improper bed], an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated; for the remaining cases, they would be offenses when caused to be made.
But for one who causes a bed or similar item to be stuffed with cotton, he incurs two offenses:
an offense of wrong-doing for that act of using, and the remaining offenses would be incurred when it has been caused to be made.
In the seventh, the eighth, the ninth, and the tenth [chapters],
the determination of offenses is indeed immediate.
The ninth section, the Ratana-vagga.
The Discussion on the Pācittiya Offenses:
The fourfold [category] and the two kinds of offenses, as well as the Pāṭidesanīyas,
have been explained without distinction by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
If a monk accepts [food] with the thought, “I shall eat,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every act of swallowing it, there shall be an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
The Discussion on the Offenses Entailing Confession.
Among the rules of training (sekhiya-dhammas), one offense is explained;
by way of disrespect alone, a dukkaṭa is proclaimed. This concludes the discussion on the rules of training.
Regarding the offense prescribed for engaging in sexual intercourse:
how many offenses are there? There are indeed four.
For one engaging in sexual intercourse, [there is the offense] in entering a non-public place.
If it is described as being dead, a monk incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if it is described as being mostly dead, a *thullaccaya*; likewise, for a [vagina] made in the shape of a mouth, a *dukkaṭa*;
and for one stuffed with jatu, a *pācittiya* is declared.
Regarding the offense of physical contact as prescribed:
how many offenses arise from the condition of engaging in it? There may be five offenses.
[These apply] to a lustful man, and likewise to a lustful nun.
It is a *pārājika* offense for one who consents to the taking of food from a dog.
If a monk touches a body with his own body, it shall be a grave offense (*garuka*);
but if he touches what is attached to a body with his own body, it shall be a serious offense (*thullaccaya*).
With a body that is bound, what is bound is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
however, a formal confession (pācittiya) is prescribed for poking another with a finger.
Regarding the remaining rules of training (sekhiya), this is the determination of the offenses.
It should be understood by one who discerns according to the very method explained above.
The Compendium of the Mahāvibhaṅga is finished.
The Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga.
For the sake of the bhikkhus' proficiency in the analysis of the Vinaya,
I shall speak briefly on the Vibhaṅga for bhikkhunīs as well.
When a man is lustful and a bhikkhunī is also lustful—
Delighting in physical contact, how many offenses does she incur?
There are three offenses for [contact] above the knees and below the collarbone;
for her who consents to being grasped, there is a *pārājika*.
For one who consents to being grasped above the collarbone or below the knees, there is a thullaccaya offense;
but for [grasping] what is attached to the body, it is a dukkaṭa.
A bhikkhunī who conceals a fault incurs three offenses.
If she conceals a *pārājika* offense knowing it to be such, she is defeated (*pārājika*).
If she conceals a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) while being in doubt,
or if she conceals a failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Those who follow one who has been suspended do not abandon that view;
by merely persisting in their conduct, they incur three offenses:
a *dukkaṭa* for the motion (*ñatti*), and two *thullaccaya*s for the two subsequent proclamations (*kammavācā*).
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), a *pārājika* offense is declared.
If she fulfills the eighth basis (*vatthu*), she incurs three offenses:
for saying "a man has come," there is a *dukkaṭa* for each instance of his coming.
But for a man, when he has entered within arm’s reach, she fulfills the eighth ground; that nun is defeated.
The Discussion on the Defeat (Pārājika).
A litigant who brings a lawsuit incurs three kinds of offenses:
upon her first announcement [of the case], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
upon her second announcement, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is declared.
At the conclusion of the motion (*ñatti*), there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*. One who ordains a thief incurs a *dukkaṭa* at the motion;
with two [subsequent proclamations], it is a *thullaccaya*; at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), it becomes a grave offense (*garuka*).
If one should go alone to another village, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) upon the act of going;
but when she has crossed the boundary enclosure with her first foot,
that female ascetic incurs an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
When [the offense] has been exceeded by the second [factor], it remains grave (*garuka*).
Regarding the fourth, the analysis is exactly like what was stated for the second;
however, in the classification of the offenses, there is no distinction whatsoever.
Having herself become lustful, if she takes even some food or other from the hand of one who is likewise lustful and then consumes it,
she incurs three offenses regarding that food and so forth. She incurs three offenses regarding that food and so forth.
For her who accepts it, there is indeed a thullaccaya offense.
In all instances of swallowing, there is the status of a saṅghādisesa offense;
if she accepts water or a tooth-stick, it is a dukkaṭa offense.
“Having taken it with your own hand, eat or consume it”—if she urges him in this way, three offenses are incurred.
There is a *dukkaṭa* for her speech; when he takes it [thinking], “I will eat,” [the offense is incurred].
If she causes all of them to swallow it, there is a *thullaccaya* offense for her.
But at the conclusion of the meal, there is the status of a *saṅghādisesa*;
and she who urges him on—these three points one should clarify.
In the seventh, the eighth, and also in the ninth and tenth [cases],
the legal determination is the same as that for the act of abducting a woman.
The Discussion on the Saṅghādisesa Offenses.
If a bhikkhunī here makes a hoard of cloths,
she incurs one offense entailing relinquishment and an offense of expiation.
She who distributes a robe given out of season as if it were a robe given in season [incurs an offense].
For the act of exchanging, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated; upon acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).
But if, having exchanged a robe, she then seizes it back;
for the act there is an offense of wrong-doing, and once it is seized, she incurs an offense entailing relinquishment.
If, having already requested one thing, she requests another thereafter,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of requesting, and it becomes an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya) once the request is fulfilled.
For if, having already had [an item] purchased, she has another purchased thereafter, [the same applies].
In the case of using [the robe], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);

if it has been acquired and given, it becomes an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya). In the same way, for the remaining seven rules beginning with the sixth, the determination of the offenses is identical to that of the immediately preceding one.
The Discussion on Forfeiture:
If one eats garlic, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of taking it;
for each act of swallowing, the offenses of expiation (pācittiya) are fully enumerated.
For one who causes hair to be plucked, there are indeed two offenses in the constriction:
a *dukkaṭa* is stated for the preliminary effort, and a *pācittiya* occurs when it has been plucked.
But while performing the striking of the palms, she incurs two offenses.
If she makes use of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); once it is made, it may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she consents to any smooth object made of lacquer, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of making use, there is an offense of wrong-doing; when it is given to her, there is an offense of expiation.
One should illuminate that the fifth [offense] is the same as the fourth;
in the classification of offenses, there is no difference whatsoever.
[The offense occurs when one] stands with water for a bhikkhu who is eating.
If [the food] is within arm’s reach, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); if one stands having let go [of the food], it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one requests uncooked grain, saying, “I shall eat it,” and takes it, it is an offense of wrong-doing; for each mouthful swallowed, it should be declared an offense of expiation.
If she discards excrement and so forth over a wall, she incurs two offenses:
a *dukkaṭa* for the act of throwing, and a *pācittiya* once it has been discarded.
However, if she discards the fourfold group beginning with excrement upon green vegetation, [the same applies].
For her, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for undertaking [the journey]; it becomes an offense of expiation (pācittiya) once she has abandoned [the journey].
If she goes for the purpose of seeing dancing and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
likewise, there is an offense of expiation for her while she is seeing or hearing [it].
The first section on garlic.
In the first, second, third, and fourth [sections],
the analysis here is equal to that of the garlic section, except for the sixth.
Having approached families and sat down on a seat,
if she departs without asking permission from the owners, she incurs two offenses:
for the first step, she incurs an offense when she has crossed beyond the shelter from rain.
It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and it may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) upon the second transgression.
If one sits on a seat without having asked permission from the owner,
there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation, and an offense of expiation once seated.
The seventh [offense] is entirely the same as the sixth; however, in the eighth, there is a *dukkaṭa* for the preliminary effort, and it becomes a *pācittiya* when one has been reviled.
And if she approaches herself, she touches two hells and so forth.
A *dukkaṭa* offense is stated for the preparation; it is a *pācittiya* when she has approached him.
But having struck herself and weeping, she incurs two [offenses];
she strikes and weeps, which is a *pācittiya*, while performing one [act] is a *dukkaṭa*.
The second chapter: On Darkness at Night.
If she bathes naked, there are two instances where an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) occurs;
at the conclusion of the bathing, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her.
If one causes a water-bath robe to be made exceeding the prescribed measure:
for the act of making it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); once it has been made, it shall be an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
However, regarding a robe, whether one has dried it oneself or caused it to be dried by another:
For not sewing [a robe], one offense of expiation (pācittiya) is stated. However,
if one exceeds the five-day period for the distribution of the outer robe (saṅghāṭī),
there is one offense of expiation clearly explained as a single rainy-season [transgression].
If one wears a robe that ought to be exchanged,
a *dukkaṭa* is stated for the act of wearing it, but a *pācittiya* when it has been worn.
If one creates an obstacle to the acquisition of a robe for the community, [one incurs an offense].
If one attempts to obstruct [the distribution], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); once it is done, it becomes an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).

Regarding the lawful distribution of robes, it is stated that while attempting to obstruct the *vibhaṅga* there is an offense of wrong-doing, but once the obstruction is completed, it is an offense entailing expiation.
If one gives [a robe] to a householder or others, and it is a robe for a recluse:
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of preparation; once given, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the rule.
If, while having only a weak expectation regarding the robe, the time limit should pass: [there is an offense].
For the act of application, a *dukkaṭa* is stated; for the transgression [of the limit], it is a *pācittiya*.
For one who obstructs a legitimate dismantling of the *kaṭhina*, there are two offenses:
a *dukkaṭa* for the act of application, and a *pācittiya* once it has been obstructed.
The Third Chapter on Bathing.
If two bhikkhunīs should lie down together on one bed, there is an offense of wrong-doing for them for every act of lying down; once they have lain down, the other [offense] shall apply.

The second [offense] is identical to the first; however, in the third case, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the effort, and it becomes an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) once it is completed.
This also applies to one who does not attend to a co-resident sister who is suffering.
However, only one offense is elucidated here: a *pācittiya*.
If, having given her a dwelling place, she then drives the bhikkhunī out, there is a *dukkaṭa* for the effort, and a *pācittiya* once she has been driven out.
But in the sixth case, if they associate together, a *dukkaṭa* offense is incurred by the motion (*ñatti*);
at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), a *pācittiya* is clearly indicated.
However, for one who wanders on a journey within her own country where there is danger:
For using [the robe], an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated;
for one who is practicing [the practice], the remainder [is as follows]. The eighth and ninth are considered equal to the seventh;
but in the tenth, only one offense of expiation (pācittiya) is clearly indicated.

She goes for the purpose of seeing everything, such as the royal palace and so forth;
for the preliminary effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for her, and it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) if she actually sees it.
For one who uses either a high seat or a couch, two offenses are stated:
an offense of wrong-doing for each instance of use, and a *pācittiya* offense once it has been used.
For one who weaves thread, there are likewise two: an offense of wrong-doing is considered for each instance of the act.
In the *Ujjavujjava* [commentary], he declared this to be a *pācittiya*.
However, for one who performs services for householders, there are only two [offenses]:
it is stated that there is a *dukkaṭa* for the preliminary effort, and once it is completed, it becomes a *pācittiya*.
In the fifth [offense], however, only one offense of expiation (pācittiya) is explained;
in the sixth, there is an act of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the preliminary effort, and once it is given, it may be an offense of expiation.
The seventh is the same as the second, distinguished by the different types of attainment.
The eighth [offense] in the second section is considered equal to the fifth.
Regarding the knowledge of animal speech (*tiracchānagata-vijjā*), there are two [types]:
for one who recites it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the preliminary action, and an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*) for every single word.
The tenth [chapter] is identical in every respect with the ninth,
except for the single word "recites" (*pariyāpuṇāti*, *vāceti*), which is the distinguishing feature.
The fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Picture Gallery (*Cittāgāravagga*).
If a nun, knowing that the monastery contains monks,

one for the first foot crossing the enclosure, and another for the second.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated in the Piṭaka, but a confession-offense (pācittiya) for the second [offense].
If a nun reviles a monk or insults him,
there is an offense of wrong-doing for her during the preliminary effort, and it becomes a confession-offense when he has been insulted.

If, out of a fierce disposition, she reviles the community, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for her in the act of application; but if she has actually reviled them, it is the other [offense].
Whether invited or already dismissed from the meal, regarding solid food or soft food—
For that nun who eats, two offenses are incurred:
for whatever she accepts with the thought, "I shall eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
in each instance of swallowing, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is declared.
If she is stingy regarding the family, however, she incurs two offenses:
for the preliminary effort, a *dukkaṭa* is stated; the rest would apply to her stinginess.
Furthermore, if she spends the rains residence in a dwelling where no monks are present, [she incurs an offense].
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the preliminary duties, and an offense of expiation (pācittiya) at sunrise.
If a nun who has completed the rains residence does not invite [criticism] from both Saṅghas by means of all three grounds,
she incurs one offense of expiation.
If she does not go for the sake of exhortation, or likewise for the sake of living together with a monk,
there shall be one *pācittiya* offense.
Even if she does not request exhortation, if she does not go to the *uposatha*, [there is an offense].
One incurs one offense entailing expiation (pācittiya); there is no doubt.

If one causes a *pasākhaja* [plant] to be split without having asked the Saṅgha, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort; once it is split, the offense of expiation is fully established.
The sixth section: On the Grove.
For one who ordains a pregnant woman, she incurs two offenses:
there is an offense of wrong-doing for the preliminary effort, and once she has been ordained, it shall be an offense entailing expiation.
The second, the third, the fourth, and the fifth as well;
the sixth and the seventh are considered equal to the first.
Having ordained a nun who was her co-resident, [she commits an offense].
If she does not assist for two years, she incurs one *pācittiya* offense.
The ninth and tenth [years] are considered equal to the eighth;
regarding the classification of offenses in these two cases, there is no difference whatsoever.
The seventh chapter is the Chapter on Pregnant Women.
Regarding the first five rules of the Chapter on Maidens:
they are entirely identical to the first rule of the Chapter on Pregnant Women.
"If you say, 'Enough with her being ordained,' she is censured;
for the preliminary effort there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and once she has been censured, it becomes an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
In the seventh and eighth [cases], one offense entailing expiation is recognized."
The five [offenses] beginning with the ninth are similar in their disadvantages.
This is the eighth chapter, the Section on the Maiden and the Nun.
Two offenses may touch one who carries a sunshade and sandals.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is declared for the act of preparing; it becomes an offense of expiation (pācittiya) once [the vehicle] is being carried.
Furthermore, for one traveling by means of a vehicle, it is said that two offenses are incurred:
there is an offense of wrong-doing for the act of preparation, and an offense of expiation if the journey is undertaken.
For one who wears a hip-cord (saṅghāṇi), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of preparation;
once it is worn, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). This same method applies even to the fourth [offense].
For one bathing with scents and colors, there is an offense of wrong-doing upon contact during the act of preparation.
At the conclusion of the bath, for her there would be a *pācittiya* offense.
The sixth [offense] is in every respect the same as the fifth;
and so too are the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth.
For the act itself, a *dukkaṭa* offense is stated; for massaging, it would be a *pācittiya*.
In the classification of offenses, there is no distinction whatsoever.
However, she who sits down in front of a monk without having asked permission [commits an offense].
For her, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of preparation, but a formal confession (pācittiya) once she has sat down.

However, for one who asks a question of a monk who has not been given leave, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the act of preparation; once the question has been asked, a formal confession is declared.
For one who enters a village on foot without wearing a bodice, one should declare it as being similar to the first section concerning the monastery.
The ninth section: The Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear.
The Discussion on the Pācittiya Offenses.
Regarding the eight [offenses] involving two kinds of transgression, and also regarding the Pāṭidesanīya offenses:
if one asks for ghee with the thought, "I shall eat it," and then takes it, [it is an offense].
Then for that nun, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for all instances of swallowing [the food], it shall be an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
The Discussion on the Offenses Entailing Confession.

and peerless state in terms of its purposeful benefit,
a bhikkhu [crosses] the great ocean that has been made easy by wisdom.

therefore, one who is possessed of ardor should apply himself to this practice.
In each instance of "being," [the word] "being";

The Discourse on the Four Failings:
How many offenses arise by reason of failure in virtue?
There may indeed be four that arise by reason of failure in virtue.
If a bhikkhunī, knowing a *pārājika* offense, conceals it,
she incurs a *thullaccaya* upon death if she was in doubt.
But if a bhikkhu conceals a *saṅghādisesa* offense, it is a *pācittiya*.
But by concealing one's own grave offense, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
As for the offenses caused by failure in conduct (*ācāra-vipatti*),
there may be only one [offense] based on failure in conduct.
If a bhikkhu, however, conceals a failure in conduct,
there is one offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for that bhikkhu.
How many offenses, moreover, arise on account of a failure in view?
Furthermore, there may be two offenses due to failure in view (*diṭṭhi-vipatti*).
By persisting in an evil view, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the formal motion (*ñatti*);
at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), the *pācittiya* is fully accounted for.
But what are the offenses due to failure in livelihood?
There are six offenses due to failure in livelihood.
On account of livelihood, one who has evil desires falsely attributes qualities to himself that he does not possess.
If one speaks of a superhuman state, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
One who engages in matchmaking incurs a *saṅghādisesa*;
if it is known that the statement was made indirectly, there would be a *thullaccaya*.
Having spoken of "exquisite food," for one who consumes it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya);
however, if it is a bhikkhunī, it would be an offense entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya).
[This applies] regarding soup or boiled rice intended for oneself, on account of one's livelihood.
Having requested it for one’s own benefit, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who consumes it.
The Discussion on the Four Failures. The Discussion on the Conditions for Legal Issues (*adhikaraṇa*).
From a legal issue arising from a dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa), how many offenses might there be?
From a legal issue arising from a dispute, there may be two offenses:
an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who is fully ordained, when one reviles another.
For a monk who reviles one who has not been fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
How many offenses are there conditioned by a legal issue arising from accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa)? There may be three types of offenses conditioned by a legal issue arising from accusation.
If a monk defames another monk with a groundless charge based on a minor matter, he incurs an offense of *saṅghādisesa*; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, if he defames him with a charge of *saṅghādisesa* itself, [he incurs the same].
A pācittiya and a dukkaṭa have been stated for failure in conduct;
as for the offenses stated by way of the condition of an offense, how many offenses are there?
By way of the condition of an offense, four indeed have been stated by the Great Sage.
If a bhikkhunī, knowing that she has committed an offense entailing defeat (pārājika), conceals it,
she incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya) upon her death if she was in doubt.
If a bhikkhu, however, conceals an offense requiring a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), he incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
But if one conceals such a failure in conduct, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
How many offenses are there caused by a legal issue concerning business (kiccādhikaraṇa)?
There are exactly five offenses caused by a legal issue concerning business.
By the very act of formal admonition, a fault of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) touches her;
like a nun who transgresses against one who has been suspended, she who follows such a person incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya) through two formal proclamations (kammavācā).
By two [proclamations], she incurs that [grave offense].
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (kammavācā), there may be a *pārājika* offense for her.
For one who follows a schismatic, even during the very process of admonition,
if she does not relinquish that adherence to the wrong view, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
Regarding formal admonition, a wicked view,
the third time [of warning], and the forfeiture of a *pācittiya* offense— this is the discussion on the conditions for legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*).
Regarding the Discussion of Questions on the Khandhakas:
Now, as for the classification of offenses that has come down in the Khandhakas, I shall explain it for the sake of the monks' proficiency; listen attentively.
In the first Khandhaka, how many offenses might there be?
In the first Khandhaka, there would be two offenses:
namely, for one who confers full ordination upon a person less than twenty years of age.
For him there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); for the remaining cases, however, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
How many offenses are there in the Khandhaka on the Uposatha?
There are three offenses;
however, regarding the Uposatha in the Khandhaka, those intent on causing schism think: "Let these perish, let them be destroyed!"
In performing the Uposatha, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is declared.
But for one who performs the Uposatha together with one who has been suspended (ukkhitaka), there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for him;
however, in other cases, it is an act of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
How many offenses are stated for the commencement of the rains retreat? Speak, [O teacher]:
only one offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated for the commencement of the rains retreat.
How many offenses are stated in the Khandhaka regarding the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā)?
Three offenses have been declared, considered equal to those on the Uposatha day.
How many offenses have been declared regarding hides? Only three are explained:
for those who kill [a cow], it is a *pācittiya*; likewise for one who takes a calf or a heifer.
For one who touches the genitals with a lustful mind, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is stated; for the remaining cases, however, it is a wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
How many offenses are stated in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka?
Three offenses have been mentioned in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka:
therein, within two finger-breadths [of the wound], a thullaccaya is declared; regarding the *bhojja* and *yāgu* [medicines], it is a pācittiya;
but for the remaining cases, it is a dukkaṭa.
In the Kathina there is no offense; it is merely prescribed.
But how many offenses are spoken of in connection with the robes?
Three offenses are spoken of in connection with the robes.
For robes made of grass or bark, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is declared.
For a robe that exceeds [the prescribed size], there is a confession involving relinquishment (nissaggiya-pācittiya);
for the remaining cases, a wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
In the Campeyyaka, the Kosambaka, the Kamma, and the Pārivāsika,
as well as in the Samuccaya, one offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is explained.
How many offenses, however, are stated in the Samathakkhandhaka?
Two offenses have been mentioned in the *Samathakkhandhaka*:
if a monk who has given his consent speaks in disapproval, it is a *pācittiya*;
in all other cases, a *dukkaṭa* is declared.
How many offenses are stated in the Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthu)?
Three offenses are stated in the Minor Matters.
However, one who cuts off his own genitals incurs a Thullaccaya offense.
In the case of a robe, it is a *pācittiya*; for the remainder, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Likewise, regarding furniture, there may be three offenses;
and in the case of giving away a heavy object, a serious offense (*thullaccaya*) is declared.
In the case of ejecting [someone] from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, there is a *pācittiya* offense;
however, in all other cases, a *dukkaṭa* is declared.
How many offenses regarding schism in the Saṅgha were spoken by the Great Seer?
Two offenses regarding a schism in the Saṅgha were taught by the Great Seer.
For those who follow the schism, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is declared;
for monks regarding the property of the group, a confession offense (pācittiya) is explained.
In the Khandhaka on the Rules of Conduct (*Vattasaṃyutta*), how many offenses are considered to exist?
In the Khandhaka on the Rules of Conduct, that is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Regarding the setting aside of the Pātimokkha, likewise only one [offense] is explained.
And in the Bhikkhunī-khandhaka, how many offenses are considered to exist?
In the Bhikkhunī-khandhaka, two offenses are considered to exist:
a Pācittiya for not inviting [criticism], and in the remaining cases, a Dukkaṭa.
The Discussion on Questions Concerning the Khandhakas is finished.
Regarding the Discussion on the Origin (Samuṭṭhāna):
however, in the two Vibhaṅgas, those rules laid down by the Great Sage—
Those rules beginning with the *pārājika* which they recite on the Uposatha day—
I shall now explain their origins hereafter,
for the sake of the monks' proficiency; listen to that with concentrated minds.
The body and speech together are "body-and-speech";
these very two, when joined with the mind, are three;
thus there is that which consists of one factor, two factors, and three factors.
They speak of a sixfold method of origination.
Among these, offenses arise through one, two, three, four,
or even all six different modes of origination.
In that regard, there is no offense that arises from all five origins;
there is one that arises from a single origin, as do those from the last three.
Likewise, there are those arising from two origins: from body and from body-and-mind.
From speech and from the mind, from the third and the sixth,
from the fourth and the sixth, and also from the fifth and the sixth—
this [kamma] arises in five ways; it does not originate from anything else.
Those called "arising from three" arise from the first three [factors] and also from the last three;
they do not arise from anything else.
Likewise, those arising from four arise from the first, the third, the fourth, and the sixth.
The second, the third, and also the fifth and sixth,
arise in two ways from four origins, but not from any other;
the one that arises in a single way from six origins indeed originates from those six alone.
And it is said:
“Threefold, they arise from one source; fivefold, they arise from two sources;
twofold, they arise from three or four sources; and onefold, they arise from six sources.”
All offenses receive their names according to the distinctions of their origination;
I shall explain them hereafter. First is the matter of the first and last [offenses], and second is the offense of matchmaking.
Formal admonition, the kaṭhina robe, wool from sheep,
the recitation of the Dhamma, traveling on a journey, a caravan of thieves, and instruction;
the announcement of what has actually occurred, and the ordination of a thief.
"And the unpermitted" (*ananuññātaka*); these are the thirteen headings for the headings [of the rules].
These thirteen methods of origination have been considered by the wise.
Among them, that which arises by way of the fourth origination;
These are explained as the sections on the first pārājika offenses.
Furthermore, those that arise from exactly three types of volitional states (citta) are indicated here,
beginning with the taking of what is not given.
An offense that arises through origins (samuṭṭhāna) is produced even from a single instance;
it is explained as being originated by the "intermediary" (sañcaritta).
However, that which arises by the sixth origin alone—by way of its origin—is [described as follows].
This *samanubhāsanā* (formal admonition) is stated according to its origin (*samuṭṭhāna*);
for that which originates from the third and the sixth [offenses] is considered to have the term *kathina* as its prefix according to its origin.
Furthermore, whatever offense arises from the body and from both body and mind,
this is explained as originating from [the category of] eḷakaloma and so forth. Moreover,
whatever offense arises from speech and from both speech and mind, [this is explained as originating from the category of] omasavāda and so forth.
This, however, is called "origination from both word and dharma.
It arises from the body, from body-and-speech, and from the fourth and sixth [bases];
furthermore, it is indicated as "origination from time."
Indeed, those offenses which arise from the fourth and sixth origins,
as well as those originating from a caravan of thieves, are here clearly explained.
Furthermore, that which is produced by the fifth origin among these—
This [offense] known as the teaching of Dhamma,
by way of its origin (samuṭṭhāna), may occur through three origins that are without consciousness (acittaka);
this [offense] known as announcing what has occurred (bhūtārocanā) is likewise by way of its origin.
Those which may arise from the fifth and sixth [offenses] by way of origination—
this one, however, is recited as originating from the ordination of a female thief (corī).
Those which [arise] from the second and third, and also from the fifth and sixth;
This may arise from non-intentional origination.
Among them, the first, second, fourth,
ninth, tenth, and twelfth have mental volition as their origination.
In each and every origin, similar cases are seen here:
the emission [of semen], bodily contact, the first *aniyata* offense,
and likewise the ripening of past karma, and being in private with a nun.
With food, in private, and two [fingers]; the fingers, in water, and laughing.
Striking, and vomiting—these are the fifty-three training rules (sekhiya);
below the collarbone, above the knees, between villages, and one who is lustful.
Purity regarding the matting of the floor, likewise regarding one who has completed the rains retreat;
not going for exhortation, and not following after the leader of the community—
these seventy-five [offenses] are specified as originating from both body and mind.
These originate from the same source; they are considered equal to sexual intercourse.
This is the origin of the first *pārājika*.
Quarreling, and furthermore, lewd speech, and self-indulgence;
The two offenses involving corrupt intent,
the second undetermined offense, taking away, diverting, lying, reviling, slandering,
announcing what is grave, and digging the earth.
Speaking falsely about a living plant, causing annoyance,
expulsion, pouring [water], likewise for the sake of food;

Intentionally, a living being, and even that which contains a living being;
reopening [an accusation], likewise, a deficient [Saṅgha], living together, and by means of expulsion;
one who speaks according to the Dhamma, for the sake of remorse, and rooted in delusion.
Regret, giving vent to criticism, and diverting [the matter] to another person—what is that to you?
It is an improper time; do not snatch it away, for a wrong grasp leads to hell.
The analysis of the Saṅgha and likewise the weak hope.
The legitimate suspension of the *kaṭhina* robe, and intentionally causing discomfort;

Pāyantī, and two years [of age], and one who has not been authorized by the Saṅgha;
three are said to be married women, and three are unmarried girls.
Two who are less than twelve years old, and likewise "sufficient for that long" (alaṃ tāva te).
Through the rules on "frightened by fear" (*sokāvassa*), as well as through the granting of consent (*chanda*) for those undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*),
and the two [rules] each year— thus there are sixty-nine training rules (*sikkhā*);
because they are equal to the rule on taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), they are established as having three origins (*tisamuṭṭhānika*).
The Origin of the Second Pārājika:
A matchmaker, a hut, a large dwelling, having it washed,

The two kinds of "prepared" robes, likewise a robe sent by messenger, silk,

The acceptance of silver—both types; the bowl with a worn binding;

as far as the gate; and the giving and sewing.
Bread, a condition, a lamp, a jewel, a needle, a small bed;

The training on requesting other items, and also exchanging [for] other items.

Schism in the Saṅgha, following a schismatic, being abusive, and being a corrupter;
