Nor should a robe that has been made allowable, nor one that is dyed, be rendered unallowable.
But for one who is dressed [in robes], there is an offense; how could there be no offense?
In this case, even if a monk has had his robes stolen, there is indeed no robe that is not considered "unfit" (akappiya).
He does not take anything from anywhere at all,
nor does he give away even a morsel of food;
how then can he incur a heavy offense?
Tell me, are you skilled in the Vinaya?
If one takes whatever has been left over by another and,
having been sent away, eats that food;
But when one has been sent away by another,
the wise declare that it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
She does not give anything whatsoever to anyone with her own hand.
And yet he does not grasp anything from anyone;
he quickly adopts what is blameworthy, but not what is weighty.
Speak, if you understand it well!
But regarding the taking of tooth-cleaning sticks or water,
a bhikkhunī who incites [another] commits an immediate offense when it is practiced;
she commits a grave offense with remainder.
"He conceals it so that he does not touch the offense; how do you know this of me?
Tell me! Having committed an offense entailing formal meeting of the Sangha, being disrespectful, even while concealing that offense, one who has been suspended does not touch another [offense]."
"Neither that which is born of living beings nor that which is not, neither the moving nor the flying;
whether it be twice-born, lovely or unlovely—if you know it, tell me.
"That which is born of living beings has been described."
"Born of mind and born of the elements;
yet because they are both produced from two [causes], the term 'twice-born' (dvija) is applied to sound."
In the Vinaya, which is unsurpassed and supreme,
a delighter in striving becomes proficient in the eye that leads to the happiness of the virtuous, yet he is not attached to sensual pleasures.
Herein, moreover, he who delights in the essential (sāramate ramate).
The verses on the Shedding of Sweat are complete.
The Discourse on the Common and the Uncommon.
I shall explain the origin and the enumeration of all the training rules (sikkhāpada) for bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs,
as well as those prescribed as non-common and those that are common.
I shall speak in brief; listen with concentrated minds.
Vesālī is known as Nidāna, and likewise the city of Rājagaha;
Sāvatthī, Āḷavī, and Kosambī, along with the Sakka and Bhagga regions, have been proclaimed.
How many were spoken at Vesālī, and how many were made at Rājagaha?
How many were prescribed at Sāvatthī, and how many were made at Āḷavī?
How many were prescribed at Kosambī, and how many were spoken among the Sakyans?
"In how many places were they designated? Tell me that when asked:
Ten were spoken at Vesālī, twenty-one at Giribbaja;
exactly one hundred minus six were made at Sāvatthī."
Six were spoken at Āḷavī, eight were enacted at Kosambī;
eight were laid down among the Sakyans, and three were explained among the Bhaggas.
Sexual intercourse, dispute, and the fourth offense involving the basic rules (vatthu);
An extra robe made entirely of black wool;
[the rule concerning] what has occurred, and likewise [the rule on] succession; the mouth-door and the naked ascetic;
and the abuse of bhikkhunīs—these ten were enacted at Vesālī.
The second and the final *vatthu*, the two *anuddhaṃsanā* (acts of reviling),
the two cases of causing a schism in the Saṅgha, and the acceptance of a robe.
Money, the requesting of thread, and likewise the act of complaining.
Eating almsfood that has been prepared specifically for oneself, likewise eating in a group;
eating at the wrong time, wandering for alms, and bathing;
giving a robe to one who is less than twenty years of age by means of the Saṅgha.
The instruction on lying down, dancing, singing, and the two modes of walking;
the gift of choice—these, O King, were twenty-one in Rājagaha.
The hut, the silk bedding, and the village of earth-beings;
They sprinkle water containing living beings; these are the six matters to be confessed.
Furthermore, there is the large dwelling, as well as being difficult to speak to;
likewise, speaking one thing while intending another, and the two cases of the door and the treasury, with the fifth being the middle case.
Disrespect, the rule on milk-drinking, and the training rules—
these eight were laid down by the One of Pure Vision at Kosambī.
Washing, wool, and secondly, the bowl.
The exhortation, medicine, and the needle, as well as those concerning forest-dwellers;
the purification by water and the arrival for the exhortation—
these eight were prescribed in the city of Kapilavatthu.
Having kindled the light, together with the material food and the rice-grains—
these three were laid down by the Kinsman of the Sun among the Bhaggas:
the four *pārājika* offenses, the sixteen grave offenses (*garuka*), and two others.
The indeterminate rules are thirty-four, and there are indeed thirty-four rules involving forfeiture.
There are one hundred and fifty-six minor rules,
and furthermore, ten rules for censure and seventy-two rules of training.
And three hundred and four [rules] were recited by one of even mind;
for all these remaining ones were established at Sāvatthī.
There are four *pārājika* rules and seven *saṅghādisesa* rules.
There are exactly eight rules involving forfeiture (nissaggiya), and thirty-two minor rules (khuddaka).
Two are censurable (gārayha), three concern those in training (sekha), and fifty-six altogether;
these were formulated in six places and are summarized by cities.
Indeed, all these training rules for the bhikkhus— both those pertaining to the seven cities and those pertaining to the seven [other] locations—
amount to exactly four hundred and fifty; they are two hundred and twenty in total.
For bhikkhunīs, however, there are four hundred and three rules:
four pārājikas, thirteen grave offenses (garuka),
two undetermined offenses (aniyata) that have been declared, and thirty offenses involving forfeiture (nissaggiya).
The ninety-two minor rules, the four offenses to be confessed,
and the seventy-five training rules were taught by the One Free from Proliferation (Nippapañca).
And there are two hundred and twenty rules of conduct for the monks alone.
The training rules come up for recitation on the Uposatha day:
eight Pārājikas, seventeen grave rules,
thirty Nissaggiyas, sixty-six, and one hundred.
There are eight minor rules to be censured, seventy-five training precepts,
and furthermore four hundred and three;
these indeed exist according to the authority of the bhikkhunīs.
The training rules come up for recitation on the Uposatha day;
there are exactly forty-six for the bhikkhus,
but the Great Sage has rendered them non-common with the bhikkhunīs.
Six Saṅghādisesa rules, likewise two Aniyata rules;
twelve Nissaggiya rules, and twenty-two Khuddaka rules.
Four Gārayha rules as well—these amount to forty-six.
These were indeed prescribed for the bhikkhus by the illustrious Gotama:
the sixty rules on bodily contact, the grave offense,
acting out of self-love, the hut, and the dwelling— these six are the heavy offenses.
In the *Nissaggiya-ādivagga*, there are the rules on washing and receiving;
likewise, in the *Eḷakaloma-vagga*, the first seven [rules] from the beginning;
and in the third *vagga* as well, the bowl is likewise the first.
The rain-cloak and the forest-dweller—thus twelve are illuminated.
These offenses entailing expiation (pācittiya) have been declared, all of them at the conclusion of the enumeration:
one hundred and eighty-eight for monks and nuns respectively.
The entire Chapter on Nuns, eating in succession,
likewise eating what is not extra, the invitation to bring food,
requesting exquisite food, and likewise the naked ascetic.
Being invited and eating with a group, concealing a grave offense,
a person under twenty years of age, and [cohabiting] even with a woman;
entering a royal harem, and a rain-cloak and a sitting mat.
These minor rules, however, number twenty-two;
four, moreover, are censurable for monks in the Pātimokkha.
Together they are prescribed as forty-six.
But those [offenses] which have become non-common to the bhikkhus by means of the bhikkhunīs,
and those which have become non-common to the bhikkhunīs by means of the bhikkhus, there are indeed thirty for both;
these were rendered non-common by the Great Seer.
There are four offenses involving defeat, ten offenses requiring formal meeting of the Saṅgha, twelve offenses involving relinquishment, and ninety minor offenses.
Furthermore, there are eight censurable offenses; thus, these amount to one hundred and thirty.
And [the offenses] of the bhikkhunīs have reached a state of non-commonality with those of the bhikkhus.

Among the bhikkhunīs, however, there are ten: the six beginning with the *saṅghādisesa* offenses, the three [offenses] that must be declared up to the third time, and the four [other *saṅghādisesas*]. Thus, these are the ten.
The out-of-season robe, likewise the stolen robe;
the seven [cases] beginning with "given by another," the bowl, both the heavy and the light [offenses].
These twelve indeed, here, are according to the nuns.
The offenses involving forfeiture were all laid down by the Teacher together.
Those laid down as non-common [to other categories] are ninety-one minor rules;
and there are eight censurable rules—this is the total number.
However, those rules for the bhikkhunīs that have become non-common with the bhikkhus are prescribed from one side alone;
they amount to one hundred and thirty.
Even when including those that are non-common and distinct, there are one hundred and seventy-six.
There are four offenses involving defeat, ten and eight grave offenses,
two undetermined offenses, twenty-four offenses requiring relinquishment,
and one hundred and eighteen minor offenses explained herein.
Twelve indeed are censurable, and seventy-six are for the virtuous;
these are explained as being both uncommon and distinct.
However, those taught by the Teacher as common to both are [the remaining ones].
Seven hundred and four are thus declared to exist:
four offenses involving defeat (pārājika), seven requiring formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa),
eighteen entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya), and seventy equal [other] minor rules (khuddaka).
Seventy-five are prescribed, as are all the Sekhiya rules;
one hundred and seventy-four are the common training for both.
This is the discussion on shared and unshared [precepts].
From here on, I shall explain the characteristics pertaining to all [the Buddhas];
listen with reverence and understand them as I speak.
The source, the person, the basis, the method of designation,
failure, non-attainment, offense, the factor of instruction, and the performance of action;
as well as perception, consciousness, origination, and the classification of blameworthy actions.
This [method] should be applied everywhere according to the two sets of three. However,
having set aside everything previously explained by way of method, as well as whatever here is self-evident, we shall provide an exposition of the meaning.
A "person" (puggala) refers to whichever monk or nun with reference to whom a training rule (sikkhāpada) was laid down; this is called a person.
They are of twenty-three kinds, such as Sudinna, Dhaniya, and others.
Regarding the Pātimokkha of the bhikkhus, there are individuals who are first offenders.
Likewise, regarding the Pātimokkha of the bhikkhunīs, there are seven beginning with Thullanandā who are first offenders; thus, there are thirty in total.
"Subject matter" (*vatthu*) refers exclusively to the individual, and to each such person in their entirety;
"transgression" (*ajjhācāra*) is said to belong to that very same subject matter.
Furthermore, that very same [subject matter] is likewise the fundamental basis for the formal rule (*paññatti*).

Designation (paññatti) may be of nine kinds: that which precedes what has not yet arisen, that which precedes everything, that which precedes a part, that which precedes a word, the common designation, the uncommon designation, and likewise those preceded by "one," "both," and "on both sides. Thus it is ninefold.
In that regard, there are such formulated rules as: "Whatever bhikkhu should engage in sexual intercourse," and "Should take what is not given," and so forth;
[and] "At the very least, a bhikkhu [should not commit it] even with an animal."
In this way, all such [rules] are explained as subsequent rules (anupaññatti).
Likewise, the rule concerning what has not yet arisen (anuppannapaññatti) was indeed introduced by means of the eight heavy rules (garudhamma), when no offense had yet occurred.
The leather mat, the sandals with and without linings,
and likewise the permanent bath— this is the fivefold formal admission (upasampadā).
This is indeed the fourfold [classification] known as the "local formulation" (padesapaññatti).
It is stated that [the term] exists only in the Middle Country and not elsewhere.
For all the remaining [terms] are declared to be designated everywhere;
in meaning, they are identical here, such as the "common dyads" and so forth.
An offense may be one involving a specific instruction (*sāṇattikā*), or it may also be one that does not involve a specific instruction (*nāṇattikā*);
this is known by the name "instruction" (*āṇatti*), which indeed refers to the act of commanding.
This applies to all offenses within all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
Indeed, every breach of the constituent factors must be understood by one who discerns:
that which arises for one who acts through body or speech is called "originated by action," just like a *pārājika* offense.
Whatever offense occurs for a monk who fails to perform what ought to be done by body or speech, that arises from non-action,
as in the case of the first Kathina robe-offering.
Furthermore, whatever offense occurs for a monk who performs [what is forbidden] or fails to perform [what is required], [that arises from action].
That which arises from both action and non-action is "from action-and-non-action," as in the case of taking up a robe.
But that which may arise for one who is acting, or for one who is not acting,
is "from action-and-non-action," as in the case of accepting money.
So it may be for one who acts;
that which belongs to the one who acts or does not act,
and that which arises from action itself.
That [offense] may also arise from both action and non-action.
Furthermore, all offenses are of two kinds according to the factor of perception (saññā).
"Deliverances with perception, not without perception"—
thus they are declared as deliverances.
This is because of the absence of any perception of transgression.
This is declared as "liberation by perception" (saññā-vimokkha);
the others, however, are declared as "not liberation by perception.
Furthermore, all of them may be twofold by way of the mind (citta).
"Those with mind and those without mind" were thus proclaimed by the Well-Awakened One;
however, that which occurs by way of origination from a state with mind—
this is what is explained as the offense called "with mind."
Or these [offenses] are "without thought" by virtue of being mixed with those involving thought.
Furthermore, all offenses are said to be twofold according to their fault:
as blameworthy or blameless, and according to the fault of worldly convention.
For one who belongs to the faction that holds the mind to be essential, if there should be an unwholesome state of mind, this [offense] is called "world-transgression" (lokavajja);
the rest are "formal-rule transgressions" (paṇṇattivajja).
Furthermore, all offenses may be of three kinds according to the nature of the action.
Bodily action, verbal action, and likewise both together—
this is called the "two triads," namely the two triads beginning with the wholesome:
a mind that is wholesome or unwholesome, and likewise a neutral mind.
Having offered [the sacrifice], one incurs an offense; while incurring it, it is not otherwise.
This applies to one possessed of pleasant feeling, as well as to one associated with painful feeling and so forth.
This, however, is stated to be the characteristic in all training rules (sikkhāpada).
Having applied [these principles], one who is confident in the Vinaya should demonstrate them:
this [tree] has three roots, nine leaves, four crests, seven fruits, and six flowers.
He who knows the two origins and the two branches,
he knows the designation in its entirety.
This has gone beyond to the unsurpassed state.
He who masters and inquires into the discipline of body and speech,
which is the unsurpassed among the unsurpassed means of approach—
he is one truly disciplined.
The Discourse on Characteristics.
After this, I shall explain the method for the complete enumeration of the entire collection consisting of sixteen ancillaries.
How many offenses have been spoken of?
How many are bodily and how many are verbal?
What offense is incurred by one who conceals [an offense]?
How many conditions for association are there?
There are six kinds of bodily offenses and likewise six kinds of verbal ones;
for one who conceals [an offense], there are three. Thus, there are five conditions for association.
How many roots of offenses were laid down by the Great Seer?
And how many offenses were spoken of regarding the concealing of a grave offense?
Indeed, there are two roots of offenses: body and speech.
There may be offenses involving expulsion (pārājika) and offenses requiring confession (pācittiya) for concealing a grave offense (duṭṭhulla).
How many are stated regarding the interval between villages, and likewise how many regarding the further shore of a river?
How many involve a serious offense (thullaccaya) in the case of meat, and how many involve an act of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the case of meats?
Within a village there are four [offenses], and likewise as many on the further bank of a river;
for the meat of humans, there is a thullaccaya, and for the nine [other meats], a dukkaṭa.
If a bhikkhu makes an appointment with a bhikkhunī, it is a dukkaṭa.
For her who enters the vicinity of a village, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
In an enclosed village, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya) at the first step;
for her walking through the interior of the village, it is a heavy offense (garuka) at the second step.
Likewise, if there is an agreement with a bhikkhunī, it is a dukkaṭa;
if he boards the boat, it is a pācittiya for the bhikkhu.
At the time of crossing a river, when his foot touches [the water], it is a thullaccaya.
In the first and second [cases], that bhikkhunī incurs a grave offense.
How many verbal [offenses] are there at night? How many verbal [offenses] are there by day?
There are two verbal [offenses] at night; there are two verbal [offenses] by day.
If she stands within arm’s reach of a man in the darkness of night, but there is no lamp present,
she incurs a pācittiya offense if she should converse with him.
If she should speak while it is concealed during the day with a man,
or if she stands within arm's reach of him, that indeed is a grave offense (dukkaṭa).
But having left the reach of the hand,
if she should speak [of it], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for her.
How many [fingers] are there for one giving, or how many for one receiving?
When giving to three or four recipients,
if a human gives poison and that person dies because of it,
it is a *pārājika* offense; for a *yakkha* or a *peta*, it is considered a *thullaccaya*.
If [the recipient] is an animal, there is a *pācittiya* offense upon its death;
likewise, if one gives a robe to one who is not a relative, it is a *pācittiya*.
Likewise, if there is taking by the hand or taking by the braid of hair, it constitutes a *saṅghādisesa*.
In the case of taking the private parts with the mouth, there is defeat (parājika).
In the acceptance of a robe from the hand of one who is not a relative, it is a confession-offense (pācittiya) involving relinquishment; thus it is fully explained.
If one accepts food from the hand of a lustful man, or if she herself is lustful,
there is a *thullaccaya* offense for her who receives the meal.
How many formal authorizations (*sammuti*) are stated here by means of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*)?
However, only one authorization for exhorting bhikkhunīs has been laid down.
How many kinds of grain-flavours are said to be allowable at the improper time?
Only salt-sour gruel is considered allowable at the improper time.
How many pārājikas are there by way of the body? How many grounds for communal living?
For how many is the interruption of the night [a factor]? How many are prescribed as two finger-breadths?
The pārājikas are by way of the body; there are two and two grounds for communal living.
The interruption of intercourse for two [persons], and the two prescribed [distances] of two finger-breadths;
the first and last bases, and also bodily contact—
these two arise from the body as Pārājika offenses.
The stage of common residence is one;
likewise, that which is preceded by various words is another.
Thus, there are indeed two stages of residence.
Spoken by the compassionate Great Seer:
for a monk who is on probation (*pārivāsika*) as well as for one who is practicing the penance (*mānatta*),
the interruption of the night for both is illustrated by [the rule] regarding what has passed beyond two nights.
The maximum length to be taken is two finger-breadths, and likewise;
it is prescribed as being either two finger-breadths or two months—thus there are two [rules] regarding the two finger-breadths.
How many [offenses] are there in the destruction of life? How many are Pārājika offenses by speech?
How many are stated regarding illumination, and likewise how many regarding matchmaking?
Three regarding the destruction of life;
three offenses involving speech are pārājika.
Three are declared in the case of illumination;
likewise three in the case of matchmaking.
In the case of an unspecific threat, a man dies from being struck or wounded.
It would be a *pārājika* offense against a *yakkha*; a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) against a *peta*;
and if it has died, one should declare a *pācittiya* offense against an animal.
These are the three offenses that may occur in the case of taking life.
The three verbal [offenses] consist of: killing a human being, taking what is not given, and giving commands; as well as speaking of superhuman qualities.
However, for one who speaks in praise of the two paths, the offense is grave.
But for him who [describes it] above the knees and below the collarbone, there is a thullaccaya offense.
However, for one who describes it above the collarbone and below the knees, a dukkaṭa offense is specified. These are the three ways of describing.
By means of the three factors beginning with receiving, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa);
by two, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is stated; but by one, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
How many offenses are there for one who cuts, and how many based on the discarded [material]?
For one who cuts [trees], there are three [offenses]; five conditions have been discarded.
For him who cuts a forest tree, it is a *pārājika*; for cutting a grove of living plants, it is a *pācittiya*;
but for cutting the male organ, it is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
If one discards poison without specifying [the recipient], and a human dies because of it, it is a *pārājika*;
if a *yakkha* dies, it is a *thullaccaya*; if an animal dies, it is a *pācittiya*.
In the case of discarding poison that has already been cast away, it is a grave offense (*garudhamma*).
It is considered a *dukkaṭa* offense for discarding feces or urine on green grass.
Tell me, how many offenses are there for one who is walking? How many for one who is standing?
How many for one who is sitting, and how many for one who is lying down?
For one walking, there are four [offenses]; for one standing, likewise;
for one sitting, likewise; and for one lying down, likewise.
For a bhikkhu who makes an appointment with a bhikkhunī, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) when one has stepped into the vicinity of a village.
There is a grave offense (thullaccaya) at the first step within an enclosed village;
it becomes a heavy offense (garuka) at the second step for one entering from one village to another.
But in a concealed place, if a bhikkhunī, being familiar with a friend,
stands within arm’s reach of a man, it is a pācittiya offense.
If she stands having left the arm’s reach, it is a dukkaṭa offense.
At the time of sunrise, for the second nun who stands having left the reach of hand,
a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) is declared; if she stands having left [the reach of hand],
there is the status of a *saṅghādisesa* (offense requiring a formal meeting of the Saṅgha).
For one who is sitting there are four [offenses], and for one who is lying down there are likewise that many;
they are of the same types as those mentioned and should be understood by one who knows the Vinaya.
Tell me, how many offenses are stated for the third time?
Listen to the three offenses stated up to the third time:
one who follows one who has been suspended incurs an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika);
one who follows a schismatic of the Sangha incurs an offense of formal meeting (saṅghādisesa).
In the case of non-renunciation, there is a *pācittiya* offense for a wicked view;
thus, in the "up to the third time" [formulas], there are these three offenses.
How many are specified for eating, and how many on account of food?
But for one eating, there are three [offenses], and five reasons for eating food.
For eating the flesh of humans, it is a thullaccaya;
for [the flesh of] other [animals], it is a dukkaṭa; but for one who eats garlic, it is a pācittiya.
For from the hand of a lustful person,
having taken any food while being lustful oneself— all that meat is unallowable.
Even if one has requested it for one's own sake and has taken the food, [it remains unallowable].
If one eats garlic mixed [with other food],
there may be five offenses: a thullaccaya, a pācittiya, a pāṭidesanīya, a dukkaṭa, and a garuka offense.
Regarding one who looks [at a woman] while she is indicated: tell me, how many offenses are there?
Regarding one who looks while she is indicated: the Great Sage has declared one offense.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one with a lustful mind toward a woman’s private parts.
While looking at the face of the one giving alms-food,
how many *ukkhepakas* (grounds for suspension) are stated, and how many *vattanās* (duties of proper conduct)?
Three *ukkhepakas* are stated, and forty-three *vattanās*.
In the case of not seeing [the offense], there are two for an offense committed;
one for not relinquishing, and one for an evil view.
How many are said to be "expelled," and for how many is there a single proclamation?
Three types of persons expelled have been declared; for three of them, the act is accomplished by a single proclamation.
These three—Mettiya, the defiler, and Kaṇṭaka—were indeed expelled respectively on account of their gender, their communal affiliation, and their punishment.
It should be specified that it is permissible for two or three [monks] to announce [the formal act] with only one preceptor and one teacher. Furthermore,
there is the formal procedure by means of a motion (*ñatti*), as well as the case where it has been interrupted.
And the "completion of what has passed": these are the three ways of classifying formal acts (*kamma*).
The "preparation" (*kappanā*) by means of a motion (*ñatti*) consists of such phrases as "let him give";
"the Saṅgha gives," "he performs," and so forth, would constitute the "incomplete" (*vippakata*).
“Given,” “done,” and so forth—these may be past participles;
for all formal acts (kamma) are indeed subsumed under these three [terms].
[They are performed] by means of a vote (salākāgāha) in the Saṅgha, or by a formal act alone.
The Saṅgha is split by two causes, and not otherwise.
For the monk who causes the schism in the Saṅgha, there is a Pārājika offense;
for the monks who follow him, a Thullaccaya is declared.
Regarding speech that is both appropriate and inappropriate, how many offenses does one incur?
Regarding speech that is both appropriate and inappropriate, one incurs six offenses.
One who, for the sake of livelihood, is evil-desirous and whose mind is overcome by craving;
One who falsely claims a higher spiritual attainment is defeated.
When one acts as a go-between, there is likewise an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
One who says to another, "He is living in your monastery," incurs a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
If a bhikkhu, having requested choice food, eats it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya);
if it is a bhikkhunī, it would be an offense of acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya).
Having requested either curry or boiled rice, if one is not ill...
If a bhikkhu eats [the food], he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, having concealed offenses for a thousand nights,
one may become a pārivāsika and be released after staying for ten nights.
There are exactly eight *pārājika* offenses, twenty-three grave offenses (*garuka*),
and two *aniyata* offenses as spoken by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
Furthermore, forty-two *nissaggiya* offenses have been declared.
There are one hundred and eighty-eight offenses entailing expiation (pācittiya);
twelve offenses to be confessed (pāṭidesanīya) were spoken by the Great Sage;
and seventy-five rules of training (sekhiya) were spoken by the Well-Trained One.
All these things were well-expounded by the illustrious Gotama of excellent wisdom;
indeed, they number three hundred and fifty.
Regarding those that should be spoken among them:
The essential analysis has been stated by me in its entirety,
in brief and in every respect.
Having investigated thoroughly the method of the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā,
and having shown respect for what has been done, this alone should be mastered.
Whether in the meaning, in the arrangement of syllables, or even in the sequence of understanding;
Therefore, one should not harbor doubt, but rather cultivate great respect for that which knows the adjudication of the Vinaya along with its superior [commentaries].
Having relinquished dependence,
he may go wherever he wishes.
One who desires to grant dependence [should do so] together with the analysis and the formal act of agreement.
Having mastered it well through recitation and understood its meaning, this very [text] should be given [to others].
One should constantly read it, reflect upon it, listen to it,
inquire about it, cause others to recite it, and examine its meaning.
But all those matters pertaining to his welfare and training stand before that bhikkhu as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of one's hand.
This is the supreme, the most excellent.
One may cross the ocean of existence, the ocean;
one may reach the autumnal clarity of wisdom, the clarity; one may become a master who has gone to the further shore, the one who has gone to the further shore.
Therefore, having forever shaken off this supreme darkness,
a person who delights in diligent application should train in that which is beneficial and endowed with virtue.
For one who aspires to proficiency in the Piṭaka— the supreme source that brings skill in the Vinaya and bestows the state that grants all limbs of happiness—
This should be mastered constantly by a clever ascetic who is skillful in the prescribed method. —
The Concluding Statement.
It was composed by the wise Buddhadatta, whose mind was pure,
desiring that the teaching of the Great Sage endure for a very long time.
And how it attained success amidst various obstacles— [so it is told].
In meaning and in composition alike, this is supreme and unsurpassed.
May the aspirations of beings connected with the Dhamma be thus fulfilled;
may the King protect the earth righteously, and may the rain-god pour down in due season.
As long as Seliṇda stands, and as long as the moon shines,
so long may the True Dhamma endure, that of the Great Seer Gotama.
May patience, gentleness, virtue, wisdom, faith, compassion, and the rest [endure].
In him all virtues are firmly established, like jewels in the ocean.
Thus requested with care and reverence by the Elder Saṅghapāla, whose mind is steadfast and who is endowed with discipline and conduct.
Desiring that the Vinaya of the Great Sage endure for a very long time,
and for the sake of the proficiency of the bhikkhus in the analysis of the Vinaya,
I have composed this supreme work named *Uttara*.
Having paid respectful attention to this recitation, one should then train in this [work].
For there are nine hundred and fifty verses;
this count is according to the *anuṭṭhubha* meter.
"Four thousand and nineteen stanzas in number are these declared as the exposition of the Vinaya.
Thus [ends] the work of the Tambapaṇṇiya, the supreme expounder,
skilled in the methods and rules of the Tipiṭaka, who caused the lotus-forest of the hearts of the foremost poets to blossom.
The *Uttaravinicchaya*, composed by Buddhadatta— the preeminent bull among the best of poets,
who pierced [the hearts of others] with the most excellent and sweet speech that produces supreme delight—
is hereby completed. The *Uttaravinicchaya* is finished.
